units.la: NOBILES & Magnifici Viri, qua fiducia hos meos tractatus, quos tanquam immaturos & crudos embryones abortii, vobis prudentia, eruditione, virtute maturis, splendoreq; gloriæ, opibus, plena autoritatis & dignitatis senecta floretibus, ausus sim ascribere, & in tutelam vestram tradere, non immerito miramini. Sed mirari desinetis, cum partim virtute, humanitate & fauore vestro, quo Musarum cultores ac politioris literaturæ studiosos semper estis complexi, partim egregia erga familiam nostră benevolentia & affectione, persuasum me ad id esse & adductum intellexeritis. Etsi autem splendore nobilitatis ac dignitatis vestræ valvalde deterrebar, ne hoc facerem, aliæ tamen etiam causæ accesserunt.
units.tr: Noble and distinguished Sirs, you may justly wonder with what confidence I have dared to dedicate these treatises of mine to you and to place them under your protection, treatises which I have brought forth like premature and raw embryos. You are mature in wisdom, learning and virtue, and flourish in old age rich in glory, resources and authority. But you will cease to wonder once you understand that I have been persuaded and drawn to this partly by your virtue, courtesy and favour, with which you have always embraced the devotees of the Muses and students of the finer literature, and partly by your outstanding goodwill and affection toward our family. Although I was greatly deterred from doing this by the splendour of your nobility and dignity, other reasons also came into play.

units.la: Primum enim, cum in primo tractatu continentur plurima in natura recondita & abstrusa, quorum causæ ex sensuali philosophia explicari satis nequeunt, in confesso autem sit omnibus, vos harum rerum inuestigatione & cognitione & plurimum delectari, & de iis vere & seuere censurā ferre posse, tū quod obseruātiæ in vos meæ, & familiæ etiam nostræ, publicum testimonium dare cupiebam, ac monimentis testatum relinquere, & satisfacere cupiditati meæ ad vos obseruandos & colendos, hæc inquā omnia & singula me impulerunt, vt hunc libellum vestris Magn. consecrare. Si quid igitur pec-catum est, quod vobis tantis viris hæc tenuia offero, spero me veniam impetraturū apud vos, qui haud minus læta fronte exi-gua ab infimis, quam magna à summis soleatis accipere. Patia-mini igitur hunc libellum nomi-nis vestri splendore decoratum illustrioremq; factum ad manus hominum peruenire. Ego vicis-sim omni obseruantiæ officio-rūq; genere vestro nomini, lau-di &honori studebo. FaxitDeus, vt vestra dignitas literis sit orna-mento, &literatis præsidio quam diutissime. Marp. è Museo meo, MDC. XII. 15. Octob.
units.tr: First, since the first treatise contains many hidden and obscure matters in nature, whose causes cannot be adequately explained by sensory philosophy, and since it is generally agreed that you take great delight in investigating and knowing these things and are able to pass true and strict judgement on them, I was moved in every one of these respects to consecrate this little book to your Worships. I wished both to give public testimony of my respect for you and for our family as well, and to leave it recorded in these monuments, and to satisfy my desire to honour and cherish you. If there is any fault in offering these slight things to men of such stature, I hope to obtain pardon from you, who are accustomed to receive small gifts from the humble with as cheerful a countenance as great ones from the high. Be pleased, then, to allow this little book, adorned and made more illustrious by the splendour of your names, to come into people's hands. For my part, in return, I shall strive by every kind of duty of respect to serve your name, praise and honour. May God grant that your dignity may be an ornament to learning and a protection to the learned for as long as possible. Marburg, from my Museum, 15 October 1612.

units.la: TRACTATVS DE VNGVENTO ARMARIO.
units.tr: A TREATISE ON THE WEAPON-SALVE.

units.la: Uoniam vetus ac laudabilis inclytæ hujus Academiæ mos est, auditores longe clarissimi, ut qui in professorum Collegium cooptantur, ij professionis suæ specimen aliquod proferant, vel de materia commissæ Spartæ consentanea Orationem habeant, non fuit mihi faciundum, ut hoc optimum majorum institutum ex honestissimis caussis rationibusq; profectum, à me neglectui habitum videretur.
units.tr: Since it is the ancient and commendable custom of this distinguished Academy, most distinguished hearers, that those who are co-opted into the college of professors should offer some specimen of their profession, or deliver an oration on a subject suited to the chair committed to them, it would not have been right for me to seem to neglect this excellent institution of our forefathers, which rests on the most honourable causes and reasons.

units.la: Sed putavi officij mei esse ut prius quædam perorando præfarer quàm ad demandatum mihi publice docendi munus me conferrem. Etsi autem non foret hîc alienum physicam scientiam ab antiquitate, dignitate utilitateque cum summa jucunditate conjuncta, commendare, tamen quia de his alibi sæpius, à doctrina judicioq; me longe superioribus erudite multa dicta esse scio, neminem quoq;, nisi cyclopicæ A
units.tr: But I thought it my duty to preface my public teaching office with some remarks before I applied myself to the task entrusted to me. Although it would not be out of place here to commend natural science, which is joined with the highest delight to antiquity, worth and usefulness, yet since I know that much has been learnedly said on these matters elsewhere, by men far superior to me in learning and judgment, and since I think no one will doubt the antiquity and usefulness of physics unless he is of Cyclopean

units.la: plane ruditatis, fore existimo, qui de physicæ antiquitate ac vtilitate sit dubitaturus, quæ etiam est tanta, vt neq; Theologus, neq; iurispe- ritus, omnium vero minimè Medicus eâ catere possit, vt non nisi à Pericle laudanda videatur, qui eam ab Anaxagora traditam percepit, & illius beneficio splendidior in dicendo extitit, omissis iam inquam iis, quæ de Physicæ vtilitate in medium afferri possent, quæstionem vnicam, quę multorum ingenia hactenus torsit, & etiam nunc fatigat, ex intimis naturæ penetralibus ac latebris depromtam, quatum quidem à me fieri poterit, impræsentiarum explicabo, persuasum habens, ex ea, admirabilem naturæ, & pene incredibilem potentiam atque maiestatem satis superque apparituram. Vos audi- tores dum in tam vastum pelagus nauigo, vestræ clementię ac benevolentię aura me subleuate & benigne prosequimini, magisq; ex voluntate dicentis, quam ex ipsa re & forma æstimate, & si forsan à scopo aberrauero, tempori nouercanti, quo ab eiusmodi exercitiis absui, amanter asscribite.
units.tr: utter crudeness. Physics is so great that neither the theologian, nor the jurist, and least of all the physician, can do without it. It seems rightly praised even by Pericles, who received it from Anaxagoras and through his benefit became more eloquent in speaking. But, setting aside what could be brought forward about the usefulness of physics, I will explain, as far as I am able at present, the single question that has tormented the minds of many until now and still wearies them, drawn from the innermost recesses and hiding places of nature. I am persuaded that from it the admirable and almost incredible power and majesty of nature will appear sufficiently, and more than sufficiently. You hearers, while I sail on so vast a sea, lift me up with the breeze of your clemency and goodwill and kindly accompany me, and judge the speaker more by his intention than by the matter and form itself; and if perhaps I stray from my aim, kindly ascribe it to the stepmotherly time from which I have been absent from such exercises.

units.la: Quæstio autem, quam tractandam suscepi, versabitur in eo potissimum, an vnguentum armarium quo etiam unum, duo vel plura miliaria vulneratus absens sanitati restituitur, telo seu instrumento, quo vulnus inflictum est, eo tantum delibuto, causam habeat in natura, an vero impostorium sit, vel veneficum? Ac principio quidem non possum hic non memi-nisse, quod, cum essem in Suecia apud I L. quē-dam & Generosum Dominum, duo ex ipsius ministris poculis inuicem certantes á verbis ad verbera devenirent, alterque alterius femur dextrum cultello satis profunde puncṫim vul-neraret. Cumque Chirurgus haberi protinus non posset, erat enim aula ab vrbe remotior, ecce vxor Generosi illius domini Fœmina no-bilißima, naturæque rerum non ignara, non applicato remedio ipsi vulneri, vllum citra do-lorem id curauit, cultello tantum, quo vulnus erat inflictum, peculiari vnguento delibuto. Et vulgi experimentum notius est, cum acule-os vel clauos pedum plantis infixos detrahunt, lardoq; elixo immittunt, & ita parte sauciatā seu vulnus absq; inflammatione & dolore conso-lidant. Quæritur igitur, qd causæ habeat in na-tura actio hæc admirabilis? Nō desunt, & inter eruditos qdā, qui naturaliter id fieri posse pla-nè negant. Alii astruunt, vulnus qdē ipsum na-turaliter curari, ceremonias a. magicas esse, im-postorias, ludicras & ad speciē confictas. Verū cū ab illis etiā frequentissimè istam adhiberi cu-ram sciā, qui religiosissimi & re & fama essent, & nullum nec dicto nec facto in diuina oracu-la fiat delistum, nondum video, quomodo su-perstitio vel impostura hic locū habere possit.
units.tr: The question I have undertaken to treat will turn chiefly on whether the weapon-salve, by which a man wounded even one, two or more miles away, being absent, is restored to health, when only the weapon or instrument with which the wound was inflicted is anointed, has its cause in nature, or whether it is a fraud or witchcraft. And at the outset I cannot help recalling that when I was in Sweden at the court of a certain illustrious and noble lord, two of his servants, competing with each other over their cups, passed from words to blows, and one of them pierced the other's right thigh with a knife, quite deeply. Since no surgeon could be had at once, for the court was rather far from the city, behold, the wife of that noble lord, a most noble lady not unacquainted with the nature of things, did not apply any remedy to the wound itself, yet cured it without any pain, merely by anointing the knife with which the wound had been inflicted with a special salve. And the common experience is better known: when people pull out needles or nails stuck in the soles of the feet, and put them into boiled lard, they heal the injured part or wound without inflammation and pain. The question therefore is, what cause does this admirable action have in nature? Among the learned there are not lacking some who flatly deny that it can happen naturally. Others assert that the wound itself is healed naturally, but that the ceremonies are magical, fraudulent, playful and feigned for show. But since I know that this cure is very often applied by those who are most religious both in deed and in reputation, and no offence is committed in word or deed against the divine oracles, I do not yet see how superstition or fraud can have any place here.

units.la: Superstitionem enim quamcunque delitam esse & inanem religionem in confesso est, quotiescunque scilicet homo dicit vel facit boni consequendi vel mali cujuspiam vitandi causa, quod neque naturalem neque præternaturalem vim habet ad effectum intentum, ut si quis in flumine seminet, vel littus aret, dicendus esset operari vanitatem, quia seminandi & arandi finis est messis, quem finem hæc ejus actio consequi nequit. Sic superstitione & vanitate non caret, cum aqua benedicta bibitur contra infirmitatem, & spargitur ad fertilitatem, balnea adhibere in vigilia nativitatis contra febres & dentium dolores, non comedere carnes in die nativitatis Domini contra febres, honorare S. Nicolaum pro acquirendis divitiis, ire ad S. Valentinum contra morbum caducum, pellere eundem prolatis gestatisve his carminibus: Caspar fert Myrrham, thus Melchior, Balthasar aurum. Hæc tria qui secum portabit nomina Regum, Solvitur à morbo Christi pietate caduco:
units.tr: For it is agreed that any superstition is a vain and empty religion, whenever a man says or does something to obtain some good or avoid some evil, which has neither a natural nor a preternatural power to produce the intended effect. If someone sowed seed in a river or ploughed the shore, he would be said to be doing vanity, because the end of sowing and ploughing is harvest, which this action cannot attain. Thus superstition and vanity are present when holy water is drunk against sickness and sprinkled for fertility; when baths are taken on the vigil of the Nativity against fevers and toothaches; when meat is not eaten on the day of the Lord's Nativity against fevers; when St Nicholas is honoured for the acquiring of riches; when one goes to St Valentine against the falling sickness; and when the same is driven away by reciting or carrying these verses: Caspar brings myrrh, Melchior incense, Balthasar gold. Whoever carries these three names of the Kings with him is freed from the falling sickness by the piety of Christ.

units.la: Dentium item dolores mitescere, si quis, dum sacrum fit, dentes contingat, hæc efferens verba, os non comminuetis ex eo: portare crucem per campos in vere circumquaq; contra tempestates, uti amuletis ad collum suspensis, quibus inscriptum est symbolum Apostolicum, licum, vel initium Evangelij Johannis, vel Psalmi alicujus particula contra incantamenta & dæmonum spectra, uti denique exorcismis & & coniurationibus, quæ absq; superstitiosa aliqua ceremonia adhiberi non possunt, quia scilicet non eruuntur ex signis & notis naturalibus, à natura ad significandum aliquid destinatis, ut ita dixisse non liceat, cur & unde creditas habent vires. Ac ejusmodi anilium deliramentorum exempla ubiq; terrarum occurrunt fere quotidie, quæ lubens silentio prætereo, ut vana enim & superstitiosa ab instituto nostro, prodigiosæq; naturæ limitibus sunt arcenda. In unguento autem armario actionem in lucem prodire sine ulla superstitione, fuco & impostura, tum ex ipso operandi modo, si quis scilicet eo utatur, tum ex iis etiam, quæ à me in medium proferentur, innotescet. Nullæ hîc audientur nugæ, nulla ænigmata, nulla commenta, fabulosum nihil, insulsum nihil, sed augustissimæ naturæ Magnalia omnem fere fidem excedentia, eam vel maxime ob causam non occultanda, non reticenda, quod ad summam Dei potentiam ac sapientiam laudandam venerandamque nos sint excitatura. Itaq; in intima naturæ latifundia nos demittemus, aliamque quàm superstitionis prætextum, exquiremus eruemusque causam, cujus inquisitio, quæ difficultate non caret, & à plerisplerisque ignoratur, ex sequentib. petenda est principiis.
units.tr: Likewise, toothaches are said to ease if someone, while the sacred rite is performed, touches the teeth, uttering these words, "You shall not break a bone of it"; or carrying a cross through the fields all round in spring against storms; or wearing amulets hung at the neck on which is written the Apostles' Creed, or the beginning of John's Gospel, or some part of a Psalm, against charms and the apparitions of demons; or finally exorcisms and conjurations, which cannot be used without some superstitious ceremony, because they are not derived from natural signs and marks, which nature has destined to signify something, so that one cannot say why or whence they have their supposed powers. Examples of such old-wives' delusions occur almost everywhere, almost daily, and I gladly pass them over in silence, since vain and superstitious things must be kept away from our subject and from the limits of natural wonders. But in the weapon-salve it will become clear that the action comes forth into the light without any superstition, pretence or fraud, both from the very manner of working, if one indeed uses it, and from those things which I will bring forward. Here no trifles will be heard, no riddles, no fictions, nothing fabulous, nothing silly, but the most august marvels of nature, almost exceeding all belief, which must not be concealed or suppressed, especially because they will stir us to praise and venerate the supreme power and wisdom of God. And so we will descend into the inner broad domains of nature, and we will seek out and bring to light a cause other than the pretext of superstition. Its inquiry, which is not free of difficulty and is unknown to most people, must be sought from the following principles.

units.la: Omnibus & cunctis vniuersi rebus congenitam quandam inter se esse consortii aut dissidii proprietatem, quâ citra visibilem contactum mutuo alterantur & afficiuntur, experientia testis est, & qui negat,
units.tr: Experience bears witness that all things in the universe have some innate property of mutual agreement or disagreement, by which they are mutually altered and affected without visible contact; and whoever denies it

units.la: Ostendi Solem postulat ille sibi.
units.tr: He asks to be shown the sun.

units.la: Harum qualitatum, viriumq; abstrusarum ac in naturæ maiestate penitus occultarum exploratio & cognitio magia naturalis est, ex sympathia rerum orta, quarum consensum dissidiumq; qui noverit, Magiæ dicetur peritus, iisq; vtens occultè, admiranda poterit producere & incredibilia vulgo, vt non nisi auxilio dæmonum talia facta esse putentur, propterea & modus efficiendi non vtiq; est manifestus. Est enim hoc mysterium aliud nihil, quàm Sympathiæ Antipathiæq; superiorum & inferiorum scientia.
units.tr: The investigation and knowledge of these qualities and hidden powers, which lie concealed in the majesty of nature, is natural magic, arising from the sympathy of things. Whoever knows their agreement and disagreement will be called skilled in magic, and by using them secretly he will be able to produce admirable and incredible effects, so that to the common people such things are thought to be done only with the aid of demons. For this reason the manner of effecting them is not at all manifest. For this mystery is nothing other than the science of the sympathy and antipathy of higher and lower things.

units.la: Sympathia mutua quædam consensio est inter res physicas, qua se amice amplectuntur: alii compassionem vocant. Galenus 3. de simpl. med. c. 5. vtitur nomine amicitiæ. Plin. l. 37. cap. 4 vocat concordiam. Cic. de sat. gravissimis veris simisq; verbis convenientiam naturæque continuationem, licet enim disiita sunt ferri & magnetis corpora, ita tamen natura in iis continuatur, vt etiam conueniant in vnum. Idem naturæ cognationem dixit. Bapt. Porta conconsensum: alii concentum & symphoniam per Metaph. alii naturalis beneuolentiæ ne-xum. Antipathia rerum mutua quædam asse-ctio est, quâ se auersantur. Gal.& Plin.pugnan-tiam vocant atque discordiam : alii dissensum, inimicitiam, dissidium, simultatem: qui verò etiam per qualitatem infestam eam definiunt, qua mediante mutuis ac cęcis dissidiis se res na-turales quædam afficiunt, non procul à veritate recedunt, vt nec hi, qui resistentiam, quæ videlicet resistit vel impedit, ne actio ab agente in patiens possit introduci.
units.tr: Sympathy is a certain mutual agreement between physical things, by which they embrace each other as friends; others call it compassion. Galen, On Simple Medicines, book 3, chapter 5, uses the name friendship; Pliny, book 37, chapter 4, calls it concord. Cicero, in weighty and true words, calls it harmony and a continuity of nature, for although bodies of iron and magnet are separated, nature is nonetheless continuous in them, so that they come together into one. The same author called it kinship of nature. Baptista Porta called it consent; others call it concord and symphony, through the Metaphysics; others a bond of natural goodwill. Antipathy is a certain mutual affection of things by which they turn away from one another. Galen and Pliny call it opposition and discord; others call it dissent, enmity, disagreement, rivalry. Those who also define it as a hostile quality, by which certain natural things are mutually affected by hidden and secret disagreements, do not stray far from the truth, nor do those who call it resistance, which namely resists or hinders the action from being introduced from agent into patient.

units.la: Quemadmodum igitur ex sympathia su-periorum & cœlestium virtutum oritur attra-ctio, & in locum terrenum inferioremq; dedu-ctio, ita ex antipathia resistentia. Vnde Platonici Magiam vocarunt attractionem vnius rei ab altera, ex naturæ quadā cognatione ortam.
units.tr: Just as attraction arises from the sympathy of the higher and heavenly powers and draws things down into the lower earthly place, so resistance arises from antipathy. Hence the Platonists called magic the attraction of one thing by another, arising from a certain kinship of nature.

units.la: Iam vero mundi huius partes omnes, ceu v-nius animalis membra, ab vno pendentes au-tore & principio, vnius naturæ coniunctione inuicem copulantur, ideò, sicut in nobis cere-brum, cor, pulmones, iecur, & reliqua à se trahunt inuicem aliquid, mutuoq; se iuuant, vt v-no illorum aliquo patiente compatiantur, ita etiam ingētis huius animalis mēbra, i. e. omnia mundi corpora connexa similiter mutuant in-uicē naturas& mutuantur, &ex cōmuni hac co-gnatione cōmunis nascitur amor, & ex amore com-
units.tr: Moreover, all the parts of this world, like the limbs of a single animal, depend on one author and principle and are joined to one another by the bond of one nature. Therefore, just as in us the brain, heart, lungs, liver and the rest draw something from one another and help each other, so that when one of them suffers the others sympathize, so too the members of this huge animal, that is, all the connected bodies of the world, similarly exchange and receive natures from one another. From this common kinship common love is born, and from common love common attraction.

units.la: communi communis attractio. Hinc magnes ferrum, Sol flores multos ad se trahit, hinc plantæ heliotropiæ ad solis, Selinetropiæ & Lunisequæ ad lunæ motum vertuntur.
units.tr: Hence the magnet draws iron to itself and the sun draws many flowers; hence the heliotrope plants turn to the motion of the sun, and the selenotropes and lunisequae to the motion of the moon.

units.la: Quamobrem in terra aspicere licet quidem Solem, Lunam & reliqua, sed pro qualitate terrena, in cælo a. & lapides, & plantas, & animalia, sed pro natura & modo cœlesti, ut ita in infimis suprema, & hæc in illis sint agnoscenda & quærenda. Fatali enim lege Deum sancivisse, ut inferiora supernis ancillentur, formamq; unicuiq; suam sidereo lapsu viribus cumulatâ immisisse, & ne continua desisteret rerum procreatio, singula semen proferre jussisse, ut quæ mutationibus obnoxia essent, cōtinua serie & lege generarentur ac corrumperentur, nemo inficiaturus est, nisi sacris pariter & profanis monimentis contradicturus, naturæq; ordinem destruturus, ut ita spectabilem illam in animalibus, mineralibus & vegetabilibus sympathian ac antipathian, non aliunde dependere, quàm ex cælesti syderū influxu impressioneq;, pro unius cujusq; specie constitutione, individuis vel omnibus, vel pro singulari complexionis gradu aliquibus tantum speciei ejusdem congenita, omnino statuendum sit. Unde cum Sapphyrus oculos non lædat, repertus tamen unus est qui prima applicatione aciem visus obtudit. Et in Austria Gemelli solis objectis ad januam corpori poris lateribus feras aperiebant, quod certe admiratione non caret.
units.tr: Wherefore on earth we may indeed see the sun, moon and the rest, but in their earthly quality; and in heaven we may see stones, plants and animals, but according to heavenly nature and mode. Thus the highest things are to be recognized and sought in the lowest, and the lowest in the highest. For no one will deny that God, by a fatal law, ordained that inferior things should serve the superior, and, having given each thing its own form by a sidereal descent with its powers increased, and so that the production of things might never cease, commanded each to bring forth seed, so that things liable to change are generated and corrupted in continuous succession and by law. Anyone who denied this would contradict both sacred and profane records and destroy the order of nature. So we must hold that the sympathy and antipathy so evident among animals, minerals and plants depend on nothing other than the celestial influx and impression of the stars, according to the constitution of each species, and are congenital either to all the individuals of the species or to some of them only, according to a particular degree of complexion. Hence, although sapphire does not harm the eyes, one was found who dulled the sight by first application. And in Austria, when twin suns were set before a door, wild beasts were made to open the pores on the sides of their bodies, which certainly is not without wonder.

units.la: Verum quibus mediis res quædam naturales sibi copulentur inuicem, difficile est hic dicere ex Philosophia communi. Quod enim alteri coniunctum est, aut est eius essentia, aut essentiæ proprietas, aut inest ei vt forma subiecto, aut id attingit, vel sicut transmutans, id quod transmutatur, vel sicut ars subiectam sibi materiam. Moses dilucide quinque inuicem connexa expressisse videtur. Cœlum & terram, terram & inanitatem, abyssum & tenebras, Spiritum Dei & aquas, lucem & corpora. Primus igitur connexionis modus designatur per terram inanem & vacuam. Vacua enim & inanis terra est materia sua, nisi formis aliunde adimpleatur.
units.tr: But by what means certain natural things are joined to one another is hard to say here from common philosophy. For what is joined to something else is either its essence, or a property of its essence, or inheres in it as form in a subject, or touches it, either as the transmuting agent touches what is transmuted or as an art touches its matter. Moses seems to have clearly expressed five mutually connected pairs: heaven and earth, earth and emptiness, abyss and darkness, the Spirit of God and the waters, light and bodies. The first mode of connection is designated by the earth being empty and void. For the earth in its own matter is empty and void, unless it is filled with forms from elsewhere.

units.la: Secundus connexionis modus per tenebras significatur super faciem abyssi.
units.tr: The second mode of connection is signified by the darkness upon the face of the abyss.

units.la: Tertius per lucem corporibus obortam.
units.tr: The third is signified by the light that arose upon bodies.

units.la: Quartus per cœlum & terram, illud enim huic coniungitur, vt efficiēs patienti, & transmutans causa corpori transmutando.
units.tr: The fourth is signified by heaven and earth; for the former is joined to the latter as the agent to the patient, and as the transmuting cause to the body being transmuted.

units.la: Quintus per spiritum Domini.
units.tr: The fifth is signified by the Spirit of the Lord.

units.la: Sed videamus quomodo hæc se habeant in nobis. Terra terrenum corpus est, inane vita, vacuum sensu, superque ipsum sunt tenebræ, torpor, mors, insensatio, immobilitas.
units.tr: But let us see how these stand in us. The earth is the earthly body, empty of life and void of sense; and above it are darkness, torpor, death, insensibility and immobility.

units.la: Lux vita est, quæ illud vegetat, monet, excitat, sensuque reddit prænditum.
units.tr: Light is life, which quickens that body, admonishes it, arouses it, and restores to it the sense it lacks.

units.la: Cœlum animus est & fons illius lucis.
units.tr: Heaven is the mind and the fount of that light.

units.la: Spiritus Dei intellectus est, lumen diuini vultus. Ratio igitur huius connexionis & consequentiæ est, corpus esse inane ex se, suas habere tenebras, tum proxime iungi luci, per lucem connecti cœlo, per cœlum substantiæ spiritali, ut videre est ex sequentibus.
units.tr: The Spirit of God is the intellect, the light of the divine countenance. The reason of this connection and sequence, therefore, is that the body is empty in itself and has its own darkness; then it is joined nearly to light, connected through light to heaven, and through heaven to spiritual substance, as may be seen from what follows.

units.la: Abyssus. Tenebræ. Inanis vita. Terra. vacua sensu Lux Vegetans vitamque reddens. Cœlum lucis fons, Spiritus.
units.tr: Abyss. Darkness. Empty life. Earth, void of sense. Light: quickening and restoring life. Heaven, the fount of light. Spirit.

units.la: VIden' quo ordine res creatæ affinitatem inuicem consequantur? Viden' naturalis beneuolentiæ nexum ac copulam? Ecquænam vero hæc philosophia est, inquit aliquis? Non certè vulgaris illa, quæ ex sensu, materia, & qualitatibus manifestis omnia diiudicat, sed cœlestis, abstrusior, scilicet & profundior.
units.tr: See in what order created things follow upon one another's affinity! See the bond and tie of natural goodwill! What philosophy is this, someone may ask? Certainly not that common philosophy which judges all things from sense, matter and manifest qualities, but a heavenly one, more abstruse and profound.

units.la: Inter corpus & animam substantias longe inuicem distantes, opus certe fuit medio vinculo, quod tam distantes naturas inuicè copula□ret, cui muneri delegatum est tenue illud & spiritale corpusculum, quod & Medici & Philosophi Spiritum appellant. Hunc Spiritu copulante diuinioré esse quàm elementa, cœloq; respondere proportione ipse Aristot. scribit: Et quemquemadmodū omnis cœlorū virtus vehiculo lucis trāsfertur ad terrā, ita omnis animi potestas, vita sc. motus & sensus lucido Spiritu intercedente ad corpus terrenū cōmeat & transfunditur. Vt autē ea quę dixi, maiorē mereantur fidē, memorabilia quædā antipathias ac sympathias exempla ex nō leuis autoritatis autoribus in medium sunt producenda. Quod dū facio, rogo vt audiar benigne, & cū attentione.
units.tr: Between body and soul, substances far distant from each other, there was surely need of a middle bond to join such distant natures. To this office was assigned that subtle and spiritual little body which both physicians and philosophers call spirit. Aristotle himself writes that this joining spirit is more divine than the elements and corresponds in proportion to heaven: just as all the power of the heavens is carried to the earth by the vehicle of light, so all the power of the soul, that is life, motion and sense, passes and is transfused into the earthly body through the intervention of the luminous spirit. But so that what I have said may deserve greater trust, memorable examples of antipathies and sympathies from authors of no small authority must be brought forward. In doing so I ask that you listen kindly and attentively.

units.la: Ac primo quidem spectabilis antipathia in venenis cernitur. Non enim omni veneno, teste Gal. l. de antid. quodlibet aduersatur antidotum, vt enim sua cuiusq; veneni species, ita sua cuiusq; est antidotus.
units.tr: And first, the notable antipathy is seen in poisons. For, as Galen testifies in his book on antidotes, not every antidote is opposed to every poison; just as each poison has its own species, so each has its own antidote.

units.la: Contra Toxicum Scytharum, quod constabat sanguine humano & sanie viperina, quo sagittas & tela inficiebant, irremediabile scelus, morte leui tactu accelerās, Cantharides peculiarē habere vim traduntur, quibus si aduersus alia venena quis vteretur, nihil certe efficeret, testante eodē l. de antid. cap. 29. Paulo Ægineta l. 5. & Diofcor. circa lib. 6. initium.
units.tr: Against the poison of the Scythians, which consisted of human blood and viper's ichor, with which they infected their arrows and weapons, an incurable crime hastening death by a light touch, cantharides are said to have a peculiar power. If anyone used them against other poisons they would certainly accomplish nothing, as the same Galen testifies in the same book, chapter 29, as do Paul of Aegina, book 5, and Dioscorides, near the beginning of book 6.

units.la: Pastinacæ marinæ seu Trigonis radio super caudam eminente nullum vsquam est venenū arboribus execrabilius, radici enim infixū eas enecare, armaq; vt telū perforare, vi ferri & veneni malo. Plin. l. 9. c. 48. autor est.
units.tr: Nowhere is there a poison more execrable to trees than that of the sea stingray (pastinaca marina, or trygon), when its ray stands up over its tail; for fixed in the root it kills them, and it pierces weapons like a missile by the force of iron and the evil of its poison. Pliny, book 9, chapter 48, is the authority.

units.la: Aconito rutham aduersari maxime idem l. 20. c. 3. Laserpitium telorum & serpentum venena extinguere.l. 22.c. 23. adamantem venena facere irrita madendo, lymphationesque abigere. l. 37. cap. 4. prodidit. Et authoritate suffragatur experientia. Scribit Galenus l.de theriaca ad Pison. trifolium coctum demorsis à vipera impositum dolores tollere : at sano cuipiam impositum dolores afferre, quales à vipera læsi patiuntur. Scaliger exerc. 353. sect. 5.huius secreti reddit quidem rationem, sed magis pro ingenio suo subtilem, quam veram. Hæc de venenis.
units.tr: Rue is especially opposed to aconite, as the same author says in book 20, chapter 3. Laserpitium extinguishes the poisons of missiles and serpents, book 22, chapter 23. He reports in book 37, chapter 4, that adamant, by being soaked, renders poisons ineffective and drives away madness induced by lymph. Experience also supports this authority. Galen writes in his book on theriac to Piso that trifolium boiled and applied to those bitten by a viper removes their pains, but applied to a healthy person it brings on pains such as those suffered by those hurt by a viper. Scaliger, Exercitations 353, section 5, does give a reason for this secret, but one more subtle according to his own wit than true. So much concerning poisons.

units.la: Sed quid dicam de inuicta illa adamantis vi duarum violentissimarum naturæ rerū contemtrice, quæ hircino rumpitur sanguine, nec aliter quam recenti calidoque macerata.
units.tr: But what shall I say of that invincible power of adamant, which scorns the strongest forces of two natures, and which is broken by goat's blood, and in no other way than when steeped in it while fresh and warm?

units.la: An non hoc præclarum naturalis dissidij specimen est: Cuius hoc ingenio inuentum? quove casu repertum? aut quæ fuit coniectura saltem experiundi rem immensi secreti, & quidem in animalium sordidissimo nimirum hirco. Numinum profecto muneris talis inuentio omnis est, inquit Plinius, nec quærenda in vlla naturæ parte ratio est, sed voluntas.
units.tr: Is this not a remarkable specimen of natural antipathy? By whose ingenuity was it discovered? By what chance was it found? Or what was the conjecture, at least, that prompted the trying of a thing of such immense secrecy, and in the filthiest of animals, the goat? Certainly such an invention is wholly the gift of the gods, says Pliny, and no reason is to be sought in any part of nature, but only the will.

units.la: Cum magnete quoq; adamantem tantum dissidere graves autores tradunt, vt iuxta positus ferrum non patiatur abstrahi, aut si admotus magnes apprehenderit, rapiat atque auferat.
units.tr: Grave authors also report that adamant so disagrees with the magnet that, when placed beside it, it does not allow iron to be drawn away; or, if the magnet is brought near, it seizes the iron and snatches it away.

units.la: Leo cunctis animalibus tremendus, qui nec tygrim metuit nec vrsum, gallum tamen his longe imbecilliorem expauescit. Quærit aliquis causam naturalem? An quia in oculis galli est vis quædam, vt quidem existimant, oculis leonis contraria. Certe huius rei causam non à materia, non à sensibus licet assignare, alias in labyrintheas perplexitates devoluere-mur, sed solùm ab ordinis superni contemplatione. Proclus lib. de Mag. hanc affert veritatem. Sunt, inquit, animalia solaria multa, vt leones, galli, luminis cuiusdam solaris participes. Gallus igitur timetur à Leone, quia præsentia luminis solaris magis convenit gallo quàm Leoni, quod inde apparet, quod gallus quibusdam quasi hymnis applaudit surgenti Soli: quandoque etiam dæmones solares visi sunt leonina fronte, quibus cum obiiceretur gallus, repente disparuerunt, quod quidem inde procedit, quia semper, quæ in eodem ordine constituta inferiora sunt, cedunt superioribus seu reuerentur superiora. Hæc Proclus,
units.tr: The lion, terrible to all animals, who fears neither tiger nor bear, nevertheless dreads the cock, which is far weaker than these. Does someone ask for a natural cause? Is it because the cock's eyes have some power, as they think, contrary to the lion's eyes? Certainly the cause of this cannot be assigned from matter or from the senses, otherwise we would be rolled into labyrinthine perplexities, but only from contemplation of the superior order. Proclus, in his book on magic, brings forward this truth. There are, he says, many solar animals, such as lions and cocks, which share in a certain solar light. The cock is therefore feared by the lion, because the presence of solar light suits the cock more than the lion. This appears from the fact that the cock applauds the rising sun with certain hymns; sometimes solar demons have also been seen with lion's faces, and when a cock was presented to them they suddenly vanished. This indeed proceeds from the fact that inferiors placed in the same order always yield to their superiors, or superiors are revered. Thus Proclus.

units.la: Aranei cum bufone & serpentibus dissidiũ notum est: hoste enim conspecto filo se librat in caput serpentis porrectæ sub vmbra arboris suæ, tantaque vi morsu cerebrum apprehendit, vt stridens subinde, vertigineque rotata, nec filum desuper pendentis rumpere, adeoq; fugere nequeat, nec finis ante mortem.
units.tr: Spiders are well known to be at odds with toads and serpents. When the enemy is sighted, the spider lets itself down on its thread onto the head of a serpent lying stretched out in the shade of its tree. It seizes the brain with such a violent bite that the serpent hisses and whirls dizzily. It cannot break the thread hanging above it, nor can it escape, and there is no end short of death.

units.la: Fraxini & serpentis antipathia tanto experimento rimento prodita est, vt ne matutinas quidem occidentesve vmbras etiam longissimas arboris huius serpens attingat, adeoque ipsam procul fugiat, sique arboris fronde accensa gyro claudatur serpens, in ignem potius quam in fraxinum fugiat.
units.tr: The antipathy between ash and serpent has been shown by such strong experience that the serpent will not even touch the shadows of this tree, whether morning or evening, even the longest, and flees it far off. And if a serpent is encircled by a burning ash-branch, it will flee into the fire rather than the ash.

units.la: Sed ad vegetabilia pergo, inter quæ conspicua quoq; & euidens simultas est. Nam quercus in oliueto nata fugit, introrsum commeat, & exarescit, olea vero in querceto radices maxime relinquit noxias, quercusq; enecat. Eadē iuglandem iuxta sata aut emoritur ipsa, aut infirma semper est, aut iuglandem nucem talem efficit. Quin & nucis vmbra omnibus satis est inimica, & quæcunque attigerit, veneno invaditilico, nocetq; stillicidij ratione, cum humorè frondibus diffunditur.
units.tr: But I move on to plants, among which there is also a conspicuous and evident enmity. The oak growing in an olive grove shuns it, retreats inward and withers, while the olive, in an oak grove, sends out especially harmful roots and kills the oak. Likewise a walnut planted nearby either dies itself, or is always sickly, or produces its nut of a certain kind. Indeed the shade of the walnut is hostile to almost everything, and whatever it touches it poisons at once, harming by dripping, as its moisture spreads from the leaves.

units.la: Sic brassicę & vitis odium spectabile est. Vitis enim cum intortis clauiculis omnia soleat complecti, solam refugit brassicam, nam prope eam sentiens, in aduersam se torquet partem, dumq; coquitur brassica, vinumq; vel si paucissimum instilles, nec coquitur, nec color ipsius constat: ipsum vero olus cyclamino & origano peraresc it, & vitis lauti odore euadit deterior, cicutaq; vino obtundi ur.
units.tr: So the hatred between cabbage and vine is notable. The vine, with its twisting tendrils, usually embraces everything, but it shuns the cabbage alone. For sensing it nearby, it turns itself toward the opposite side. And while cabbage is being cooked, even if you drip in a very little wine, it neither cooks properly nor keeps its colour. The vegetable itself is dried up by cyclamen and oregano, and the vine is made worse by the smell of laurel, while hemlock is subdued by wine.

units.la: Polipodium cancro adeo est antipatheticū, vt hic illi admotus tum integentes crustas, tum vngues abiiciat à pedibus. Filix & arundo in tantum sibi aduersantur, vt neutra iuxta se alteram ferat; vnde nec in arundinetis filices, nec in filicetis arundines videntur.
units.tr: Polypody is so antipathetic to the crab that when it is brought near, the crab casts off both its shell coverings and its claws from its feet. Fern and reed are so opposed that neither will bear the other beside it. Hence ferns are not seen in reed beds, nor reeds in fern beds.

units.la: Alyssum, hypericum, & moly herbas in tantum malignis spiritibus antipatheticas esse, vt quemadmodum luporum capita ianuis affixa, sic has herbas in aedibus suspensas, ab hominibus & pecore, veneficia, ne fascinentur, arcere, grauissimi autores tradunt. Homer. Odyss. 10. 11. Plin. l. 28. cap. 10. Dioscorid. l. 3. c. 17. Vnde Homerus, Magiae peritissimus, Mercurium contra veneficia Circes Molij herba Vlyssem muniuisse cecinit. Et in historia Tobiae, vt sacra etiam huc referamus, legitur, angelum cordis particulam, piscis e flumine extracti docuisse Tobiam super carbones proiicere, sicq; excitato fumo omne daemoniorum genus extricati tam a viro quam muliere. Proinde his & similibus Periaptis & amuletis, quae ratione nituntur naturali, fides non est deroganda, de quorum scilicet substantia, profluuia inspirata vires corporis reficere, venenisque possunt resistere.
units.tr: Alyssum, hypericum and moly are herbs so antipathetic to malignant spirits that, just as wolves' heads fixed to doors, so these herbs hung in houses keep men and cattle from witchcraft, lest they be bewitched, as the most weighty authors hand down. Homer, Odyssey 10 and 11; Pliny, book 28, chapter 10; Dioscorides, book 3, chapter 17. Hence Homer, most skilled in magic, sang that Mercury protected Odysseus against Circe's witchcraft with the herb moly. And in the history of Tobias, so that we may bring sacred things in here too, we read that the angel taught Tobias to throw a piece of the heart of a fish drawn from the river onto coals, and so, with the smoke raised, every kind of demon was driven away, from both the man and the woman. Therefore these and similar periapts and amulets, which rest on natural reason, are not to be disbelieved, since from their substance breathed-in exhalations can restore the powers of the body and resist poisons.

units.la: Sic Peoniae albae radix & alcis vngula epilepsiae, semen melanthij catarrhis antipathetica sunt: stercus lupi doloribus colicis, non quidem vt inepte & inscite quidam putant, incantationis viribus, sed quod ab illorum substantia, vapores quidam velut atomi defluunt, qui inspirati cerebrum siccent, morbique causam suis viri-bus alterent. Vnde Galenus experientia horum edoctus, periaptis, inquit, hic confidere oportet, vt substantia ipsorum, non incantationis verba, iuuet l. 6. & 10. de simplic. medic.
units.tr: So the root of white peony and the hoof of the elk are antipathetic to epilepsy, and the seed of melanthium to catarrhs. Wolf's dung is good for colic pains, not, as some foolishly and ignorantly think, by the power of incantation, but because certain vapours flow off from their substance like atoms, which, when breathed in, dry the brain and alter the cause of the disease by their powers. Hence Galen, taught by experience of these things, says: "Here one must trust in periapts, so that their substance, not the words of incantation, may help" (books 6 and 10 On Simple Medicines).

units.la: Contacta tridente torpedine marina, piscatoris manus obstupescere, & Echneida piscículum, quamuis velocem ventorum agitatæ procella nauis cursum sistere videmus, non quidem incantationis verbis, sed ob causas modo commemoratas. Stupendum certe naturæ miraculum, minutissimum etiam piscículum, qui maris & terræ portenta sua natura superat, remis velisq; concitatam nauim quantumvis magnam, non alio modo quàm adhærendo remorari.
units.tr: We see that when the trident of the sting-ray is touched, the fisherman's hand grows numb, and the echeneis, a small fish though swift, stops the course of a ship driven by a storm of winds. This is not by words of incantation but for the causes just mentioned. Surely a stupendous wonder of nature: the tiniest fish, which by its nature surpasses the portents of sea and land, holds back a ship, however large, driven on by oars and sails, by nothing other than adhering to it.

units.la: Videatur Plin. l. 9. cap. 25. & l. 32. cap. 1. Fertur Actiaco Marte tenuisse imperatoriam naué Antonij, properantis circuire & exhortari suos, donec transiret in aliam, ideoque Cæsariana classis impetu maiore protinus venit. Tenuit & nostra memoria Principis Caij ab Astrua Antium remigantis. Quin & auspicalis piscículus est, siquidem nouissime in vrbem reuersus Imperator ille, suis telis confossus est. Nec longa fuit illius morae admiratio, statim causa intellecta, cum è tota classe quinqueremis sola non proficeret, exilientibus protinus, nus, qui id quaerarent, circa nauim inuene- runt adhærentem gubernaculo, ostenderunt- que Caio, indignanti hoc fuisse, quod se re- uocaret, quadringentorumque remigum ob- sequio contra se incederet. Constabat peculi-ariter miratum, quomodo adhærens tenuis- set, necidem polleret in nauigium receptus. De hoc Laurentius Lippius Oppiani interpres, erudite lusit his versibus:
units.tr: See Pliny, book 9, chapter 25, and book 32, chapter 1. It is said that at the battle of Actium it held back Antony's imperial ship, which was hurrying to go round and encourage his men, until it passed into another; therefore Caesar's fleet came on at once with greater force. In our own memory too, a fish held back the ship of Prince Caius as he rowed from Astura to Antium. Indeed it is also a portent-fish, since that emperor, returning lately to the city, was pierced by his own weapons. The wonder at its delay was not long, for the cause was understood at once: out of the whole fleet, only the quinquereme did not advance. Those who leapt out at once to find out the reason found a fish clinging to the rudder near the ship, and they showed it to Caius, who was indignant that it had been done to call him back, and that with the obedience of four hundred rowers he was advancing against it. It was commonly remarked on how it, clinging on, had held the ship back, and how it could be so small and yet be taken aboard. Lorenzo Lippi, translator of Oppian, wittily played on this in these verses:

units.la: Pellebant velis, pellebant remige nauem,Ventus erat, coeptum sum remoratus iter.Solus ego Actiacam potui retinere carinam,Et potui Caij rostra tenere ducis.Semipedalis ego: quis hac corpuscula credatIn cursu tantas detinuisse rates.
units.tr: They drove the ship with sails, they drove it with oars; the wind was there, and yet I halted the journey they had begun. I alone could hold back the Actian keel, and I alone could hold the beak of the leader Caius. I am a half-foot long: who would believe that such a tiny body could hold back so many ships in their course.

units.la: Fatendum certe, naturam hic abstrusam, & sensibus inexplicabilem. Præter enim ea, quæ dicta modo sunt fatale quoddam indi- cium & præsagium in eo obseruatum est, qua- si futuri mali præscio periculum imminens cu- pienti auertere. Tenuit legatos Periandri de castrandis pueris nobilibus, tanquam indi- gnum iudicante natura homini, id, quod con- seruationi ipsius donatum esset, auferre, iccirco nauem inhibuit, & à cursu reuocauit. Tenuit nauem Caij Cæsaris non multo post Romæ interfecti, condolens misero Cęsaris exitio ipsa natura cupiit ab ipso malum auertere, atq; ab infausto cursu reuocare. Hæc de Echneide fere omnia ex Plinio.
units.tr: Certainly this must be admitted: nature here is hidden and inexplicable to the senses. For besides the things just mentioned, a certain fatal sign and omen was observed in it, as if, foreseeing an impending evil, it wished to turn away the danger. It held back the envoys of Periander, who were to castrate noble boys, as nature judged it unworthy for a man to lose what had been given for his preservation; therefore it checked the ship and called it back from its course. It held back the ship of Caius Caesar not long after he was killed at Rome; grieving at Caesar's wretched death, nature herself wished to turn evil away from him and call him back from his unlucky course. Almost all of this about the echeneis is from Pliny.

units.la: Cæterum in experimentis est, hirundinis cor palpitans deuoratum memoriam deperditam restituere, adque ingenium valere & intelligentiam.
units.tr: Moreover, it is in experiments that the heart of a swallow, eaten while still palpitating, restores lost memory, and makes the mind and understanding strong.

units.la: Cor turturis viuum calensque comesum ad febres intermittentes omnes.
units.tr: The heart of a turtledove, eaten alive and warm, is good for all intermittent fevers.

units.la: Anatem viuam ventri admotam compescere tormina.
units.tr: A live duck applied to the belly checks gripes.

units.la: Viuentem araneam iuglandis testis inclu-sam colloque subnexam pellere quartanam: ranarum oculos ante Solis ortum erutos, viuis illis in aquâ dimissis, alligatos, sicut & vnguiū præsegmina in pedibus & manibus febricitan-tis, cancri viui dorso superligata, cumq; eo in aquam fluentem proiecta, tertianas febres.
units.tr: A live spider enclosed in a walnut shell and tied around the neck drives away quartan fever. Frogs' eyes torn out before sunrise, tied on while the frogs are alive and put into water, and the parings of the nails of the feet and hands of a feverish person, tied on the back of a live crab and thrown with it into flowing water, cure tertian fevers.

units.la: Talpæ viuentis dentem odontalgiam sanare contactu:
units.tr: Touching a living mole's tooth heals toothache.

units.la: Hominis caluam mederi epilepsiæ.
units.tr: A man's skull cures epilepsy.

units.la: Ossiculum è poplite leporis nephritidi & spasmo flatulento.
units.tr: A little bone from the hare's knee cures kidney stone and flatulent spasm.

units.la: Intestinum lupi colicis doloribus.
units.tr: A wolf's intestine cures colic pains.

units.la: Cor corui gestatum ad inhibendum so-mnum, cor vespertilionis ad eundem valere accersendum.
units.tr: A raven's heart carried about prevents sleep; a bat's heart, for the same purpose, is good for bringing sleep on.

units.la: Ossa capitis equæ fugare erucas palo in hor-tis affixa.
units.tr: Bones of a mare's head, fixed on a stake in gardens, drive off caterpillars.

units.la: Graminis genus, 7. habens internodia, effi-cacissime cacissime contra capitis dolores adalligari.
units.tr: A kind of grass with seven internodes, tied on, is most effective against headaches.

units.la: Herbam, canis vrina irrigatam, euulsam, ne ferro tangatur, luxatis mederi celerrime.
units.tr: An herb watered with dog's urine, pulled up and not touched by iron, cures dislocations very quickly.

units.la: Florente cicuta & violis, si qui morbi homini acciderint, quoties florere eas herbas cötigerit, licet sanatum, recidiuam tamen quandã eorum sentire compertum est. Non prætereunda hic, quæ Plin. lib. 24. cap. 17. & 19. Item lib. 25. cap. 4. & lib. 26 cap. 4. ex Pythagora, Crateua, Democrito, Apollidoro, Cleemporo Medico & aliis recêset, de mira quarundã herbarũ efficientia ac virtute. Adamantide herba, Armeniç & Cappadociç alumna, admota, leones resupinari cum laxo hiatu.
units.tr: When hemlock and violets are in flower, if any illness has befallen a man, then whenever those herbs flower, although he has been cured, a certain relapse is found to be felt. Not to be passed over here are the things Pliny recounts from Pythagoras, Crateuas, Democritus, Apollodorus, Cleemporus the physician and others, about the wonderful efficacy and power of certain herbs: book 24, chapters 17 and 19; likewise book 25, chapter 4, and book 26, chapter 4. The herb adamantis, a nursling of Armenia and Cappadocia, when applied, makes lions fall on their backs with their jaws loosely gaping.

units.la: Arianide, quæ in Arianis nascitur colore ignea, collecta Sole existente in Leone, ligna accendi tactu oleo peruncta.
units.tr: Arianis, which grows among the Arians and is fiery in colour, when gathered while the sun is in Leo, makes wood catch fire when touched, if it is anointed with oil.

units.la: Æschynomenem, appropinquante carpentis manu contrahere folia.
units.tr: Aeschynomene draws in its leaves when a hand approaches to pick it.

units.la: Theangelide in Libano Syriæ, Babylone, & Susis Persidis proveniente, pota, homines diuinare.
units.tr: Theangelis, growing in Lebanon of Syria, in Babylon and in Susa of Persia, when drunk, makes men prophesy.

units.la: Gelotophyllide in Bactris & circa Borysthenē nascente, & pota cum myrrha & vino, varias obseruari species, ridendique finem non fieri, nisi potis nucleis pineæ nucis cum pipere & melle in vino palmeo.
units.tr: Gelotophyllis, growing in Bactria and around the Borysthenes, when drunk with myrrh and wine, shows various appearances, and laughter does not end unless one drinks the kernels of pine nuts with pepper and honey in palm wine.

units.la: Æthiopiden in Meroe crescentem hydropicos vtilissime bibere è mulso. Ophiusam in Elephantine Æthiopiæ conspicuam, potam, terrorem ac metum serpentū imprimere & quandoq; ex eo mortem, obque id sacrilegos cogi illam bibere: aduersari autem vinum palmeum.
units.tr: The Ethiopian plant growing in Meroe is most useful for dropsy when drunk in mulled wine. The ophiusa, conspicuous in Elephantine in Ethiopia, when drunk causes terror and fear of snakes, and sometimes death from it; for this reason sacrilegious people are forced to drink it. Palm wine, however, counteracts it.

units.la: Helianthe in Cilicię montibus maritimis cum adipe leonino decocta ac inuncta, corpus aspectu reddi iucundum ac venustum, Persarum Regibus in frequenti olim vsu.
units.tr: Helianthes boiled and smeared with lion's fat in the mountains of Cilicia by the sea make the body pleasing and attractive in appearance; this was once in frequent use among the kings of Persia.

units.la: Crocidis contactu phalangia mori.
units.tr: At the touch of the crocis, spiders die.

units.la: Oenotheridis è vino aspersu omnium animalium feritatem mitigari:
units.tr: The oenotheris, sprinkled with wine, softens the fierceness of all animals.

units.la: Herbam in capite statuę natam alligatam in lino russo, capitis dolores sedaie confestim.
units.tr: A herb that grows on a statue's head, tied in red linen, quickly relieves headaches.

units.la: Herbam quæ nascitur supra fimeta ruris, efficacissime pollere contra anginas ex aqua potam:
units.tr: The herb that grows on dunghills in the countryside is most effective against quinsy when drunk in water.

units.la: Contra summa veneficia pollere Moly laudatissimam herbarum Homero, circa Pheneū & in Cyllene Arcadiæ prouenientem : & Dodecatheon herbam omnibus mederi morbis aqua potam, quæ maximam etiam à Moly authoritatem obtinuit.
units.tr: Moly, the herb most praised by Homer, which grows near Pheneus and on Cyllene in Arcadia, is powerful against the strongest poisons; and the herb Dodecatheon, drunk in water, cures all diseases, and it has gained even greater authority than Moly.

units.la: Æthiopide amnes ac stagna siccari coniectu, tactu clausa omnia aperiri.
units.tr: By being thrown in, the Ethiopian plant dries up rivers and pools; by touch, it opens everything that is closed.

units.la: Achimenide coniecta in aciem hostium, trepidari agmina, ac terga vertere.
units.tr: When the achimenis is thrown into the enemy's battle line, the ranks tremble and turn their backs.

units.la: Latacen, à Persarum Rege dari solitam legatis, ut quocunq; venissent, omnium rerum copia abundarent. Æmi-
units.tr: Latace, which the King of the Persians was accustomed to give to envoys, so that wherever they went they would abound in every kind of goods. Aemi-

units.la: Æmilianum Scipionem Carthaginis patefecisse portas peculiari herba, & pontinas paludes Æthiopide siccatas antiquæ historiæ memorát: Et quis occulta naturæ insignia omnia attigerit? Quis vero causas hic explicare vnquam valuit? aut quæ saltem fuit coniectura omnia hæc experiundi? Verè numinis cuiusdam muneri hanc inuentionem acceptam ferunt naturæ Prudentes.
units.tr: The ancient histories record that Aemilius Scipio opened the gates of Carthage with a special herb, and that the Pontine marshes were dried up by the Ethiopian plant. And who has ever grasped all the hidden marvels of nature? Who has ever been able to explain their causes here? Or what conjecture, at least, led anyone to try all these things? Truly, the wise students of nature say that this discovery was received as a gift of some divinity.

units.la: Atqui ex hoc fundamento pendent quoq; Physicæ ligaturæ, vt cum præsentia adamantis Magnetis actionem, ne ferrum trahat, & oleū ne succinum paleas alliciat, sistit, cohibet & ligat. Quemadmodum igitur, si alterum cum altero conspicitur habere inimicitiam ad noxas, quas illud inferre posset, vsum eius esse posse veteres p remedio arbitrati sunt, in quo etiam successus fauit coniecturæ, sic in sympathiis occulti aliquid venerari licebit, quod ad aliquod malum amouendum vel expellendum vires habeat socias.
units.tr: Indeed, physical charms also depend on this foundation: when the presence of the magnet-adamant stops, restrains and binds the action by which it draws iron, and when oil keeps amber from attracting straws. Therefore, just as, if one thing is seen to have enmity with another regarding the harms that it could inflict, the ancients thought that its use could serve as a remedy, and in this the conjecture also met with success, so in sympathies it will be permitted to revere something hidden, which has allied powers for banishing or expelling some evil.

units.la: Et quidem herbarum cum astris, consensus admirandus spectatur quotidie. Euidentissimum Solaris præsentiæ testimonium & documentum præbent cichorij flores, Epaticis affectibus singulare remedium, qui Sole oriente se expandunt, eodem occidente se contrahunt.
units.tr: Indeed, the wonderful agreement of herbs with the stars is seen every day. The chicory flowers provide the clearest evidence and proof of the sun's presence; they are a unique remedy for liver complaints, opening when the sun rises and closing when it sets.

units.la: Lupinus quotidie cum Sole circumagitur, ita vt nubilo etiam cœlo agricolis horas monstret:sistret: similiter & malua motui se Solis accom‐modat. Pulegium in coronarijs florere ipso brumali die pleiadibus occiduis , quis non animaduertit ?
units.tr: The lupin is turned about with the sun every day, so that it shows the hours to farmers even under a cloudy sky; the mallow likewise adapts its movement to the sun's. That pennyroyal blooms in garlands on the very winter solstice day, when the Pleiades are setting, who has not noticed?

units.la: Veratrum nigrum adulterinum, flores cir‐ca Decembris finem in viridi flauescentes pro‐ferre,conspicuum omnibus est.
units.tr: It is plain to everyone that the false black hellebore produces flowers that turn from green to yellow around the end of December.

units.la: Laurum & ficum è cœlo nõ tangi, sicut nec vituli marini tergus,nec hyænæ pellem,nec vir‐tim albam autores non proletarij prodiderűt, quare nautæ iis vela muniunt, ne fulmine icta deflagrẽt atqȷ decidant. Hoc Octauius se mu‐niebat Augustus,Lauro Tiberius Cæsar,quam pro corona gestabat,ne vterqȷ scilicet tonitrű afflaretur,ɔ̃ solum enim contra fulminis im‐petum, verum ętiã aduersus fulminis ictű re‐torquentem habent naturam. Sed mirabilis est Sympathia illa inter metalla & diuinã vir‐gulam seu bifidum illum furculum ex corylo decīsum,quo metallarij venas auri argentique feraces explorant, frustra certe quis hic ad ma‐nifestas qnalitates confugerit.
units.tr: Authors who are not mere common writers have recorded that the laurel and the fig are not touched by lightning, nor is the hide of the sea calf, nor the skin of the hyena, nor the white virgin stone; therefore sailors protect their sails with these, so that they do not burn and fall when struck by lightning. Octavius Augustus protected himself with this, and Tiberius Caesar with the laurel, which he wore as a crown, so that, of course, neither would be struck by thunder; for these things have the nature not only of resisting the force of lightning, but also of turning back its stroke. But that sympathy between metals and the divining rod, or that two-pronged little fork cut from hazel, by which miners search out veins rich in gold and silver, is wonderful; certainly no one who seeks here to take refuge in manifest qualities would get anywhere.

units.la: Verum enim vero Orpheo, Theophrasto,& Proclo iudicibus,lapidibus longe efficacior cũ astris & spiritibus consensus est quam herbis, non astrorum enim nominibus , sed animis quoqȷ hominum imperitare videntur. Nam iaspis non modo sacrificia diis reddit accepta, sed Achates animos coniugum conciliat supplices voti quoq; reddit compotes. Et lapides virtutis astrorum consortio frui, nemo inficiabitur, qui ferreum compasti perpendiculum, cuius obtutu atq; inspectione nauclearis velificatio perficitur, magnete confricatum Septentrionalis poli stellam semper spectare animaduertit, & qui Selenitin lapidem ex Arabia candidum, pro Luna incremento crescere & decrescere obseruat.
units.tr: Indeed, in the judgment of Orpheus, Theophrastus and Proclus, the agreement of stones with the stars and spirits is far more effective than that of herbs; for they seem to rule not only by the names of the stars but also over the minds of men. For the jasper not only renders acceptable sacrifices to the gods, but the agate also wins the hearts of spouses and brings about the fulfilment of their prayers. And no one will deny that stones enjoy a share in the power of the stars, if he who has measured the iron plumb line, by whose sight and inspection the sailing of ships is carried out, observes that a magnet, when rubbed, always looks toward the star of the North Pole, and if he observes that the white Selenite stone from Arabia grows and wanes with the increase of the moon.

units.la: Turcosia gemma, quoties mutari, atq; expallescere, natiuoq; colore destitui conspicitur in gestante, vel languescente, vel valetudinario? Sed magis stupendum, quod imminens periculum coloris huius gemmæ in fuliginosum, vel serenissimi cœli contrarium mutatio, vel etiam maculæ alicuius aut fissuræ apparentia præsagire dicitur.
units.tr: When the Turkish gem is seen to change, to grow pale and to lose its natural colour, does this happen in its wearer when he is weak, languid or sick? But what is more astonishing is that a change of this gem's colour to smoky, or to something contrary to a most serene sky, or even the appearance of some spot or crack, is said to foretell an impending danger.

units.la: Smaragdum aduersus febres valere & venenum, autores non leuis autoritatis tradunt, imo frangi, si à veneno vincatur, rumpi quoq; in prima virginei pudoris excussione, ac quouis illegitimo coitu inquinari, nitoremque amittere, quo oculorū lassitudinem demulcere solebat. Deperit enim vis insita omnisq; nitor fordescit. Itaq; dubiū nullum est, inuisibilē latentemq; vim gemmas eiaculari atq; cuibrare. Licet enim sint res solida, calor tamen natiuus, & confricatio contactusque vim eliciunt, cordique ac cerebro illam communicant. Hanc vero astrorum & lapidum Sympathian, seu conuenientiam non puto quenquam fore qui ad manifestas qualitates sit relaturus, cum sint saltem vmbrae rerum, & instrumenta organaque naturae cuiusdam sublimioris ac præstantioris, præterea q; nec odores habeant, nec colores, similesq; potestates, vt ita iniurius sit in naturam iniusta ac fallaci quatuor qualitatum censura omnia explorare. Medicamenta quedam à similitudine prodesse, miroque modo à morbis liberare, quotidiana documenta testantur & experimenta, ob nullam causam aliam, quam quia vnũ alterius Anatomiam habet & signaturas. Atq; huc pertinet modus demonstrandi per similitudinem, quo sæpe summus rerū Creator diuinas ac occultas res solet patefacere, vt supremam idearum similitudinem referant atq; demonstrent.
units.tr: Authors of no small standing hand down that the emerald is effective against fevers and poison; indeed, that if it is overcome by poison it breaks, and it also breaks at the first loss of virginal modesty, and is stained by any illicit intercourse, and loses its lustre, by which it used to soothe weariness of the eyes. For its inherent power perishes and all its brightness grows foul. Therefore there is no doubt that gems send out and emit an invisible and hidden power. For although they are solid things, their native warmth, rubbing and contact nevertheless draw out their power and communicate it to the heart and brain. But I do not think anyone will be found who would refer this sympathy or agreement of stars and stones to manifest qualities, since they are at least shadows of things and the instruments and tools of a certain higher and more excellent nature; moreover, they have neither odours nor colours, nor powers of a similar kind, so that it would be unjust to the nature of things to examine everything by the unjust and deceptive judgment of the four qualities. That certain medicines benefit through likeness and deliver from diseases in a marvellous way, daily proofs and experiments testify, for no other cause than that one thing has the anatomy and signatures of another. And to this belongs the method of demonstrating by likeness, by which the supreme Creator of things often sets out to reveal divine and hidden matters, so that they may display and demonstrate the supreme likeness of the ideas.

units.la: Omnes enim herbæ, flores, arbores, aliaque ex terra nascentia sunt signa magica à Deo concessa, per quorum cognitionem ad veram medicinā id est, signatum peruenitur. Signa igitur quæ natura externe prodit, intrinsecæ cuiusdã aclarétis virtutis indicia sunt, semperq; signatum internusq; nucleus per externam physiognomiam designatur.
units.tr: For all herbs, flowers, trees and other things that grow from the earth are magical signs granted by God, and through knowledge of them one arrives at the true medicine, that is, at the thing signified. Therefore the signs which nature displays outwardly are indications of a certain inner and hidden virtue, and the thing signified, and the inner kernel, is always marked by its outward physiognomy.

units.la: Hinc multorum morborum curatio, quia promanant ab astrali impressione firmamenti maioris mundi, non promiscuis remediis perficienda ficienda est, sed per influentiam astronomi-cam, id est, per ea vel cum iis, quæ analogiam habent ad majorem & minorem mundum, in quibus est vera magnetica vis firmamenti, & impressio cœlestis morbis resistendi. Hanc influentiam ac signaturam à stellarum complexu ac radiis plantis quibusdam illis subjectis, videmus impressam, quæ in hyperico ne ac persicaria est evidentissima maximeq; conspicua, illud enim exilibus foraminibus perforatum, hæc foliis macula rubentibus, ac si gutta sanguinis super ea decidisset, cernitur.
units.tr: Hence the cure of many diseases, since they arise from the astral impression of the firmament of the greater world, is not to be accomplished with indiscriminate remedies, but through astronomical influence, that is, through those things which have an analogy to the greater and the lesser world, in which lies the true magnetic power of the firmament and the celestial impression that resists diseases. We see this influence and signature, impressed from the conjunction and rays of the stars on certain plants lying beneath them, most evident and most conspicuous in the hypericum and the persicaria: for the former is pierced with tiny holes, and the latter shows on its leaves reddish spots, as if a drop of blood had fallen upon it.

units.la: Ejusmodi quoq; signaturæ reperiuntur, in aro, dracunculo & aliis, morborum cognitioni maxime inservientes, ut ita non sufficiat Botanico naturasque herbarum investiganti, in externis signaturis acquiescere, hoc est, externa tantum plantarum vestimenta diversoria & habitationes describere, internum autem illud principium operandique virtutem, quæ est creatoris imago creaturis implantata, somnolento & noxio præterire silentio. Omnino enim necesse est, in rerum natura dari aliquid, in quo rosa latitet hieme, quod scilicet elementis utcunq; etiam modo corruptis, speciem signaturas inviolatas contineat, adque novorum individuorum procreationem servet incorruptas, alioquin novæ rerum species produci non possent. Id vero nihil aliud est quàm balsamum radicale, vitale, spirituale, Cœleste, actionum omnium in natura principium, cui vni & soli accepta sunt ferenda, quæ nec crasi elementariæ, nec sensui, nec manifestis qualitatibus assignari possunt & debent. Hoc enim in corruptionibus rerum non interit, sed elementis & mixtis qualicunq; etiam modo dissipatis, seruatur. Sic granum, quod terræ committitur, putrescit, resoluitur, perit, ac radicale balsamum seruatur, in quo totius seminis anatomia & potestas viget, nouaq; reuolutione in mundanum theatrum progrediens nouũ fabricat corpus officiis destinatis accommodatur. Hoc ipsum principium variis nominibus appellatur, ab aliis dicitur enim balsamus vniuersæ naturæ, sulphur vitale, radicale semen, materia prima, mumia balsamita. Delitescit autem non in alimentario quo perfunditur humore, nec in fæculentis & crassis sordibus, sed in excellentiori quadam humiditate deprehenditur, quoniam externis iniuriis impressionibusq; magna vi solet resistere, speciérumq; signaturas inuiolatas ad nouorum indiuiduorũ productionem conseruat. In animantibus & plantis vniuersam corporis anatomiam animalé hoc balsamum occupat, in certis tamen animantibus certam magis partem vt cor, proque diuersa impressione, tinctura & confluentia, proprietate, & differentiis diuersas quoq; producit citationes. Huius igitur balsami virtute plantæ quædam partesq; animalium morbis quibusdam antipatheticæ sunt, huius inquam balsami vi ac virtute, animalium quorundam partes, corporis humani partibus sunt sympatheticæ, iuuando illa, corroborando atq; in vigore radicali conseruando : testatum id facit medicamentum à me confectum, liquor scilicet ille potabilis, cordis vitæq; spiritibus gratissimus, debili memoriæ roborandæ, iudicioq; firmando, cerebro prætetea vertiginoso, paralytico, ac epileptico sanando, colicæ flatulentæ ac frigidæ, nec non podagricis chiragrisq; infirmitatibus & doloribus profligandis, (absit fucata iactantia, quotidianis enim experimentis id patefactum habetur & compertum, & testabuntur sanati) accommodatissimum. Hoc est medicamentum, cui præparando integra fere æstas danda est, omnis vulcanicæ violentiæ, corrosionis & malignitatis expers, constatq; ex merè vegetabilibus, animaliumq; quorundam partibus. Reperitur autem id ipsum quocunq; tempori apud me præparatum.
units.tr: Signatures of this kind are also found in the arum, the dracunculus and others, which are most useful for knowing diseases; so it is not enough for the botanist who investigates the natures of herbs to rest in external signatures, that is, merely to describe the outward coverings, varying forms and habitations of plants, while passing over in drowsy and idle silence that inner principle and power of operating, which is the image of the Creator implanted in creatures. For it is necessary that there be something in the nature of things in which the rose lies hidden in winter, something which, even when the elements have been corrupted in some way, keeps the outward signatures of its form uninjured and preserves them unimpaired for the production of new individuals; otherwise new kinds of things could not be produced. This is nothing other than the radical, vital, spiritual and heavenly balsam, the principle of all actions in nature, to which alone these powers are to be attributed, and which cannot and should not be assigned to elemental mixture, to sense, or to manifest qualities. For this does not perish in the corruptions of things, but is preserved when the elements and mixed bodies are dissipated in any way whatever. Thus the grain committed to the earth rots, dissolves and perishes, and yet the radical balsam is preserved, in which the whole anatomy and power of the seed flourishes, and, proceeding in a new revolution into the theatre of the world, it fashions a new body fitted to the functions appointed for it. This principle itself is called by various names: by some it is called the balsam of the whole of nature, vital sulphur, radical seed, prime matter, balsamic mummy. Now it lies hidden not in the nourishing moisture by which it is bathed, nor in the dregs and thick filth, but is found in a certain more excellent moisture, because it is accustomed to resist external injuries and impressions with great force, and preserves the signatures of the species unviolated for the production of new individuals. In animals and plants this animal balsam occupies the whole anatomy of the body, though in certain animals it occupies a particular part more, such as the heart; and according to different impressions, tincture, confluence, property and differences, it also produces diverse motions. Therefore by the virtue of this balsam certain plants and parts of animals are antipathetic to certain diseases; and by the power and virtue of this balsam, I say, parts of certain animals are sympathetic to parts of the human body, helping them, strengthening them and preserving them in radical vigour. The medicine prepared by me bears witness to this: that potable liquor, most welcome to the spirits of the heart and of life, suitable for strengthening a weak memory and firming judgment, and also for curing the brain of vertigo, paralysis and epilepsy, and for banishing colic, flatulent and cold, as well as the disorders and pains of gout and chiragra (let there be no feigned boasting; for it is known and proved by daily experiments, and those who have been healed will bear witness). This is the medicine for which almost a whole summer must be given to its preparation; it is free from all the violence, corrosion and malignity of volcanic fire, and it consists purely of vegetables and certain parts of animals. This same medicine is found prepared by me at any time.

units.la: Ac licet quidam hoc meum inuentum, superciliosa quadam fatuitate sibi omnia tribuentes sint derisuri, aliis persuadentes, non posse Hippocratis aut Galeni assecias, nisi ex Paracelsico aut Lullianio commentario sapere, malo tamen ἐν πυρὶ &experimento cum omnibus iis, qui eo ad nominis Diuini celebrationem, & dictorum morborum profligationem utuntur, & usuri sunt, acquiescere, quam blandis ac bracteatis, ut illi faciunt, verborum lenociniis, mundum decipere. Sed ad priora. Hoc igitur radicale principium, has inquam rerum signaturas qui neglexerit, nec intimius inspexerit atq; cognoverit, medici nomen non meretur. Et certe si per nihil aliud, hujus tamen mysterii cognitione admirabilis in sua arte evadit medicus, quod Hippocrates de iis pronunciat, qui morituros & salvandos praenoverint.
units.tr: Although some people, with a certain haughty foolishness that claims everything for themselves, will mock my discovery and persuade others that one cannot understand Hippocrates or Galen without the Paracelsian or Lullian commentaries, I would rather agree, "by fire [ἐν πυρί]," with all those who use this remedy, and will use it, for the glory of the divine name and the cure of the said diseases, than deceive the world with the flattering and gilded verbal charms that those others employ. But to return to what came first. Whoever neglects this radical principle, these signatures of things I mean, and has not examined and understood them more deeply, does not deserve the name of physician. And certainly, even if for nothing else, the physician becomes admirable in his art through knowledge of this mystery, in the sense that Hippocrates speaks of those who foreknow who will die and who will be saved.

units.la: Morbos singulos habere sua signa morborum cognitioni inservientia, negari non debet, eademq; quoq; signa reperiri in remediis a natura ita signatis, ut in totum & vere dixisse liceat, hic morbus est hujus remedii morbus, & hoc remedium est hujus morbi remedium, ut tussilago est remedium obstructi pulmonis, quia gerit ejusdem signa, lingua cervina & scolopendrium infarcti & tumefacti splenis remedium sunt, quia splenis exhibent signaturam. Unde apparet, ex signis remediorum naturas cognosci posse, Sympathiasq; ac antipathias mysterium, tum rerum tum qualitatum medico maximo esse emolumento, proindeq; secretioris ejusmodi philosophiae peritos, sagaces que rerum naturalium exploratores admirandas actiones posse producere.
units.tr: It cannot be denied that each disease has its own signs that serve the recognition of the disease, and that the same signs are found in remedies which nature has so marked that one may say, wholly and truly: this disease is the disease of this remedy, and this remedy is the remedy of this disease. Thus coltsfoot is the remedy for a blocked lung, because it bears the same signs; hart's tongue and spleenwort are remedies for an obstructed and swollen spleen, because they display the signature of the spleen. From this it appears that the natures of things can be known from the signs of remedies, and that the mystery of sympathies and antipathies, both of things and of qualities, is of great advantage to the physician; and therefore those skilled in this more secret kind of philosophy, and sagacious investigators of natural things, can produce admirable effects.

units.la: Et quoniam modus ut in aliis non utique manifestus est ac evidens, sed occultatus, miraculosarum illarum actionum causam dæmonum præstigiis ascribunt imperitiores, tali sc. Magiæ,quæ Goëtia dicitur, àluctu, & dæmoniaca,est enim malorum spirituum iuxta sepulcra invocatio, cujus germana soror est Necromantia, quæ ad vocandos defunctorum manes sanguinem humanum, quo dæmones effuso delectantur, vel saltem nigri pecoris cruorem requirit.
units.tr: And since the mode of these actions, as in other cases, is not plainly manifest and evident but hidden, the less learned ascribe the cause of those miraculous actions to the tricks of demons, namely to that magic called goëtia, which is of lamentation and demonic, for it is the invocation of evil spirits near the tombs. Its true sister is necromancy, which in order to summon the shades of the dead requires human blood, in which demons delight, or at least the blood of a black animal.
