So all those bodies between which there is sympathy and antipathy act on one another mutually and perform their operations without any visible contact; that is, the power of one is conveyed to the other through the intervening Spirit, so that, however great the space, it is not dissipated by the winds nor seized and shaken by the vast, moist or cold air without any alteration, but is preserved and continued by natural communion, likeness and bond.

units.la: Sic in contagionibus quoq; nullus fit contactus corporum, vt in certo lippitudinis genere afficiuntur oculi illorum qui lippum intuentur, item grassantibus febribus pestilentialibus multi inficiuntur, qui ad ægrotos nunquam accesserunt, hoc est, quorum extrema nunquam fuerunt simul: maligna enim & putrida istarum febrium qualitas corpora contaminat propagando se diffundendo & continuando. Itaque qui alium morbo inquinat, non necessario eundem tangit, nam putridum halitum vaporemq;
units.tr: So too in contagions there is no contact of bodies: thus in a certain kind of inflammation of the eyes, the eyes of those who look upon the inflamed are affected; likewise when pestilential fevers are raging, many are infected who never approached the sick, that is, whose extremities were never together. For the malignant and putrid quality of these fevers contaminates bodies by spreading, diffusing and continuing itself. So he who infects another with a disease does not necessarily touch him in the same way.

units.la: NB. temq; in pannum vestemue aliquam (in his enim & similibus seminarium contagii sæpè delitescere experimentis patefactum est) expirans, qui postea aliû multos dies post inficit, nõ rectè dicitur infectum sic contaminatumq; tetigisse, cum nihilominus tamen citra dubium affirmari possit, morbos de homine vno ad alium non transfire absque corpore aliquo, id est non transportari absq; fauore seu spiritu vel humore. Ac spirituales qualitates hîc plurimû valent. Licet enim secundum modum & existentiam, quæ existunt, per se actionem corpoream non edant: per accidens tamen nihil prohibet, quo minus per medium idoneum propagetur, quod medium nihil est aliud quam spiritus vaporue mediæ cuiusdam inter corporatas & incorporatatas substantias naturæ, qui spirituales actiones in se recipiat, aërique repræsentet, cum sit corporeus, contactu suo realiter alteret.
units.tr: NB. ...and the vapour, breathed out into a cloth or some garment (for it has often been shown by experiment that the seed of contagion lurks in such things and similar ones), which afterwards infects many others for many days, is not rightly said to have touched the infected and so contaminated person; yet it can be affirmed beyond doubt that diseases do not pass from one man to another without some body, that is, they are not transported without a vapour, spirit or moisture. And spiritual qualities here count for very much. For although, according to their mode and existence, they do not by themselves produce a bodily action, yet nothing prevents them, per accidens, from being propagated through a suitable medium; and this medium is nothing else than a spirit or vapour of a certain intermediate nature between corporeal and incorporeal substances, which receives spiritual actions into itself, represents them to the air, and, since it is corporeal, really alters by its contact.

units.la: Vnde verissimum euadit, multas esse actiones, ad quas non sit opus eo, qui vere & solus contactus est, cum in se mutuam actionem exercent corpora multa, quæ sunt simul non per contactum corporis, sed virtutis, estque hæc virtus, quam per intervalla exercent corpora, effunduntque, qualitas corporis expers, in qua sola inest efficacitas. Sic vis ex vnguento exiens effundit se non in lapidem, ferrum vel lignum, quibus cum nullam habet coniunctionem, sed virtute motoris ad vulnus se propagat.
units.tr: Hence it turns out most truly that there are many actions for which no contact is needed, in the strict and only sense of contact, since many bodies exert a mutual action on one another while they are together, not by contact of body but by virtue; and this virtue, which bodies exert and pour out across intervals, is a quality free of body, in which alone efficacy resides. So the power that issues from the ointment pours itself not into stone, iron or wood, with which it has no conjunction, but propagates itself to the wound by the virtue of the mover.

units.la: Primum enim mouens in vnguento est vis balsamica in sanguine & vsnea, quae mediante spirituali vinculo ad vulnus vsque continuatur, & nisi intercapedo sit nimia, fiunt vnum per vtriusque formae coniunctionem, coniunguntur inquam, quia formae se ipsas propagant & promouent, ita vt etiam egredientes in media intercapedine mutuo occursu vniantur. Simul igitur sunt mouens & quod mouetur, ita vt vel secundum immediatam superficierum applicationem se contingant, vel vt vnius virtus ad superficiem alterius, atque ita in corpus alterius deducatur, siue id fiat lumine, siue radiis, siue qualitate occultiore & contactu spirituali. Quare vnguentum attingit vulnus seu coniungitur vulneri, vt efficiens & agens patienti, seu vt causa transmutans alteransque corpori transmutando, quo etiam modo coelum coniungitur terrae, quae tamen secundum superficiem illi non est contigua, hoc est extrema coeli & terrae se non contingunt, vt ita verissimum sit, agentia longo saepe interuallo diuulsa esse ab iis quae patiuntur, vt si quis eminus videt hostem, etsi hic vicissim illum non videat, repente tamen commouetur, expallescit, trepidatque & contremiscit, qui certe moti sanimimi mi ab externo agente, à specie hostis obiecti ob oculo recepta, & ad sensum interiorem delata, in mentem primum, ab ea in corpora deinde deriuatur, agensq; longo interuallo à patiente est diuulsum, vnde spiritualis hic & insensilis actio est, non realis operatio.
units.tr: For the first mover in the ointment is the balsamic power in the blood and the unguent, which, by means of a spiritual bond, is continued all the way to the wound; and unless the interval is too great, they become one through the conjunction of the two forms. They are conjoined, I say, because the forms propagate and promote themselves, so that even as they go out they unite in the middle interval by their mutual meeting. The mover and what is moved are therefore together, so that they touch either by the immediate application of their surfaces, or by the power of the one reaching the surface of the other and so being conveyed into the body of the other, whether this happens by light, by rays, or by some more hidden quality and spiritual contact. Hence the ointment touches the wound, or is joined to the wound, as agent to patient, or as a cause transforming and altering the body by transforming it; in the same way heaven is joined to earth, although by its surface it is not contiguous with it; that is, the extremities of heaven and earth do not touch. So it is most true that agents are often separated by a long interval from what they affect: as when someone sees an enemy from afar, and although the enemy does not see him in return, he is suddenly moved, grows pale, trembles and shakes. Certainly he is moved by an external agent, by the image of the hostile object received by the eye and carried to the inner sense, first into the mind and then from there derived into the body; and the agent is separated from the patient by a long interval. Hence this is a spiritual and imperceptible action, not a real physical operation.

units.la: Itaq; mouens cum re mota simul est, intelligi debet de agente proximo, hoc enim semper simul est cum remota, vt sunt imaginatio & Spiritus, id quod in titillatione quoq; constat, q; sæpè fit sine contactu & attrectatione, & nihilominus tamen mouens & motum simul esse recte dicuntur, scilicet per contactum internum occultum, qui fit vi spirituum ab imaginatione impulsorum, partesq; illas, quæ titillationem perpeti possunt, ferientium, est enim motus illorum celeberrimus. Ex his quis non intelligit, falsas in physica positiones esse generaliter acceptas, 1. agentium & patientium extrema se semper contingunt. 2. Non est vis aliqua agentis in patiens, nisi illud hoc secundum extrema & superficiem contingat. Qualitas enim seu virtus cœlestis & magnetica mediante spiritu istius deductionis directionisque in unguento causa est & quasi vehiculum, quo moto res vecta mouetur similiter, nam in vehiculo requiritur, vt sit aptum ad vehendum, ad vehendum autem aptissima virtus est magnetica cœlestis, quæ quasi interuenit & interiicitur inter ter telum obligatum& vulneratum locum,mo uetq; seu dirigit vim ad effectum consequen-dum. Et qui ignorat vel negat, virtutem quan-dam ætheris naturis elementarib. à cœlo com-municatam ( quam Astrologiæ periti dicunt formas earum complere & absoluere) qua me-diante vis ac proprietas quarundam naturarū formis implantetur, ac inter se Corpora con-nectantur atq; cohæreant,& ab hoc ordine ne-xuq; similitudinis naturalis ortum esse, indeq; mirandarum actionum causas eruendas, is in toto hoc mysterio plane cæcutit. Inter virtu-tem enim & vehiculum primo sympathia est, quæ posteà deducitur transitque in telum, de-hinc in vulnus ob familiaritatem & similitudi-nem, hæc enim efficiens causa est, vt res inui-cem vinciantur. Vnde inter telum obligatum & vulnus contactum fieri nemo inficiaturus est, licet is non fiat immediate extremis simul, & tangat quod remotum est primum, id enim in hoc mysterio necesse non est,cum enim prin-cipiorum hic actio corporea non sit, cōtactum corporeum etiam requiri opus non est. Vis e-nim seu virtus peruenit ad vulnus mediate, non per dæmonem,sed interuentu, vt dictum est, virtutis cuiusdā sublimioris & incorporeæ, quàm Magiæ naturalis Doctores magneticam rectè appellitarunt. Impostoria igitur sa-natio non est, Magica tamen. Impostores enim verè sunt, qui omne magicum dicunt su-perstitiosum impostorium.
units.tr: Therefore the moving thing is at the same time with the thing moved, and this must be understood of the proximate agent, for that is always simultaneous with the remote one, as imagination is with the spirit. This is also clear in tickling, which often happens without contact or touching, and yet the mover and the moved are rightly said to be together, namely through a hidden internal contact, which comes about by the force of the spirits driven by the imagination and striking those parts that can feel tickling, for their motion is very rapid. From these points, who does not see that the positions in physics commonly accepted are false? (1) The extremities of agents and patients always touch one another. (2) There is no force of an agent upon a patient unless the one touches the other at the extremities and surface. For a celestial quality or virtue, through the spirit of this drawing and direction, is the cause in the ointment and, as it were, its vehicle, which, when moved, moves the thing carried along. For in a vehicle it is required that it be fit for carrying, and the most fit virtue for carrying is the celestial magnetic virtue, which intervenes and is interposed, as it were, between the weapon that is bound and the wounded place, and moves or directs its force to bring about the effect. Whoever does not know or denies that a certain virtue of the ether, communicated from the heavens to the natural elements (which those skilled in astrology say completes and perfects their forms), by means of which the force and property of certain natures are implanted in forms, and bodies are connected and cohere with one another, and that from this order and natural bond of likeness the origin arises, and from it the causes of wonderful actions are to be drawn out, is quite blind in the whole of this mystery. For between the virtue and the vehicle there is first a sympathy, which is afterwards drawn down and passes into the weapon, and then into the wound, on account of familiarity and likeness, for this is the efficient cause by which the things are bound to one another. Hence no one will deny that contact takes place between the bound weapon and the wound, even though it does not happen immediately at the extremities together, and does not touch what is remote first; for in this mystery that is not necessary, since the action of these principles is not corporeal, so bodily contact need not be required either. For the force or virtue reaches the wound mediately, not through a demon, but by the intervention, as has been said, of a certain more sublime and incorporeal virtue, which the teachers of natural magic have rightly called magnetic. The healing is therefore not imposture, but it is magical. For those are truly impostors who say that everything magical is superstitious imposture.

units.la: Ad extremum ipsius vnguenti descriptio-nem & compositionem placuit subiicere, vt nemo non intelligat, ex mere naturalibus re-bus & quidem ipso homine id componi: Baptista Porta l. 8. c. 12. id describit, refettq; ad auto-rem Paracelsum, quem tamen huius illustrato-rem amplificatoremque extitisse tantum, non autorem reperio.
units.tr: Finally, I have thought fit to add the description and composition of the ointment, so that no one fails to understand that it is compounded from purely natural things, and indeed from the human body itself. Baptista Porta describes it in book 8, chapter 12, and refers it to the author Paracelsus, though I find that he was only the illustrator and amplifier of it, and not its author.

units.la: Rec. vesnæ concretæ in caluaria furis suspen-si & in aëre derelicti.
units.tr: Take moss grown on the skull of a hanged thief and left exposed to the air.

units.la: Mumiæ veræ;
units.tr: True mummy.

units.la: Sanguinis humani adhuc calentis sing. vnc. vnam.
units.tr: One ounce of human blood, still warm.

units.la: Adipis humani vnc. ij.
units.tr: Two ounces of human fat.

units.la: Ol. linij.
units.tr: Linseed oil.

units.la: Terebinthin.
units.tr: Turpentine.

units.la: Boli armen. sing. ʒ ij.
units.tr: Two drachms of Armenian bole.

units.la: Miscceantur omnia simul in mortario, seruen-turq; in vitro vel vrna oblonga & angusta.
units.tr: Let all these be mixed together at once in a mortar, and kept in a glass or long, narrow urn.

units.la: Alii, recipiunt vineam abrasam è cranio ho-minis violentâ morte perempti, duarum auel-lanarum pondere:
units.tr: Others take moss scraped from the skull of a man who died a violent death, the weight of two hazelnuts:

units.la: Adipis verris aprugni,
units.tr: Fat of a wild boar,

units.la: Vrsini sing. vncias vj.
units.tr: of a bear, six ounces each,

units.la: Lumbricorum terr. ex vino lotorum, inque Pistoris fornace ollâ tecta torrefacto-rum rum (non adustorum) vnc. iij. horum in pul-uerem redactorum vnciæ vni adiiciunt
units.tr: earthworms washed in wine and roasted in a baker's oven in a covered pot (not burnt), three ounces; of these, reduced to powder, they add one ounce

units.la: Cerebri aprugni siccati,
units.tr: of dried brain of a wild boar,

units.la: Santali rubri odorati, mumiæ & hæmatitis, fingul. vnc. j. omnibusque mixtis cum adipe faciunt vnguentum. Hæc descriptio optima esset, si succo & neruis, hoc est, sanguine & adi-pe humano, (in quibus maximè dominatur Spiritus ille vitalis, vegetabilis & balsamicus) non careret. Itaq; in vera huius vnguenti compositione sanguis & adeps humanus non sunt omittenda, quo etiam modo confecтum apud me quouis vt tempore possit haberi (quoniam Chirurgi sæpè vel non sunt præsentes, vel etiam à vulnerato remotiores) nunc operam impendo, quantam possum.
units.tr: of red scented sandalwood, mummy and haematite, one ounce each; and when all are mixed with the fat, they make the ointment. This description would be excellent, if it did not lack the juice and sinews, that is, human blood and fat, in which that vital, vegetative and balsamic spirit especially prevails. Therefore in the true composition of this ointment, human blood and fat must not be omitted. I am now devoting as much effort as I can to having it made in such a way that it can be kept by me at any time (since surgeons are often either not present or even further away from the wounded man).

units.la: Conficiendum a. est Sole existente in libra, vsnea vero colligetur cum Luna crescente, inq; Veneris existente domo, si fieri potest, non Martis aut Saturni. Si in Veneris domo locum habere Luna non potest, diligenter attende, vt possit abradi vsnea Luna versante in piscibus, hoc enim signum est omnium conuenientissimum propter Iovis domicilium, & Veneris exaltationem, proximum huic est taurus & libra.
units.tr: It must be prepared while the Sun is in Libra, but the moss is to be gathered while the Moon is waxing, and when Venus is in her house, if that can be done, and not when Mars or Saturn is. If the Moon cannot be in Venus's house, take care to scrape the moss while the Moon is in Pisces, for this is the most suitable sign of all because of the house of Jupiter and the exaltation of Venus; next to this are Taurus and Libra.

units.la: Sanantur hoc vnguento sic confecto omnia vulnera, quæ ferro, ictu vel iactu infligun-tur, modo haberi possit instrumentum. Excipi-untur untur tamen illa vulnera, quæ fiunt in arteriis, & vno è membris principalioribus, vt corde, cerebro, &c.
units.tr: All wounds inflicted by iron, by a blow or by a throw, are healed by this ointment prepared in this way, provided that the instrument can be had. Those wounds are excepted, however, which are made in the arteries and in one of the principal members, such as the heart, the brain, and so on.

units.la: Immergendum autem ferrum seu telum est quod sauciauit (vel in huius defectu lignum, seu ramus salignus in apertura cruenta madefactus) in vnguentum, & ita relinquendum: æger quotidie suâ vrina vel purâ aqua vulnus eluat, deligatq; mundo panno lineo, semper pus extergendo vulnusque aurora qualibet mundificando & absq; vllo dolore sanabitur, Hoc Maximilianum Imp. comprobasse in confesso est. Si instrumentum, quo vulnus inflictum est, haberi nequit, aliud ducatur per vulnus, & loco veri teli id inunge vtroque latere, reponatur loco mundo & temperato, si enim aëri vel frigori nimio exponatur, excitabitur dolor. Attendendum est etiam, cæsimne an punctim factum sit vulnus. In punctura enim telum inungendum est à cuspide capulam versus, in cæsura ab acie versus tergum. Meminisse præterea oportet obligare tela. Si non apparet quam alte sint infixa, tota sunt inungenda, sint apparet, pars illa tantum, quæ fuit in vulnere. Cito sanaturus sæpè illine (præsertim vero si vulnus est magnum & profundum) si maturatione opus non est; necessitasque non urget, intermitti quidam dies poterunt, imo sufficit, si senis diebus id fiat bis, vel ad summum ter, semper tamen vulnus mane abluendo, ex- tergendo, iterumq; deligando.
units.tr: The iron or weapon that wounded must be immersed in the ointment (or, if that is lacking, a stick or willow twig soaked in the bloody opening), and left there in that way. The patient should wash the wound each day with his own urine or with pure water, and bind it with a clean linen cloth, always wiping away the pus and cleansing the wound at dawn; and it will be healed without any pain. That this has been approved by Emperor Maximilian is beyond dispute. If the instrument with which the wound was inflicted cannot be had, another is to be drawn through the wound, and the true weapon is to be anointed with it on both sides, and it is to be placed in a clean and temperate place; for if it is exposed to air or to excessive cold, pain will be aroused. One must also attend to whether the wound was made by a cut or by a puncture. For in a puncture the weapon is to be anointed from the point toward the hilt, in a cut from the edge toward the back. It is also necessary to remember to bind the weapons. If it does not appear how deeply they are fixed, the whole must be anointed; if it does appear, only that part which was in the wound. If you wish to heal quickly, anoint often (especially if the wound is large and deep); if there is no need for hastening and no necessity presses, some days may be left out; indeed, it is enough if this is done twice in seven days, or at most three times, always, however, washing and wiping the wound in the morning and binding it again.

units.la: Ad extremum de vsnea non est consensus: alii petitam eam enim volunt ex capite strangulati, alii parum referre aiunt, siue sit ex strangulati, siue ex alterius cuiusdam capite. Verum cur ex strangulati potius quàm alterius cuiusdam capite vsnea petenda, causas adhuc à nemine scripto explicatas atq; allatas vidi. Ego qui tamen aliorum eruditorum iudicio hic me subiicio, hanc afferri rationem posse existimo, quod in strangulando, spiritus vitales ob praesentiam mali praesentis in caput ac cerebrū refugiant, unde quia regressus illis ob violentam illam constrictionem ad principium suum non patet, remanere eos, & cum spiritibus balsamoque capitis ac cerebri misceri ac confundi necesse est. Et licet omnes functiones animales intereant, manet tamen calor ille in ossibus, neruis, aliisq; partibus similaribus, qui & in lapide est, & pipere emortuo, &c. elementalis. His ita commixtis in balsamico sanguine, vi caloris circumfusi ambientisq; humorem vitâ imbuentis, coeliq; influxu cooperante, vsneam ceu vegetabili quadam vi & virtute in caluaria tandem progenerari verisimilimū est, maioris potentiae, quam est ea, quae in alterius cuiusdam ex morbo defuncti capite reperitur. In decollatis spiritus non retineri, sed diffugere, eua- nes. hescere ac dissipari omnibus in confesso est.
units.tr: Finally, there is no agreement about the moss: some want it taken from the skull of a hanged man, others say it matters little whether it comes from a hanged man or from the skull of some other person. But I have seen no one who has yet written and set out the reasons why the moss should be taken from a hanged man rather than from the skull of some other person. I, however, who submit myself here to the judgment of other learned men, think this reason can be offered: that in strangling, the vital spirits, because of the presence of the present evil, flee into the head and brain; and since their way back to their source is not open to them on account of that violent constriction, they must remain there and be mixed and confused with the spirits and balsam of the head and brain. And although all the animal functions perish, that heat remains in the bones, sinews and other similar parts, which is also elemental, as it is in stone and in dead pepper, and so on. With these things thus mixed in the balsamic blood, by the force of the surrounding heat and of the moisture that surrounds and imbues it with life, and with the cooperating influence of the heavens, it is most probable that the moss, by a certain vegetable force and virtue, is at last generated in the skull, of greater power than that which is found in the head of some other person who died of disease. It is agreed by all that in beheaded men the spirits are not retained, but flee away, evaporate and are dissipated.

units.la: De mumia intellige non vulgatam illam in Seplasiariorum taberna vbiq; fere prostantem, quæ nihil aliud est quam arefacta cadauerum conditorum caro, non autem eorum infarctus & liquor ex carne humana manans. Perperam etiam faciunt Seplasiarii, qui carnes ossaque contusa medicamentis Mumiæ necessariis commiscent.
units.tr: On mumia, understand not that common stuff which is hawked almost everywhere in the apothecaries' shops, which is nothing other than the dried flesh of embalmed corpses, and not their marrow and the liquor that flows from human flesh. The apothecaries also act wrongly when they mix crushed flesh and bones with the medicines required for mumia.

units.la: Itaq; vt legitima mumia haberi possit, in penuria Ægyptiacæ & Arabicæ, quæ concinnabatur ex myrrha, aloe, croco, ballamo, aliisque pretiosis odoramentis, in hospitalibus nostris cadauera obeuntium aloë, myrrha, croco, & aliis ad eam idoneis rebus, replenda sunt & imbuenda, idoneoque tempore eximenda, & ad vsus custodienda, hanc enim plurimis pollere facultatibus, præter experientiam grauissimi autores tradiderunt. Sed de Mumiæ viribus compertis aliâs plura.
units.tr: Therefore, so that genuine mumia may be had, since there is a shortage of Egyptian and Arabian mumia, which used to be made from myrrh, aloe, saffron, balsam and other precious perfumes, the bodies of those who die in our hospitals must be filled and steeped with aloe, myrrh, saffron and other things suitable for this purpose, and then taken out at a suitable time and kept for use. For the most serious authors have handed down that this mumia possesses very many powers, apart from experience. But more about the proven powers of mumia elsewhere.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: FINIS.

units.la: TRACTATVS ALTER DE LVXVRIOSIS CONVIVIIS NOstri seculi.
units.tr: Second Treatise on the Luxurious Banquets of Our Age.

units.la: VIX puto quenquam fore qui existimet, aut ostentatione aliquâ me adductum, aut fiduciâ ingenii ad dicendum in hoc celeberrimo congressu accessisse: abhorret enim ab vtroque natura & genius: Nam si in minimis rebus ostentatio reprehenditur, quo tandem odio dignus essem, si quem admodum Phormio apud Hannibalem de re militari declamauit, sic ego apud vos doctrina & eloquentia praestantes, inepte aliquid ostentando meam importunitatem in theatrum producerem. Sed quoniam officii ratio mihi hoc loco & tempore dicendi necessitatem imponit, humaniter à vobis peto, vt pro vestra pietate & candore qualemcunq; orationem, mensesab hinc quatuor plus minus, commentari à me coeptam boni consulatis : CoColophonem huic adiicere, intercurrentes quidam strepitus musas meas interturbantes tunc non sinebant: Nunc vero non sine labo-re ad finem eam perduxi, luce etiam tandem donandam. Etsi autem hic locus postulat, ut eas artes & doctrinas, in quibus explicandis versor,ornem & prædicem, tamen cum de iis ab aliis, eloquentiâ excellentibus, splendidè & copiosè dictum sit, sumpsi aliud argumentum huic tempori conuenientissimum; quando-quidem ad nos redierūt dies bacchanaliorum, qui apud Ethnicos fuerunt hominum aut si-mulantium furores, aut ebrietate insanienti-um; qui ad portentosas atq; monstrificas hel-luationes ac conmessationes instistuuntur, sola simulatione insaniæ & repræsentatione gestus bacchantium: horum inquam recordatio, & memoriæ similiumq; monstrificarum baccha-tionum, quibus nostrum seculum se contami-nauit,celebratio, in hanc potissimum me sen-tentiam adduxit, ut de luxus in conuiuiis origi-ne & primis autoribus ex hoc loco ornatissimo quædam dicere non erubescerem: idq; eo fa-cio lubentius in hoc consessu, quoniam scio vos de eo seuerè & verissimè censuram ferre posse:nullæ hic sunt nugæ: nihil monstrosum, fabulosum nihil, neque item insulsæ traditio-nes, haustæ ex fæce quorundam tribulariorum scriptorum,sed ex autoribus Græcis pariter at-que que Latinis percelebribus atq; perueteribus: rem tradam corporis non modo saluti, sed animæ quoque non parum conferentem: ipsa rerum grauitas atque varietas fastigium vestrum propulsabit, attentioresque vos reddet: de primo & postea vario gentium victu & quibusdam prisci seculi insanæ gulæ irritamentis, quæ ganeosorum portentosa ingenia excogitarunt, magna mehercule naturæ iniuriâ, si considerate dicenti auscultaueritis, non improbabitis scio institutum meum, dicendiq; occasionem, propterea quod confuse hæc & intercisè tractata conscriptaq;, apud priscos autores inueniantur. Meæ institutæ orationis hic erit ordo. Primò dicam de prima mortalium & postea vario gentium victu, tum de prodigioso conuiuiorum apparatu & celsis luxuriæ fastigiis: quæ singula dum pertracto, rogo vt perbenignè me audiatis & cum silentio.
units.tr: I think no one will suppose that I have come to speak in this most distinguished assembly either led by some display or relying on my own talent, for both my nature and my disposition shrink from such things. For if display is blamed even in trifling matters, how deserving of hatred would I be if, like Phormio who once lectured Hannibal on the art of war, I were to put my own presumption on show by foolishly parading before you, who excel in learning and eloquence. But since the duty of my office and the occasion of this place and time lay the necessity of speaking upon me, I courteously ask you, in your kindness and fairness, to accept with good will whatever oration this is, which I began to prepare about four months ago. I wanted to add a colophon to it, but certain disturbing noises interrupted my Muses and would not allow it then. Now at last I have brought it to an end with considerable effort, and it is at length to be given to the light. Although this place requires that I praise and proclaim the arts and sciences with which I am concerned, still, since others, excelling in eloquence, have spoken of them splendidly and fully, I have taken up another subject, most fitting to this time. For the days of the Bacchanalia have returned to us, which among the heathen were days of men either pretending to be mad or raving in drunken frenzy, who went in for monstrous and prodigious gluttony and drinking bouts, with nothing but a pretence of madness and the acting out of the gestures of Bacchants. This recollection, I say, and the celebration of the memory of similar monstrous Bacchic revels, with which our age has defiled itself, has led me chiefly to this purpose: that I would not be ashamed to say something, from this most distinguished place, about the origin of luxury at banquets and its first originators. I do this the more willingly in this gathering, since I know you can pass a strict and most accurate judgment on it. There is no nonsense here: nothing monstrous, nothing fabulous, nor again any silly traditions drawn from the dregs of certain hack writers, but taken from Greek and Latin authors alike, both very famous and very ancient. I shall relate a matter that contributes not a little not only to the health of the body but also to the soul. The very weight and variety of the subject will carry your attention forward and make you more attentive. Concerning the first and afterwards the varied diet of peoples, and certain incitements of the insane gluttony of the old age, which the monstrous minds of gluttons devised, to the great injury of nature, I think, if you listen to me attentively as I speak, you will not disapprove of my plan and of the occasion for speaking, because these matters are found in the ancient authors treated and written down in a confused and fragmentary way. The order of my oration will be this. First I shall speak of the earliest diet of mortals and afterwards of the varied diet of peoples, then of the prodigious array of banquets and the lofty heights of luxury. As I deal with each of these, I ask that you hear me most kindly and in silence.

units.la: Primò constat, victum mortalium, eruditissimorum iudicio, quibusdam gradibus distinctum fuisse, quibus à summa rusticitate vel potius feritate ad humaniorem primò deuentum sit, postremò ad summa luxus culmina.
units.tr: First, it is agreed, by the judgment of the most learned, that the diet of mortals was divided into certain stages, by which people advanced from the greatest rusticity, or rather savagery, first to a more humane condition, and finally to the highest peaks of luxury.

units.la: Primum hominum genus, vt feræ in syluis & nemoribus versabatur: conueniq; inter omnes, glandiferas bacciferasque arbores mortales tunc præcipuè aluisse, nutricesque extitisse feræ ac inopis illius sortis.
units.tr: The first kind of men lived like wild beasts in the forests and groves; and it is agreed among all that mortals of that time were chiefly nourished by acorn- and berry-bearing trees, and that the wild beasts served as their nurses, in that poor condition.

units.la: Deinde ex hac vita in secundam descende-runt, pastoritiam scilicet, etenim ex animalibus ob eandem vtilitatem syluestria deprehende-tunt atque mansuefecerunt, inter quae primum oues assumtas esse autumant, propter placi-tatem, aptissimae enim sunt ad vitam hominū, ad cibos, caseum simul ac butyrum, ad corpo-ris vero tutelam & vestitum vellera adhibue-runt.
units.tr: Then from this life they descended into a second, the pastoral: for for the same usefulness they caught and tamed the wild animals; among these, they say, sheep were first taken up, on account of their gentleness, for they are most suited to human life, providing food, cheese as well as butter, and for protection of the body and clothing they used their fleeces.

units.la: Tertio deniq; gradu à vita pastorali ad agri-culturam animum adhibuerunt, quam maxi-mè acceptam vitae fuisse satis testantur popu-lorum erga eam amor ingens & diligentia ad-mirabilis. Illis enim seculis nihil antiquius ha-buerunt, quàm agros studiosè excolere, illum-que amplissimè laudasse existimabant, quem virum bonum Colonum dixissent, tumq; pas-cua & fruges sola regum & gentium vectigalia erant, annonæq; vilitas erat incredibilis: haud-que dubium est, aurea illa secula veré extitisse, in quibus tam innocenti victu mortales vte-rentur, iis videlicet, quae benigna tellure pro-uenirent vescentes, & eo quod honestis ma-nibus excultū esset, vt vita merito censendū sit, humanioré liberalioremq; victus ratione non extitisse, quàm quae salutari frugū inuento ad vitā sustentandā vsa est, quæq; vel pauperrimo cuiq; paratu facilis fuit. In hoc cœlesti munere quantum vita postea profecerit, & quan-tum tum solertia ingeniaq; hominum curam eam auxerint atq; locupletarint; satis superque testatur aureum illud vitæ genus sublatum, cùm ad postremum gradum luxuriæ peruentum, ferreaq; tunc proles repentè exorta est: hæc vltima vita, hic vltimus gradus nostri seculi est, quem feliciorem solent dicere, qui nouis moribus & luxui fauent.
units.tr: Thirdly, at last, from the pastoral life they turned their minds to agriculture, which is amply attested to have been the most welcome of ways of life, by the immense love of peoples for it and their admirable diligence. For in those ages they regarded nothing as more important than cultivating the fields with care, and they thought that the man who could be called a good farmer deserved the highest praise; pasture and crops were then the sole revenues of kings and peoples, and the cheapness of grain was incredible. And there is no doubt that those golden ages truly existed, in which mortals lived on such innocent food, eating what the kindly earth produced; and because it was worked by honest hands, life may rightly be judged to have had no more humane or generous manner of sustenance than that which used the salutary discovery of grain to sustain life, and which was easy even for the poorest. How much life afterwards advanced in this heavenly gift, and how much human skill and talent increased and enriched that care, is amply shown by the loss of that golden way of life, when luxury had reached its last stage and the iron race suddenly arose. This is the final life, this the last stage of our age, which those who favour new customs and luxury are accustomed to call the happier.

units.la: Hinc varius gentium victus mirabilisque, quem non vnum esse, sed innumeros, & penè totidem quot gentes, hominumq; linguæ, testatur inter alios, qui res populorum historiâ prodiderunt, quiq; de situ orbis monumenta reliquerunt. Iul. Cæsar in illis suis clarissimis commentariis de rebus bellicis. Non solum enim Cæsar alium Gallorum fuisse victum, alium Britannorum, alium vero Germanorum prodidit, verùm etiam inter Germanos variū extitisse eumq; mirabilem, atque etiam inter ipsos Gallos, quos agricolationi fuisse deditos & mitiorum frugum alimentis vsos, pomorumq; & vitium succis atque liquoribus extra dubium est: Galliarum enim agros feracissimos, quin & vitibus maxima parte consitos omnium fere scripta prædicant.
units.tr: Hence arose the varied and wonderful diet of peoples, which is not one but countless, almost as many as there are peoples and tongues of men. This is attested, among others, by those who recorded the affairs of nations in history and left records of the world's geography, and by Julius Caesar in his famous commentaries on the war. For Caesar reported that the diet of the Gauls was one thing, that of the Britons another, and that of the Germans another still; and that among the Germans too there was variety, and a remarkable one. And that among the Gauls themselves, who were devoted to farming and used the foods of milder crops, and also the juices and liquors of fruits and vines, is beyond doubt: for almost all writers praise the very fertile fields of Gaul, most of which are planted with vines.

units.la: Belgæ à pristinis moribus longè recesserunt, quoniam summo studio vina externa conquirunt terræ marisque, et enim apud eos vites nullæ conseruntur: vescuntur præterea carnibus bus pecorum, quæ illic abundant propter pabulorum vbertatem : verum ante cuncta panificia fingunt varia ex caseo, lacte, butyro, quę in summo honore mensarū & commessationum habentur : ebrietati autem magis indulgent quam cæteri Galli, honorificamq; maxime putant non solum viris, sed & fœminis crapulam, præsertim qui Rheno sunt proximi.
units.tr: The Belgians have departed far from their former customs, since with great zeal they seek out foreign wines from land and sea, for no vines are planted among them. Moreover they eat the flesh of herds, which abound there because of the richness of the pastures; but above all they make many kinds of pastry from cheese, milk and butter, which are held in the highest honour at tables and feasts. They indulge in drink more than the other Gauls, and they think drunkenness honourable, not only for men but also for women, especially those who live nearest the Rhine.

units.la: Apud Petragonos & Lemouicos castaneæ & rapa à vino & messe tertium honorem adipiscuntur : rapa etiam Allobrogibus & Subaudis in cibo mirifice grata, sicut & castaneæ montanis Lugdunensibus.
units.tr: Among the Petragorians and the Lemovices, chestnuts and turnips take third place after wine and grain. Turnips are also wonderfully pleasing as food to the Allobroges and the Subaudi, just as chestnuts are to the mountain people of Lyonnaise Gaul.

units.la: Montium Cemannorum populi Aruernis proximi vice panificij castaneis vtuntur, quippe festis tantum diebus, vel non infimæ sortis homines panificium illic ex frugibus vsurpant.
units.tr: The peoples of the Cemmenian mountains, near the Arverni, use chestnuts in place of bread, and only on feast days; or, men of no low rank there make bread from grain.

units.la: Gasconum gens Aquitaniæ nobilissima inter præcipua pulmentaria allia habet, cepasque, quorum olfactum & gustatum in delitias gulæ vertit & suauia condimenta : hi nunc quoque præter cæteros Gallos ventri indulgere magis existimantur, vulgatum enim & maxime nobilitatum apud eos iactatur Prouerbium ; Satius esse belle farcire ventrem epulis, quam corpus veste molli & pretiosa ornare: aiuntq; Burgundioni ventrem esse fericeum. Aruerni vero caseo frequentius victitant. Nortmanni malis pyrisque crudis ac coctis liberaliter vescuntur, suosque ex illis concinnant potus, carnibus quoque vescuntur omnigenis.
units.tr: The Gascons, the most noble people of Aquitaine, have garlic and onions among their chief relishes, which they turn into delights of the palate and pleasant seasonings by their smell and taste. These people are now also thought to indulge the belly more than the other Gauls, for a commonly repeated proverb, much praised and famous among them, runs: it is better to stuff the belly well with feasts than to adorn the body with soft and costly clothing; and they say the Burgundian has a silken belly. The Arverni live more often on cheese. The Normans liberally eat apples and pears, raw and cooked, and make drinks from them; they also eat meats of every kind.

units.la: Narbonensis Gallia fœcunditate frugum, vitium pomorumque mira varietate ac suavitate nullis aliis terris cedit: Verum morum civilitate & vitæ nitore atque lautitia à cæteris Gallis videtur discessisse; pisces habet frequentes, tum recentes, tum sale conditos, ante cuncta autem oliuas conditas, capparesq; manducat, ficus item vuasque recentes, mala citria, arantia, limones inter lautiores cibos habet & irritamenta: vina apud eos generosissima: oues pascuntur thymo, quo pabulo mire pinguescunt.
units.tr: Narbonese Gaul yields to no other lands in fertility of crops and in the remarkable variety and sweetness of its vines and fruits; yet in civility of manners and in the elegance and refinement of its living it seems to have departed from the other Gauls. It has plenty of fish, both fresh and salted, and above all it eats preserved olives and capers, and also fresh figs and grapes; it counts lemons, citrons and oranges among its more refined foods and stimulants. Its wines are most noble, and the sheep feed on thyme, by which fodder they grow remarkably fat.

units.la: Armonicarum regionum populi inter se vivendi ratione non consentiunt. Brittones enim & Britonisantes victu magis barbaro & fero vtuntur: at Gallobrittanes maximam partem ciuilitatis vrbanitatisque Francicæ seruant, apud quos panificia lauta ex frugibus parantur, vinaque non ignobilia absorbentur. Mediterraneos autem fere omnes Gallos lautiores in cibis haberi atque humaniores Possidonius Stoicus scribit apud Athenæum.
units.tr: The peoples of the Armorican regions do not agree with one another in their manner of life. The Britons and those who imitate the Britons live on a rather barbarous and savage diet, but the Gallo-Britons keep most of the civility and urbanity of the French, among whom fine breads are made from grain and not unrefined wines are drunk. Posidonius the Stoic, as cited by Athenaeus, writes that nearly all the inland Gauls are regarded as richer in their food and more refined.

units.la: De moribus Germanorum prodidit Cornelius Tacitus, quod cibi illis olim fuerint simplices; agrestia poma recensq; fera aut lac concretum cretum sine apparatu, sine blandimentis ad famem sedandam, sed aduersus sitim non eandem fuisse temperantiam, quoniam diem noctemque in potu continuarent, qui mos apud illos nostra etiā memoria pertinacissime perdurat, vt videantur ad perdenda vina geniti: eoque nomine nunc apud Romanos & Hispanos pessime audiant: Germanos quoque carnibus vesci, ac bibere vinum meracum, historia scriptum reliquit Possidonius Stoicus: sed certum est totam Germaniam à Romanis minime fuisse cognitam: hodie, quanquam longe mitiori & vrbaniore victu degant Germaniæ populi, nihilominus ferinæ cuiusdam & prisca vitæ vestigia quædam retinuerunt, maxime quanto magis vergūt in Septētriones.
units.tr: Cornelius Tacitus wrote about the customs of the Germans, that their food was once plain: wild apples, fresh game, or curdled milk, with no preparation and no delicacies, served to satisfy hunger. But their self-restraint was not the same in drinking, since they kept on drinking day and night. This habit has persisted most stubbornly among them even within our own memory, so that they seem born to squander wine, and for this reason the Romans and Spaniards now speak very ill of them. Posidonius the Stoic also left it recorded in his history that the Germans eat meat and drink undiluted wine. But it is certain that the whole of Germany was little known to the Romans. Today, although the peoples of Germany live on a much milder and more civilized diet, they have nonetheless kept certain traces of a savage and ancient way of life, especially the further north they lie.

units.la: Britanni, qui nunc Angli, si Cæsari credimus, pecorum magnum alebant numerum, leporem vero, gallinam anseremque gustare fas non putabant, animi tamen voluptatisque gratia educabant: conuecto & deportato fumento, præcipue vero gallico vtebantur, vina etiamnunc ab exteris petunt, Gallis, Lusitanis, Hispanis & Germanis, quæ potentiora sunt, nam imbecilla vecturam non ferunt: carnibus vescuntur largiter præcipue à pistoribus incrustatis, magni enim illic pecorum greges & armenta boum. Cœlum vero temperatius esse quam apud Gallos, asperitatemq; frigoris ab iis abesse experientia testis est. His adiacent Scoti, quibus D. Hieronymus feritatem ac barbariem asscribit, quos etiam adhuc feros inuenias, ni aliæ gentes eos cicurarint atq; expolierint, miseramque omnino victus condi-tionem iis fuisse historiæ testantur: bubulam in cibis assumunt largissime, armenta enim huiusmodi animalium fert tellus alitque: frumenta non multum habent, sed aduentitiis vtuntur.
units.tr: The Britons, who are now the English, if we believe Caesar, kept large herds of cattle. They did not think it lawful to eat hare, hen or goose, though they reared them for pleasure and amusement. They imported and brought in grain, and used especially French grain. They still seek wines from abroad, from the Gauls, Lusitanians, Spaniards and Germans, and the stronger wines, for weak ones do not survive the carriage. They eat meat in large amounts, especially from the bakers' ovens. For there are great flocks of sheep and herds of cattle there. That the climate is milder than among the Gauls, and that the harshness of the cold is absent from them, is attested by experience. Next to them are the Scots, to whom St Jerome ascribes savagery and barbarism. You would still find them wild, unless other peoples had tamed and refined them, and histories testify that their condition of life was altogether wretched. They take in beef very freely as food, for the land bears and feeds herds of such animals. They have little grain, but use imported supplies.

units.la: Italia pro tractuum differentia imperijque incremento victum pariter mutauit. Romani enim qui initia imperio dederunt, tum etiam qui id prouexerunt, cibos expetebant tantum qui vitam sustinerent famemque depellerent. Capitale erat bouem mactasse gulæ causa: pi-scibus statim à Roma condita præsertim marinis vsos esse constat eruditorum antiquorum monumentis, omnino carnes parcius semper esitasse quam cæteros populos, verum videri potest, nam & nostra memoria parcissime iis vescuntur, herbis oleribusque varie vtuntur tum crudis, tum coctis. Vini autem obseruationes memorabiles apud Romanos fuerunt, nam auctoritatem post centesimum vrbis annum coepisse aiunt, Romulumque ipsum lacte, non vino libasse? & Numam sanxisse ne rogum vino respergerent, nec licuisse fœminis primum id bibere, postea concessum valetudinis tudinis tantum causa: eorum autem qui secuti sunt, cura fertilior & industria felicior fuit in vitibus colendis: vini quidem in vniuersum sunt auidi, sed modum potionibus adhibent, pariterq; Hispani.
units.tr: Italy, according to the differences of regions and the growth of its empire, likewise changed its diet. For the Romans who gave the beginnings of the empire, and those who advanced it, sought only food that would sustain life and drive away hunger. It was a capital offence to slaughter an ox for the sake of gluttony. It is agreed by the monuments of the learned ancients that from the founding of Rome they used fish, especially sea fish, and that they always ate meat more sparingly than other peoples. This may well be true, for even in our own time they eat meat very sparingly, and they use herbs and vegetables in various ways, both raw and cooked. The Romans' rules about wine were noteworthy. For they say that its use began among them after the hundredth year of the city, and that Romulus himself poured libations with milk, not wine. Numa decreed that they should not sprinkle funeral pyres with wine, and that women were not allowed to drink it at first, but later it was permitted only for the sake of health. Of those who followed, however, their care in cultivating vines was more fruitful and their diligence more successful. They are indeed greedy for wine in general, but they keep to moderation in drinking, and so do the Spaniards.

units.la: Victus autem Romanorum rationes variasse pro Reipublicæ recta vel depravata institutione, & postea Imperatorum virtute temperantiaque, atq; etiam libidine & luxuria, dubium non est, vnde tot emerserunt leges sumptuariæ & censoriæ, quibus cibaria non exotica solum, sed & domestica prohibebantur, atque etiam ex sue pernæ cœnis detrahebantur. Romani etiam veteres pisces simul cum carnibus vna in patella seu lance mensis apponebāt, pariterq; herbas quasdam vt asparagum: Panificia varij generis conficiebant: lepusculi & perdices raro Romanas mensas subibant ob inopiam scilicet, cætera autem alitum genera frequentius: capreas in macello venales passim reperias, primis semper mensis acetaria imponuntur, æstate peponibus liberalissime vescuntur, nam plerumque iis solis contenti & pane, prandia sua cœnasque incoant & finiunt: ficus item simul ac vuæ recentes per autumnum. Vitulina nulla caro pretiosior illis gustatur. Veruecina non admodum placet, piscinarum non sunt tam studiosi, neq; ita auide pisces expetunt, quam sui maiores, quippe rarissime vel marinos attingunt, nisi religio cogat. Hispani sordes in viuendo aliquibus in locis peculiares habent, quoniam si suis alantur loculis domi esuriunt & famelici hiant, at quando aliena quadra frui licet, nulla gens æque vorax cernitur, viuunt carnibus immodicis, piscibus cum amnicis tum marinis, panificia quoque lauta faciunt, pomorum vbertas illic varia atque multiplex maxime citriorum omne genus & punicorum, ficuū, vuarum, quas siccatas alias in terras mittunt: ante cuncta vina illic vehementissima sunt. Secundis mensis querenas glandes adhibent dulcedine præstantes. Strabo Lusitaniæ montanas gentes querna glande vesci autor est: sunt praterea apud mōtanos quosdam Hispaniarum populos condimenta & saccharata innumera, officinarum & Seplasiariorum commenta, ea mensas secundas exornant bellariorumque vices supplent. Siculas mensas & in his Syracusanas potissimum nobilitauit luxuria, quas prudentissimus Plato damnauit: fruges in Sicilia repertas à Cerere narrat antiquitas, quoniam solum illic sit omnium frumentorum fertilissimum, unde & terra illa Romaorum horreum nuncupabatur.
units.tr: That the Romans' ways of eating varied according to the sound or corrupt constitution of the commonwealth, and afterwards according to the virtue and temperance of the emperors, and also according to lust and luxury, is beyond doubt. From this came forth so many sumptuary and censorial laws, by which not only foreign but also domestic foods were forbidden, and even ham was removed from dinners. The ancient Romans also set fish on their tables together with meat, on one dish or platter, and likewise certain herbs such as asparagus. They made bread of various kinds. Hares and partridges seldom came to Roman tables, obviously from scarcity, but other kinds of birds more often. You could find roe deer on sale in the market everywhere. Salads were always set at the beginning of the meal. In summer they ate melons very freely, for they were usually content with these alone and with bread, and began and ended their lunches and dinners with them. Likewise figs and fresh grapes in autumn. No meat was more prized among them than veal. Mutton did not much please them. They were not so keen on fishponds, nor did they seek fish as eagerly as their forebears did, for they very rarely touched even sea fish, unless religion required it. The Spaniards have a peculiar meanness in living in some places, for if they are fed from their own purse, they go hungry at home and gape with hunger; but when they may enjoy someone else's table, no people is seen to be so greedy. They live on immoderate meats, both river and sea fish, and they also make fine breads. The abundance of fruit there is varied and manifold, above all every kind of citron and pomegranate, figs and grapes, which they send in dried form to other lands. Above all, their wines are very strong. At dessert they serve acorns of the oak, which are excellent in sweetness. Strabo is the authority that the mountain peoples of Lusitania eat oak acorns. Besides, among certain mountain peoples of Spain there are countless seasonings and confections, inventions of apothecaries and perfumers, and these adorn the dessert courses and take the place of the sweets served in turn. The Sicilian tables, and especially those of Syracuse, were made famous by luxury, and Plato, the most prudent of men, condemned them. Antiquity tells that grain was discovered in Sicily by Ceres, since the island has the most fertile soil of all for grain, and for this reason that land was called the granary of the Romans.

units.la: Græci crapulæ gulæq; admodum fuerunt dediti, quare pergræcari pro indulgere genio proverbio circumfertur. Constat tamen diuersam victus rationem & studia illis fuisse: aliter enim Lacedæmonii, aliter Athenienses viuebant: Lycurgus leges Lacedæmoniis condens tantum ciborum vnicuique elargiri iussit, quod ad bonam corporis valetudinem satis esset: certum itaque numerum frumenti singulis in singulos annos emetiri mandauit, & liquores pro ratione, atque id vberius viris, fœminis vero parcius. Præter ea instituit conuiuia publica, in quibus nullæ præter vulgares escæ apponerentur, probrosum existimans simul ac inutile animis corporibusque coquorum condimentis & saporum coaceruationibus saginari.
units.tr: The Greeks were very much given to drunkenness and gluttony, and hence the proverb "to live like a Greek" for indulging one's genius is in circulation. Yet it is agreed that their manner of life and their pursuits were different. For the Spartans lived differently from the Athenians. Lycurgus, when he made laws for the Spartans, ordered that each person be given only as much food as was sufficient for good bodily health. He therefore commanded that a fixed measure of grain be doled out to each person each year, and drinks in proportion, more generously for men but more sparingly for women. Besides these things, he instituted public dinners, at which no food was served apart from the common fare, regarding it as shameful and at the same time harmful to minds and bodies to be fattened on the seasonings of cooks and the piling up of flavours.

units.la: Solebant præterea Lacedæmonii epulas suas condire labore in venatu, sudore, cursu, fame, siti: unde Dionysio Siculo neganti, se iure illo nigro, (erat enim hoc inter obsonia illis celebratissimum) quod caput cœnæ fuerat, delectatum, respondisse fertur, qui illud coxerat, minime mirum, condimenta enim defuerunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the Spartans used to season their feasts with labour in hunting, sweat, running, hunger and thirst. Hence, when Dionysius of Sicily said that he did not enjoy that black broth (for this was the most celebrated of their dishes, and was the chief part of the dinner), they are said to have replied: "It is not at all surprising, for the cook who made it lacked seasonings."

units.la: Sybaritæ gloriæ virtutisque loco delitijs mollitieique dediti vitam despiciebant, quoniam mortem non timerent. Spartani vero & viuendum liberaliter & moriendum censebant, sed vtrunq; cū virtute, teste Plutarcho.
units.tr: The Sybarites, given to delights and softness, regarded a life of pleasure as a substitute for glory and virtue, because they did not fear death. But the Spartans thought that one should both live generously and die bravely, yet both with virtue, as Plutarch testifies.

units.la: Verum Athenien siium longe alia fuit viuendi ratio, quippe luxui omnino deditos fuisse,
units.tr: But the manner of life of the Athenians was very different, since they were wholly given over to luxury,

units.la: Græci fere omnes testati sunt, ipsique Poetæ Comici imprimis Atticas cœnas riserunt. Socrates enim cibos detestabatur, qui non esurientem invitarent ad edendum, similiter & potus, qui non sitientes ad bibendum.
units.tr: as nearly all the Greeks have testified, and the comic poets above all have mocked Attic dinners. For Socrates detested foods that invited to eating those who were not hungry, and likewise drinks that invited to drinking those who were not thirsty.

units.la: Athenienses in cœnis solebant lances apponere, quæ quinque alias paruas lances continebant, quarum una referta erat allio, altera duobus Eschinis. Tertia placenta, quarta conchis decem, quinta antaceo paruo. Est in exemplis parasitum quendam interrogatum, nū cœnæ Atticæ Chalcidis lautiores essent, an vero hæ Atheniensibus præstarent, respondisse, Chalcedoniacum proœmium pretiosius esse & suauius quam Atticorū totum apparatum, appellans videlicet Proœmium cœnarum, ostrearum multitudinem & varietatem: nihil ad peregrinos exportari licebat præter solum oleum, nam qui ficus exportantes ostenderent Sycophantæ apud illos dicebantur.
units.tr: The Athenians at their dinners used to set out platters, which held five other small dishes, one of which was filled with garlic, another with two Eschines. The third held a cake, the fourth ten shellfish, the fifth a small anchovy. There is an example of a certain parasite who was asked whether the Attic dinners were more lavish than those of the Chalcidians, or whether these surpassed the Athenians. He replied that the Chalcedonian prelude was more costly and pleasant than the whole Attic preparation, meaning of course the prelude to the dinners, that is the multitude and variety of oysters. Nothing could be exported to foreigners except olive oil alone, for those who displayed figs for export were called sycophants among them.

units.la: Persarum victum exponens Xenophon ad panem quicquam eos adhibuisse negat præter nasturtium. Sed de eorum luxu & ganea nihil hic ascribendum duxi, cum apud omnes fere scriptores passim complura tradita legantur, & in altera parte obiter quædam sim relaturus.
units.tr: Describing the diet of the Persians, Xenophon says they ate nothing with their bread except cress. I have decided not to set down anything here about their luxury and feasting, since many accounts of these are read everywhere among almost all writers, and I shall touch on some matters in passing in the second part.

units.la: De Ægypto certum est & frugum & vitium fœcunditate eam felicissimam fuisse, quin pomorum omni genere, olerum quoque ac herbarum cibis supra modum visam, piscesque amnicos marinosque & salsamenta immodice esitasse.
units.tr: It is certain that Egypt was most fortunate in the abundance of its crops and vines, and indeed it was seen to abound beyond measure in fruit of every kind, in vegetables and herbs, and it ate its river and sea fish and salted meats to excess.

units.la: De aliarum gentium victu, quæ à gravissimis auctoribus literis assignata sunt & quasi per monumenta tradita, scio permulta esse eiusmodi, ut vix fidem impetrare valeant, multisque ea videatur incredibilia. Sed quia ex illis mundi partibus, quarum gentium multiformes mores, rirus, mirabilemque victum enarraturus sum, homines, fruges, legumina, aves, animaliaque nostris incognita terris creberrime ad nos terra marique conuehuntur, fidem facile adhibendam ijs censeo, præsertim si naturæ eximia benignitas & vis eius immensa perpendatur, fateor permultos qui à patrio solo non discesserunt, multa hic non sine fastidio audituros: veruntamen candide meum hunc laborem velim interpretentur, quippe si omnino à Musis remoti non fuerint, erunt non pauca quæ animum delectabunt per tot gentium cibaria discurrentem.
units.tr: As for the diet of other peoples, which the most weighty authors have recorded in writing and handed down as if in monuments, I know there are very many such accounts, so incredible that they can scarcely win belief and seem unbelievable to many. But since the men, grains, pulses, birds and animals unknown to our lands, from those parts of the world whose manifold customs, rites and wonderful diet I am about to describe, are very often carried to us by land and sea, I think they should readily be believed, especially if one weighs the remarkable kindness of nature and its immense power. I admit that many who have never left their native soil will hear much here not without disgust; yet I would like them to interpret my labour fairly, for if they are not altogether strangers to the Muses, there will be not a few things to delight them as they run through the foods of so many peoples.

units.la: Sed hoc præfari lubet, ut non unus clim fuit, ita nec hodie quoq; mortalium victum vnum, sed innumeros esse & quidem totidem, quot hominum linguæ:
units.tr: But I wish to premise this: just as there was not one diet of mortals at any time, so today too there are not one but countless diets, as many as there are human languages.

units.la: Ferinum ante aliquot annos & absurdum apud nostrates fuit, cochleis vesci, ranis, testutestudinib°, at in vniuersa fere Gallia inter precipuas mensarum delicias reponuntur.
units.tr: Some years ago it was wild and absurd among our countrymen to eat snails and frogs and tortoises, yet across almost all of France they are now counted among the chief delicacies of the table.

units.la: Thraces quosdam canibus vičtitasse Picus Francifcus auctor est.
units.tr: Picus Franciscus is the authority for saying that certain Thracians lived on dogs.

units.la: Arcades carnes & mahamin cibatu habuisse ferunt, quin & glandes, vnde & balanophagi dicuntur.
units.tr: The Arcadians are said to have had flesh and mahamin as their food, and even acorns, whence they are called acorn-eaters (balanophagi).

units.la: Hircani vescebantur venatibus quorum varietate abundabant Marcellino teste.
units.tr: The Hyrcanians fed on game, of which they had abundance in great variety, according to the witness of Marcellinus.

units.la: Getis quibusdam vini vsus omnino ignotus, quin & frugum, vičtum illis ouillum pecus cōmodat, ex quo Nomadum Getharumq; plurimi, teste Columella, galačtopotæ dicuntur.
units.tr: Some Getae knew nothing at all of wine, and not even of grain; flocks of sheep supply their food, and from this, according to Columella, many of the Nomads and Getae are called milk-drinkers (galactopotae).

units.la: Xenophon prodidit Mosynecos ostentasse diuitum liberos bene curatos, non alio tamen cibo quam elixis nucibus enutritos.
units.tr: Xenophon reports that the Mossynoeci displayed the children of the wealthy, well cared for, yet nourished on nothing but boiled nuts.

units.la: Armeniam minorem fœcunditate percelebrem referunt, qui paulo ante nostram ætatem eam peragrarunt, nulliusq; quod ad victum hominis pertinet, indigam, quin etiam cœlum saluberrimum & clementissimum. Præterea Persarum regionem omni frugum abundantia nobilem narrant, vinoq; & pomis felicem, sicut & palmetis, quæ dačtylos vberrime ferant, pistaceis præterea & malis quæ paradisea appellantur:
units.tr: Writers who travelled through Lesser Armenia shortly before our own time report that it is very famous for its fertility, lacking nothing that pertains to human sustenance, and that its sky is most healthful and mild. They also relate that the region of Persia is renowned for its abundance of every kind of grain, and is blessed with wine and fruit, as well as with palm groves that bear dates most plentifully, and besides with pistachios and apples called paradise apples.

units.la: Tartarorum victus parum distat ab eo, quo Nomadas Scythasque vti prodidit antiquitas, quo etiam vtuntur non paucæ Septentrionis gentes, quippe plurimus his lactis vsus & caseï.
units.tr: The diet of the Tartars differs little from that which antiquity said the Nomads and Scythians used, and which many peoples of the north still use, for among them the use of milk and cheese is very common.

units.la: Orientis populi plurimi qui Imperio Magni Cham parent, potus suos ex oryza & genere aromatum concinnant: carnes crudas contritas primum, deinde aromatis respersas oleisque odoratis imbutas vorant: Serpentibus etiam nunc quæ illic nascuntur copiosissimæ & grandissimæ in cibis suis vtuntur, in deliciis quoque habent hominum carnes, qui morbo non extinguuntur, quales sunt qui in bello ab iis trucidantur.
units.tr: Many peoples of the East who obey the empire of the Great Khan prepare their drinks from rice and a kind of spice. They first eat raw meat, crushed, then sprinkled with spices and soaked in fragrant oils. They also use in their food the serpents that are born there, which are most plentiful and very large, and they even count among their delicacies the flesh of men who have not died of disease, such as those who are slaughtered by them in war.

units.la: Solinus autor est, Essedones Scythiæ populos parentum suorum funera cantibus lætos prosequi fuisse solitos, conuocatisque propinquorum coetibus cadauera ipsa, (horrenda parentalia,) dentibus laniasse, pecorumque visceribus mixta inter epulas apposuisse, Cranio vero populi loco vsos fuisse, quod & auro circumcirca ornarunt.
units.tr: Solinus is the authority that the Essedones, a people of Scythia, used to escort the funerals of their parents with joyful songs; and when the groups of relatives had been gathered, they tore the corpses themselves with their teeth (horrid funeral rites), and served them at the feast mixed with the flesh of cattle. They used the skull in place of a cup, and they even adorned it all round with gold.

units.la: Matthias Michon de Sarmatia Asiana scribens Tartarorum quoq; meminit & omni frumento carere asseuerat, omniq; leguminum genere, excepto milio, quod magna cura ab iis seri idem tradit: equorumque greges educant, quorum carnes manducant, sanguinem vero equinum milio commiscent, coquuntque simul & manducant: quin etiam ipsum potant solum, idque & barbaris olim placuisse testa-tur Virg. carmine bucolico, & lac concretum cum sanguine potat equino: acido lacte oble-ctantur, id namque tum stomacho salutare esse sibi persuadent, tum aluo deijciendæ ex-perimentis idoneum comprobarunt: si quan-do vero epulantur splendidius, lac sublima-tum, si liceat eo vocabulo uti in elegantioris penuria, bibunt, quod mirabile dictu, prom-tissime atque ocyssime in cerebrum penetrat inebriatque.
units.tr: Matthias Michov, writing of Asiatic Sarmatia, also mentions the Tartars and asserts that they lack all grain and every kind of pulse except millet, which he records they sow with great care. They rear herds of horses, whose flesh they eat, and they mix horse blood with millet, and they cook and eat them together; indeed they drink the blood alone as well, and Virgil testifies in his bucolic poem that this pleased the barbarians of old too: "and drinks curdled milk mixed with horse blood." They anoint themselves with sour milk, for they are persuaded that this is both good for the stomach and proved suitable for purging the bowels. If at any time they feast more splendidly, they drink sublimated milk (if one may use that word in the lack of a more refined one), which, marvellous to say, penetrates the brain most readily and swiftly and makes it drunk.

units.la: A Tartaris Turcas oriundos idem censet, quare ab eorum victu non procul recede-re. Qui de Rhodi expugnatione historiam scri-pserunt, omnino gentem illam immundam & obscœnam tradunt. In Sarmatia Europæa Po-dolia fertilitate nobilitata est, quppe illic fruges feliciter & læte pueniunt, cibaria igitur ex fru-gibus, potus vero ex melle cocinnant, quod il-lic abundantissime gignitur, atque etiam in Ruscia: aquæ omnes sponte illic pisculentæ sunt, in quibus lucij capiuntur amplitudinis mirandæ saporisque suauissimi.
units.tr: The same author holds that the Turks are descended from the Tartars, which is why I do not stray far from their diet. Those who have written the history of the capture of Rhodes say without qualification that this people is unclean and obscene. In European Sarmatia, Podolia is renowned for its fertility, for grain grows there richly and happily, so they make their food from grain and their drink from honey, which is produced there in great abundance, and so too in Russia. All the waters there teem with fish of their own accord, among which pike are caught of wonderful size and most delicious flavour.

units.la: Verum & Lithuaniæ Moscouiæque amni-bus usu venit, ut sponte & copiose alant gene-rentque pisces, qui & magnitudine & suauitate nobilitantur. Moscouiæ idem Matthias men-tionem faciens potum eis esse scribit ex aqua & melle confecto: aromatis crebrius utuntur, nam & ea cum melle arte Chymica sublimant existimantes hac potione visceribus calorem excitari adeo insignem & salutarem, vt possit inclementissimis frigoribus fortiter repugnare: aliam ipsam sublimant, ex qua sublimatione elicitur liquor, quam aquam ardentem vocât, æque ac apud Germanos, Gallosq; & Italos ex vinis vehementioribus: Principis edicto seuerissimo vini potus aliorumque liquorum, qui ebrietatem concitant, prohibetur, nec licet ea bibere, nisi eiusdem Regulí indulgentia.
units.tr: Indeed, in the rivers of Lithuania and Muscovy it happens that they nourish and breed fish abundantly of their own accord, and these are famed for both their size and their sweetness. Matthias, again speaking of Muscovy, writes that their drink there is made from water and honey. They use spices more often, for they also distil these with honey by chemical art, believing that by this drink so remarkable and healthful a heat is kindled in the vital organs that it can strongly resist the harshest cold. They distil another spirit as well, from which a liquor is drawn off that they call burning water, just as the Germans, French and Italians do from stronger wines. By the strictest edict of the prince, the drinking of wine and of other liquors that induce drunkenness is forbidden, nor is it lawful to drink them except by the indulgence of the same ruler.

units.la: Muscovitis parent Scythæ & Antropophagi humanis corporibus vescentes, sine vllo degentes panificio, vino, alijsque potibus.
units.tr: The Scythians who are subject to the Muscovites, and the cannibals who eat human bodies, live without any bread, wine or other drinks.

units.la: Paulus Iouius literis mandauit Moscouiam melopepones ferre, quod mirari subit, quippe gelidissimis Boreæ flatibus tenerrima quæque exurūtur. Certissima messis in melle atq; cera est, namque illic apes in arborum campis mella conficiunt & probatissima & copiosissima: domi opipare & laute epulantur, gallinæ siquidem & anates singulæ pro singulis argenteolis nummis vænciunt: venatio & aucupia mensas magnatum opulentant, vina nesciunt præter exotica, iisque vtuntur in Sacrificiis & conuiuiis luxuriosioribus ostentationis gratia.
units.tr: Paulus Jovius has committed to writing that Muscovy bears melons, which is surprising, since the most tender kinds are burned up by the icy blasts of the north wind. The most reliable harvest is of honey and wax, for there the bees make honey in the fields of the trees, and it is both excellent and abundant. At home they feast sumptuously and elegantly, for hens and ducks are sold singly for single small silver coins. Hunting and fowling enrich the tables of the great; they know no wines except imported ones, and they use these in their sacrifices and in more luxurious feasts, for show.

units.la: Lapponum gens, supra quam credibile sit, fera est & agrestis, neque enim fruges, neque vina, neq; poma nouit: sagittandi arte sola victum quaeritat & ferarum occisarum tergoribus vestitur.
units.tr: The race of the Lapps is wild and rustic beyond what one could believe; they know neither grain, nor wine, nor fruit. They get their food by archery alone, and they clothe themselves in the hides of the wild beasts they have killed.

units.la: Colmogora Moscouiae contermina regio frugibus abundat, seminaque terrae mandata nullo illis beneficio aratri proueniunt, admirabili celeritate naturae festinantis, vt Iouius testatur. In subiectis Moscouiae campis, caprearum, leporumque incredibilis multitudo cernitur, quae nemini aut plagis aut canibus venari licet: lacus quoque habent, vnde piscium admirabilem copiam expiscantur: eademque pene de moribus & victu caeterorum populorum Septentrionis literis mandata reperiuntur, tum apud veteres tum apud recentiores.
units.tr: The region of Kolmogora, bordering on Muscovy, abounds in grain, and seeds committed to the earth come up for them without any help from the plough, through the wonderful speed of nature hurrying on, as Jovius attests. In the open fields of Muscovy an incredible multitude of roe deer and hares is to be seen, which no one may hunt either with snares or with dogs. They also have lakes from which they catch an astonishing quantity of fish. Almost the same things about the customs and diet of the other peoples of the north are found recorded in writing, both by the ancients and by more recent authors.

units.la: In Oriente porro traditur esse quosdam populos, qui sine vllis arboribus, sineque frutice degant. Plurimae quoque gentes frugum, arborum, quin etiam pecorum expertes inueniuntur.
units.tr: Further, in the East it is reported that there are certain peoples who live without any trees or shrubs. Very many nations are also found to lack grain, trees, and even livestock.

units.la: Scytharum multa genera, qui corporibus humanis vescerentur, olim fuerunt, & esse nostro aeuo in noua India Cannibalos vocatos accepimus. Adde quod quidam in remediis summis habent viscera ossaque humana vorare sanguinemque gladiatorum bibere, & quidem ex homine ipso sorberi ex ipsa vena secta calidum adhuc & spirantem efficacissimum putant. Fuerunt apud Graecos qui scrupulose homihominum viscera sunt persecuti, eorumque sapores.
units.tr: There were formerly many kinds of Scythians who fed on human bodies, and we have heard that in our own age there are Cannibals, so called, in the New India. Add to this that some hold it the highest remedy to eat human viscera and bones and to drink the blood of gladiators; and indeed they think it most efficacious to drink it from the man himself, straight from a severed vein, while it is still warm and breathing. There were also Greeks who carefully investigated the viscera of men and their flavours.

units.la: Æthiopum gens, cuius regio à Neroë ad fluuium Hydaspin porrigitur, scorpionibus vescebatur aspidibusque.
units.tr: The people of Ethiopia, whose country stretches from Meroë to the river Hydaspes, fed on scorpions and asps.

units.la: Quintinus Heduus scribit, se vidisse in insula Melita, qui scorpionem ederet innoxie. Sunt enim illic scorpiones veneni expertes. Supra Borysthenem esse gentem Sauromatum, quæ tertio semper die capiat cibum: Ad extremos vero Indiæ fines gentem Astomorum fuisse, sine ore, corpore toto hirtam, vestitam frondium lanugine, halitibus tantum viventem & odore, quem naribus trahebant, memoria proditum est: quæ si vera sunt, quis miretur Democritum mellis odore vixisse.
units.tr: Quintinus Heduus writes that he saw a man on the island of Malta who ate a scorpion without harm, for there are scorpions there that are free of poison. Beyond the Borysthenes there is a people of Sauromatians who take food only every third day. At the farthest limits of India there was, it is recorded, a people of Astomi, without a mouth, with their whole body hairy and clothed in a down of leaves, living only on breath and on the smell they drew in through their nostrils. If these things are true, who would wonder that Democritus lived on the smell of honey?

units.la: Qui Athon montem incolebant, viperinis carnibus alebantur, itaque nec capiti nec vestibus eorum noxia corpori animalia innascebantur.
units.tr: Those who inhabited Mount Athos were fed on viper flesh, so that no animals harmful to the body were bred in their hair or their clothes.

units.la: Pandoræ locustas in cibis habuerunt atque etiam Parthi.
units.tr: The Pandorae ate locusts with their food, and so did the Parthians.

units.la: Gens Medunnorum appellata animalium, quæ Cynocephalos vocabant, lacte viuebant. Arimphæi gens baccis alebatur.
units.tr: The people called Medunni lived on milk, and they were called animals, which they named Cynocephali. The people of the Arimphaei were fed on berries.

units.la: Celenophagi testudinibus vescebantur, quarum testis casas suas integebant, idque genus hominum noua India alit: Candei
units.tr: The Celenophagi fed on tortoises, whose shells they used to cover their huts; and this race of men the New India still feeds: the Candei.

units.la: Cădei serpentibus vesci assueti, & ob id Ophiophagi dicti.
units.tr: The Cadei were accustomed to eat serpents, and for this reason they were called Ophiophagi.

units.la: Libes ouillam non gustabant, erat enim apud eos id inexpiabile, si quis edisset.
units.tr: The Libyans did not taste sheep's flesh, for among them it was an inexpiable offence if anyone ate it.

units.la: Iudæi atque Ægypti non vescebantur suilla.
units.tr: Jews and Egyptians did not eat pork.

units.la: Troglodityæ specus subibant, alebanturque serpentibus.
units.tr: The Troglodytes went down into caves and were fed on serpents.

units.la: Riphæis baccæ erant alimenta. Nonnullis Indiæ populis cæsorum parentum visceribus epulari fas erat.
units.tr: The Riphaei had berries for food. Some peoples of India were permitted to feast on the flesh of their slain parents.

units.la: Carmani sine fruga ac veste, sine pecore, sine sedibus degebant, piscibus vescebantur, atque eorum cute sese velabant. Pharusii pecoribus tantum alebantur.
units.tr: The Carmanians lived without grain or clothing, without livestock and without dwellings; they fed on fish and wrapped themselves in their skins. The Pharusii were fed only on livestock.

units.la: In Æthiopia tum hominum multiformes miræque effigies reperiuntur, tum victus ratio varia & incredibilis: illic enim gentes esse ore concreto & naribus carentes, vnoque tantum foramine spirantes, tradiderunt Prisci, & potu aucnę calamis trahere. Quibusdam ignotum fuisse ignis vsum narrat ante Ptolomæum Latyram Ægypti Regem, atque illic fuisse Nomadas, qui Elephantis vescerentur.
units.tr: In Ethiopia there are found both men of many shapes and wondrous appearance, and a manner of food both varied and incredible. For the ancients handed down that there are peoples with fused mouths and no nostrils, breathing through a single opening and drinking through reeds. For some the use of fire was unknown, as is related of the time before Ptolemy Latyrus, king of Egypt; and there were Nomads there who fed on elephants.

units.la: Fortunatarum insularum incolas inprimis beatos existimare possumus, quibus sua sponte tellus abundantissime suppeditat alimenta, alis super aliis scilicet innascentibus, quam felicitatem in quibusdam orbis Indici nuper patefacti insulis spectari accepimus.
units.tr: We may consider the inhabitants of the Fortunate Islands especially blessed, for their soil supplies food most abundantly of its own accord, one crop growing upon another. We have heard that such happiness is seen on some islands of the Indian world lately opened up.

units.la: Agriophagi Pantherarum carnes leonumque edebant.
units.tr: The Agriophagi ate the flesh of panthers and lions.

units.la: Pamphagi omnia vorabant, Æthiopum pars quædam locustis tantum vixisse fertur, fumo saleq; duratis in annua alimenta, sed quadragesimum vitæ annum non excedere.
units.tr: The Pamphagi devoured everything. A certain part of the Ethiopians is said to have lived on locusts alone, preserved with smoke and salt for the year's food, yet they did not live beyond their fortieth year.

units.la: Alii Orientis populi piscibus viuunt, tum siccaris tum recentibus, quorum captura vberrima fit Martio, Aprili, Maioq; mensibus, contritos eos & in massam redactos in panificia cogunt, siccataq; in annua cibaria reponunt.
