units.tr: Other peoples of the East live on fish, both dried and fresh, whose catch is most abundant in the months of March, April and May. They crush the fish, press them into a mass, form it into loaves, and dry and store them as food for the year.

units.la: De victu & cibo nouæ Indiæ, siue noui orbis non ita pridem à Christianis patefacti constat varium eum esse, fertilitate soli alibi; alibi vero infœcunditate nobilem, herbarum quoque, fruticum, arborum, pomorum odorumq; & alituum innumera genera esse reperta, quæ non minorem admirationem præbent, quàm incognitæ olim res Indicæ: alit præterea oues, & alia pecora, aprosq;, affatim abundat melle, saccharo & vitibus quæ plus fundunt vuarum quàm foliorum.
units.tr: Concerning the food and diet of New India, or the new world lately opened up by Christians, it is established that it is varied: in some places it is remarkable for the fertility of the soil, in others for its barrenness. Innumerable kinds of herbs, shrubs, trees, fruits, spices and birds have been found there, which give no less wonder than the once unknown things of India. The land also feeds sheep and other cattle, and wild boars; it abounds in honey, sugar and vines, which yield more grapes than leaves.

units.la: Qui terras incolunt prima Americi Vespucii nauigatione visas, omninò frumenta ignorant, cibaria autem iis sunt poma atque herbæ, pisces quoq; radicem quandam in farinam redigunt qua vice panis vescuntur, hanc alii iuccam, alii Chambi appellant: porro carnes nullas las attingunt præter humanas: Eadem nauiga-tione reperta gens est quę in cibo habet animal quoddam magnitudine quidem capræ, specie verò serpentem referens.
units.tr: Those who inhabit the lands first seen on the voyage of Amerigo Vespucci know nothing of grain at all. Their food is fruit and herbs. They also grind a certain root into flour, which they eat in place of bread; some call this root iuca, others chambi. Otherwise they touch no meat except human flesh. On the same voyage was found a people who eat an animal the size of a goat but resembling a serpent in appearance.

units.la: Qui primi è Christiano orbe in eas terras habitatum deducti sunt, durarunt quidem aliquot annis solis herbis, pomis, radicibusque viuentes, verum postea ad alia cibaria transierūt, quippe venter ingenii largitor docuit, inuenitque cibos, quos primùm exitiales experti sunt, innoxios reddere. Etenim iucca radix primùm degustata illis mortifera fuit. Verùm procedente tempore, cum id venenum in radicis solo succo esse comperissent, aqua coctam ac igne tostam mandere cœperunt absque noxa navigatione Iosephi Indi compertum habetur, regionem Indicam, quæ Carangonora dicitur, sitim inter æstiuum tropicum & æquatorem, nucibus, quas Indicas appellamus, abundare, herbarum insuper 24. radicibus vesci, ex oryza verò panes conficere: Sunt etiamnum Palmeta, ex quorum fructibus panes conflant, vinum eliciunt, acetum temperat, oleum exprimunt, atq; etiam saccharum: quod ideò minus mirabile videtur, quod Strabonem auctorem grauem eadem penè in libris suis de orbis situ, tradidisse reperio. Ex palma enim fieri panem, mel, acetum, & oleum, scripto mandauit: multa quoque illic arborum genera, multa herbarum, rum, multa quadrupedum, alium & piscium videri, quæ non alibi, testantur, qui in eam navigare, poma quibusdam instar messium sunt, aliis herbarum radices.
units.tr: The first people from the Christian world who were taken into those lands lasted for some years living only on herbs, fruit and roots. But afterwards they turned to other foods, for the belly, the giver of talent, taught them and discovered ways of making harmless the foods that had first proved deadly to them. For the root iuca, when first tasted, was fatal to them. But in time, when they had found that the poison lay only in the juice of the root, they began to eat it boiled in water and toasted over fire, without harm. From the voyage of Joseph the Indian it is known that the region of India called Carangonora, lying between the summer tropic and the equator, abounds in the nuts we call Indian, feeds on the roots of 24 herbs, and makes bread from rice. There are also palm groves, from whose fruit they make bread, draw wine, produce vinegar, press oil and even sugar. This seems the less remarkable because I find that the weighty author Strabo wrote nearly the same in his books on the situation of the world; for he set down in writing that bread, honey, vinegar and oil are made from the palm. Many kinds of trees, herbs, four-footed beasts, birds and fish are seen there which are found nowhere else, as those who have sailed there attest. For some people the fruits are like crops, for others the roots of herbs.

units.la: Sed ne quid prætereamus, Calechutana cibaria attingemus: qui in eam terram primi è Christianis navigationem instituerunt, narrät incolas lacte & butyro vesci, panesque factitare sine frumento in foco tantum coctos & cinere. Oryzæ apud eos summa abundantia, eamq; cymbalis, saltationibus, omniqué lætitiæ genere ferunt, sua dæmonia precantes, vt sit oryzæ vberrimus proventus, hac enim varias epulas conficiunt: ex palmis potant liquorem, carnibus piscibusque promiscuè vescuntur, à bubula tamen abstinent, boues namque sacrosanctos putant.
units.tr: But lest we pass over anything, we shall touch on the foods of Calicut. Those of the Christians who first undertook the voyage to that land report that the inhabitants live on milk and butter, and make breads without grain, baked only on the hearth and in the ashes. There is the greatest abundance of rice among them, and they celebrate it with cymbals, dances and every kind of rejoicing, praying to their demons that the rice harvest may be most abundant, for from it they make varied feasts. From the palms they drink a liquor. They eat meat and fish indiscriminately, but abstain from beef, for they consider oxen sacred.

units.la: Qui colunt Insulam, quæ S. Iohannis porta dicta est, canes alunt ac saginant in vsum cibarium, verum nullus illis latratus est, rostrumq; habent vulpinum. Infima plebs piscatu nutritur, muriumq; venatu. Incredibilia profectò sunt, quæ de felicitate illius Soli tradita legimus, & præsertim in arboribus & pomis producendis.
units.tr: Those who inhabit the island called the Gate of St John feed and fatten dogs for eating. Yet these dogs never bark, and have foxlike snouts. The lowest common people live by fishing and by hunting mice. What we read handed down about the fertility of that soil, especially in producing trees and fruit, is truly incredible.

units.la: Mameluchi, qui Sultano Ægyptio parebant, equorum, camelorum bubalorumq; carnibus victitârunt. Arietes in illis locis nascuntur memorabiles, quorum aliqui caudam gestant 40. li40. librarum, adeoq; obesos vt vix progredi valeant: nonnulli arietes cornua damis similia gerunt, quorum vno aureo duodenos veniisse tantum proditum est: capras praeterea grandes admodum illic reperiri traditur, quae vno partu 4. haedos enitantur: Atque haec de vario mirabilique gentium victu huic orationi adiicere volui, vt is ne rudis omninò, qui non audierit, in istiusmodi rerum auditionibus reperiatur.
units.tr: The Mamelukes, who obeyed the Egyptian Sultan, lived on the flesh of horses, camels and buffaloes. Remarkable rams are born in those places: some carry a tail of forty pounds and are so fat that they can scarcely walk; some rams bear horns like those of fallow deer, and one of these was reported to have fetched twelve gold pieces. Goats there are also said to be very large, and to bring forth four kids at one birth. I wished to add these things about the varied and wondrous diets of peoples to this discourse, so that the reader may not be entirely unversed, having never heard of such things.

units.la: Nunc ad alteram orationis meae partem progredior in qua monstrosa & fabulosa omittam, tantum, quae tum Graecorum, tum Romanorum historiis nobilioribus mandata inueni viuendi, illustrium quorundam virorum exempla attingam, victus cibosq; ostendam, vnaque opera luxum & sobrietatem aperiam: vbi adnotasse oportet, aliquando bene nos debere de moribus nostris & viuendi ratione sperare, aliquando vero peßime, quandoq; enim parsimonia indicabitur, quandoque insanus luxus eiusq; asseclae. Monstrificas vobis hic exhibebo coenas, prodigiosas atque portentosas, auribus eas percipietis, non gustabitis, & si cui forsan laliuam mouerim, lautiore tamen & vlteriore quodam ferculo palatum explere non valeo. Nolim, inquit Cicero de finibus, mihi fingere asotos, qui in mensam veniant & de conuiuiis auferantur, crudiqué postridiè rursus ingurgitent. Cer-
units.tr: Now I proceed to the second part of my discourse, in which I shall omit the monstrous and fabulous, and touch only on the examples of certain illustrious men which I find recorded in the more noted histories of the Greeks and Romans. I shall set out their ways of life and their foods, and at the same time reveal luxury and sobriety. Here it must be noted that sometimes we may hope well of our morals and way of life, and sometimes very badly, for sometimes frugality will be shown, and sometimes insane luxury and its followers. I shall here set before you monstrous, prodigious and portentous dinners; you will perceive them with your ears, not taste them. And if perhaps I stir anyone's appetite, I cannot satisfy the palate with a richer or more exotic dish. "I would not wish," says Cicero in De Finibus, "to imagine for myself gluttons who come to the table and are carried away from the banquets, and who gorge themselves again the next day, still drunk." Cer-

units.la: Certum est autem à Græcis & Romanis omnem ad nos fluxisse luxum, Victo enim Mardonio Magni illius Xerxis duce, Græci aurum inter se partiti sunt, vnde apud eos primum luxuria cœpit, si Iustino credimus, quemadmodum Asia primùm deuicta luxum misisse in Italiam fertur: Tempore enim Manlii Curii Respub. Rom. nondum luxuriabat, nec ad luxum inclinabant mores.
units.tr: It is certain, however, that all luxury flowed to us from the Greeks and Romans. For when Mardonius, the commander of the great Xerxes, was defeated, the Greeks shared out the gold among themselves, and from this, if we believe Justin, luxury first began among them; just as Asia, once conquered, is said to have sent luxury into Italy. For in the time of Manius Curius the Roman commonwealth was not yet given to luxury, nor were its morals inclined to it.

units.la: Diebus festis Græci inferias agentes poculis certabãt, & qui cæteris præbibebat, promachus nuncupabatur quasi præpugnans, quatuorque choas, id est, congios ebibebat. Cremato Calano, Alexander conuocatis amicis & ducibus solenne conuiuium instituit, in quo vinariæ potationis certamen indixit, victori coronam proponens vnius talenti, quam promachus quidam quatuor congios ingurgitans accepit bibacissimus omnium.
units.tr: On festival days the Greeks, offering funeral rites, would compete in drinking. Whoever drank more than the others was called the promachus, as if to say "the champion," and he drank four choae, that is, four congii. After Calanus was burned, Alexander called together his friends and commanders and held a solemn banquet, at which he announced a contest in wine-drinking, offering a crown worth one talent to the winner. A certain promachus, the most drink-loving of all, who gulped down four congii, won it.

units.la: Luxum autem Romam & inuexisse, & auxisse atque ornasse etiam Lucullus perhibetur, quem hoc nomine inprimis nobilitatum inuenio apud autores. Deuictis enim duobus maximis & potentissimis Regibus Mithridate & Tigrane ingentes sibi comparauit opes, quas Romam ingressus conterere omnino studuit, quod tamen efficere non potuit, neque hortorum amoenissimorum intolerabili impensa, neque ædium coenationumque amoenissima structura, ĉturâ[?], quin nec conuiuiorum quotidiano ap-paratu, vnde adagio etiamnunc celebrata eius luxuria est, inque proverbium abierunt delitiæ Luculli. Cœnationes ita ordinatas habebat, vt taxata cœnarum summa vnicuiq; loco esset, id est, singulis conuiuiis definitum erat pretium, & apparatus splendor. Quod vel testatur cœ-na illa impendio quinquaginta millium appa-ratu, hoc est, mille ac ducentorum quinquagin-ta aureorum, tanta celebritate ac lautitia epula-rum, vt Pompeius & Cicero, quibus illa daba-tur, obstupescerent. Liuius de bello Macedo-nico de triumpho Manlii loquens, epulæ quo-que ipsæ, inquit, & curâ & sumptu maiori ap-parari cœptæ, tunc coquus vilissimum antiquis mancipium, & æstimatione & vsu in pretio esse cœpit, & quod ministerium fuerat, ars haberi cœptâ: Coquos enim singulos pluris, quam e-quos quiritabantur.
units.tr: Lucullus is also said to have brought luxury into Rome, and to have increased and adorned it, and he is found in the authors as especially famous for this. After he had conquered the two greatest and most powerful kings, Mithridates and Tigranes, he acquired immense wealth, and on entering Rome he took great pains to squander it entirely. He could not manage this, neither by the unbearable expense of his most pleasant gardens, nor by the most elegant construction of his houses and dining halls, nor even by the daily preparation of his banquets. From this his luxury is still celebrated in a proverb, and the "delights of Lucullus" have passed into a saying. He arranged his dinners so that the total cost of each dinner was fixed for each place: that is, a price and a level of splendour were set for each banquet. This is attested by that dinner which cost 50,000 denarii for its preparation, that is, 1,250 gold pieces, with such crowds and such lavish feasting that Pompey and Cicero, to whom it was given, were astonished. Livy, speaking in his account of the Macedonian war about the triumph of Manlius, says: "The banquets themselves began to be prepared with greater care and expense; then the cook, who was among the ancients the cheapest slave, began to be valued both in price and in use, and what had been a menial service began to be regarded as an art; for they were valued at more than horses, individually, as they were ranted about."

units.la: Et hodie nullus prope mortalis æstimatur pluris, quàm qui peritissimè censum Domini mergit. Non tulit tamen hanc palmam solus Lucullus, quippe eius prodigen-tiam M. Apitius nepotinis helluationibus si non exsuperasse, æquasse tamen dicitur, ob quod in proverbium abierunt cœnæ Apitia-næ, sexcenties enim sestertium, id est, quindeci-es centena aureorum millia inexplebili illa in gluuie helluatus est, cumque posset adhuc du-centis quinquaginta millibus vitam lauto ele-gangantique victu producere, tamen venenum miser hausit, ne patrimonio tanto superesset, quod iam defecturum eum videbatur. Plinius aptissimum omnium nepotum appellauit gu gitem. Suidas sic de eo mentionem facit: Apicius Marcus in Luxum & inusitatos sumptus multas argenti myriades in ventrem absumpsit.
units.tr: And today almost no mortal is valued more than the man who most skilfully sinks his fortune. Yet Lucullus did not bear this palm alone. For M. Apicius, if he did not surpass his extravagance in the gluttony of his successors, is said at least to have equalled it, and it is because of him that "Apician dinners" have passed into a proverb. He squandered 60 million sesterces, that is, 1,500 hundred thousand gold pieces, in that insatiable gullet; and although he could still have prolonged his life on 250,000 in lavish and elegant fare, the wretch swallowed poison, lest he be left with a patrimony so great that he seemed about to run out of it. Pliny called him the most fitting glutton of all the spendthrifts. Suidas speaks of him thus: "Apicius Marcus, given to luxury and unusual expenses, consumed many myriads of silver on his belly."

units.la: Huius meminit quoque Athenæus lib. 1. asserens eum delicatum & locupletissimum, ab eoque complura placentarum genera Apitiana nuncupata esse: Quin & tanta erat insania gulæ hominis illius, ut in Lybiam ventris explendi gratiâ nauigârit.
units.tr: Athenaeus also mentions him in book 1, asserting that he was dainty and very rich, and that many kinds of cakes were named Apician after him. Indeed the madness of that man's gluttony was so great that he sailed to Libya for the sake of filling his belly.

units.la: Constat autem non aliunde maiorem epularum luxuriam fuisse apud Romanos quàm è piscibus: Unde piscinarii nobilissimi Romanorum dicti: Inde ostrearum viuaria illa celebratissima Sergii Auratæ, qui primus optimum laporum ostreis adiudicauit: nec cessauit gula quin & reliquorum piscium viuaria instituere: Huius inuenti autor fuit Licinius Murena, cuius exemplum deinde nobilitas secuta est, Philippus, Hortensius, Lucullus, cuius piscinæ quadringentis [?] stertiis vaniere: pretia enim piscium insana extitisse docet Mullus ille tantopere iactatus ac nominatus à Plinio, Iuvenale & Macrobio. Hunc ab Asinio Celere viro consulari emptum millibus nummum Plinius tratradidit, id est, ducentis aureis æstimatione Bu-dæi.
units.tr: It is agreed that the Romans had no greater luxury in their banquets than in fish. Hence the most noble fishmongers of the Romans were so called. From this came those most celebrated oyster-beds of Sergius Orata, who first judged the best oysters to be those of the lakes. Nor did the gluttony stop there, but they also set up fish-ponds for the rest of the fish. The inventor of this was Licinius Murena, whose example the nobility afterwards followed: Philippus, Hortensius, Lucullus, whose fish-ponds cost four hundred thousand sesterces. For the prices of fish became mad; this is shown by that mullet so much boasted of and named by Pliny, Juvenal and Macrobius. Pliny relates that it was bought from Asinius Celer, a man of consular rank, for 8,000 denarii, that is, by Budaeus's valuation, 200 gold pieces.

units.la: Meritò igitur Imperii Romani ruinam præ-dixit Cato ille, cum præmoneret vix posse rem-publicam illam, in qua quidem piscmiculus plu-ris quàm bos væniret, consistere, nam pariter Luxuria inuecta est, & Carthago deuicta, cuius excidii autor & suasor extitit Cato, sumpto ar-gumento à præcoci ficu triduo inde allata.
units.tr: Rightly, therefore, did that Cato foretell the ruin of the Roman empire, when he warned that that commonwealth could hardly stand, in which a little fish sold for more than an ox. For luxury was brought in at the same time as Carthage was conquered, and Cato was the author and promoter of its destruction, taking his argument from an early fig brought in three days before.

units.la: Cæterùm mira & immensa auium pretia, si quis animo reputet, facilè coniiciet auro & ar-gento Romanos exuperasse, vrbemq; Romam quasi arcem quandam expilatorum orbis toti-us videbit. Singula paria columbarum veniisse denariis quadringentis, Plinius testis est. Varro verò ait singula paria ducenis nummis vulgò væniisse, sique essent eximia, singulæ millibus nummûm.
units.tr: Moreover, if one considers in one's mind the wonderful and immense prices of birds, one will easily conjecture that the Romans surpassed the world in gold and silver, and one will see the city of Rome as a kind of citadel of the plunderers of the whole world. Pliny is witness that a single pair of doves fetched 400 denarii. Varro, however, says that a single pair commonly sold for 200 coins, and if they were exceptional, a single one for 1,000 coins.

units.la: Coruum loquacem viginti millibus num-mûm emptum constat, id est, aureis quingen-tis: turdos singulos ternis væniisse denariis hi-storia proditum est: horum igitur s. millia hoc pretio diuendita sexaginta millia nummûm fa-ciunt, & certum est tanta fuisse Romæ turdorû auiaria tempore Varronis, vt ex eorum fimo a-gri stercorarentur. Pauones quoq; in sum-mo pretii culmine fuisse aiunt. Marcus enim Aufidius Lurco saginare eos primus instituit, ex eoque quæstus redditus is sestertium lexage-na
units.tr: It is agreed that a talking raven was bought for 20,000 coins, that is, 500 gold pieces. It is recorded in history that single thrushes sold for three denarii each. Therefore, if they sold 5,000 at this price, they make 60,000 coins, and it is certain that at the time of Varro the aviaries of thrushes at Rome were so great that fields were manured with their dung. They also say that peacocks were at the very height of price. For Marcus Aufidius Lurco was the first to set about fattening them, and from this his profit was [...] sesterces [sixty thousand], as Pliny attests; Varro said more than sixty thousand coins, which Budaeus also confirms, that is, by his valuation 1,500 gold pieces. From this tax one can see how great the devastation of gluttony was. Their eggs sold for five denarii each.

units.la: na ha millia habent, vt testatur Plinius: Varro su-pra sexagena millia nummum dixit, quod & Budæus confirmat, hoc est eius æstimatione mille & quingentos aureos, ex quo vectigali potest patere quanta fuerit gulæ populatio. O-ua eorum venierunt denariis quinis. Hortensius Orator pauonem primus cibi gratia Romæ occidit, & augurali cœnæ appositum, cuius exemplum posteritas secuta in priuatas epulas transtulit: Sed neq; in anseribus ingenia Romanorum impigra visa sunt, præcipue vero epatis bonitatem nouêre, fartilibus enim in magnam altitudinem crescit.
units.tr: Hortensius the orator was the first in Rome to kill a peacock for food, and it was served at an augural banquet; his example the later generation followed and transferred to private feasts. But the Romans did not find geese unproductive either, and they knew especially the goodness of their liver, for it grows to a great size when stuffed.

units.la: Aviaria primum instituit omnium generum avium inclusis Marcus Lælius Strabo. Pretia quoq; pomorum mirabilia tradidit Plinius, nam singula Persica primum sestertiis quaternis venisse ait, deinde augescente gratia, auctoritate scilicet iis vescentium, pretium quoq; adauctum ad trecentos nummos.
units.tr: Marcus Lollius Strabo first set up aviaries holding birds of every kind. Pliny also records the wonderful prices of fruits: he says that single peaches were first sold for four sesterces each, and then, as their fashion grew, and surely through the esteem of those who ate them, the price too rose to 300 coins.

units.la: Quare mirum videri non debet, singulas arbores, vt tradit Plinius, millia nummum annuo reditu meruisse, cum septem & sexaginta poma hanc summam conficere potuerint tricenis nummis singula venundata. Ergo singularum arborum circa suburbana Romæ maius erat vectigal, quam apud antiquos prędiorum. Præterea vt nihil intentatum luxus relinqueret, inuentum quoque est quadrupedes sagi-nare, nare, tum feras tum domesticas, & mensis solidas apponere.
units.tr: It ought not therefore seem strange that single trees, as Pliny relates, brought in a yearly yield of a thousand coins, since seventy-seven apples could make up this sum, each sold for thirty coins. So the revenue from single trees in the suburbs of Rome was greater than the income from estates among the ancients. Moreover, so that luxury might leave nothing untried, it was also discovered to fatten quadrupeds, both wild and domestic, and to serve them whole at table.

units.la: Seruilius Rullus primus Romanorum in epulis aprum solidum apposuit, Persarum Magnates credo imitatus, qui in suis mensis solidos asinos, equos, camelos & boues assatos ponebant, vt Græci autores tradunt, nec solum in feris ventris insania visa est, sed & in domesticis, Suem enim celerius castratione pinguescere repertum est, neq; ex alio animali numerosior materia ganeæ inuenta est, quare Censoriæ leges de nullo alio pecore frequentius paginas suas nobilitârunt. Interdicta n. cænis glandia, abdomina, testiculi, vuluæ, sincipita & verrina.
units.tr: Servilius Rullus was the first of the Romans to serve a whole boar at a banquet, I believe imitating the magnates of the Persians, who, as Greek authors relate, placed whole roasted asses, horses, camels and oxen on their tables. And the madness of the belly was seen not only in wild animals but also in domestic ones; for it was found that a pig fattens more quickly by castration, and no other animal yielded a more abundant material for gluttony. Therefore the censorial laws have made their pages famous for no other cattle more often. For they forbade acorns, bellies, testicles, wombs, heads and sow's flesh at dinners.

units.la: Minus profecto mirabilis videtur lancium amplitudo tantopere celebrata, quando pecora integra mensas Romanorum subiisse, Romanorum historiâ proditum inuenietur.
units.tr: The vast size of the platters, so much celebrated, seems indeed less wonderful, since it will be found in Roman history that whole animals were brought to the tables of the Romans.

units.la: Vitellius in principatu suo ducentorum sestertiorum, id est, quinque millium aureorum commentus est patinam, cui faciendæ fornax in campis exædificata est. Escaria insuper vasa ex murrhinis fieri cœperunt post Pompeii victoriam, non tamen sine magna eius infamia, qui tanti luxus autor fuisse visus est. Nero capedinem vnam murrhinam quadringentis sestertiis parauit. Verùm alios fuisse mores Romanorum ante Carthaginem euersam clarum est, etenim legati Carthaginensium dixisse aliquanquando feruntur, nullos hominum benignius inter se viuere, quam Romanos, eodem enim argento apud omnes coenitauisse ipsos: at post- quam de ea triumphauit Scipio, aurumq; illud grande Punicum transtulit, totum in appara- tus mensarum paulò post transiit. Verùm ad ci- bos redeamus.
units.tr: Vitellius, in his reign, devised a dish costing 200,000 sesterces, that is, 5,000 gold pieces, for the making of which a furnace was built in the fields. Moreover, vessels of food made of murrhine began to be produced after Pompey's victory, not without great infamy to him, who seemed to be the author of such luxury. Nero acquired one murrhine dish for 400,000 sesterces. But it is clear that the Romans had other customs before Carthage was overthrown. For it is said that the envoys of the Carthaginians once remarked that no people lived more kindly among themselves than the Romans, for they dined on the same silver among all; but after Scipio triumphed over Carthage and carried off that great Punic gold, shortly afterwards it all passed into the furnishing of tables. But let us return to the foods.

units.la: Glirium somniculosorum sagina quoque instituta est, & viuaria, ne quid venter non de- uoraret. Cochlearum pariter & saginam & vi- uaria commentus est Fuluius Hirpinus, vt illæ altiles ganeam quoq; implerent. Sed & vermes qui in ligno humore scilicet nimio nascuntur, Cossos appellant; saginare altilesq; facere luxus inuenit, quin & alia fœdiora animalia in deli- tias gulæ verterunt.
units.tr: The fattening of sleepy dormice was also instituted, and their enclosures, so that the belly might not devour anything. Fulvius Hirpinus likewise devised fattening and enclosures for snails, so that these fattened birds too might fill the gullet. Moreover, the worms which are born in wood from excessive moisture, which they call cossi, luxury discovered how to fatten and make into fat birds; and indeed it turned other more foul animals into delights of the gullet.

units.la: In vinorum quoque differentiis insaniuisse victorem orbis populum in confesso est. Primū enim fuit magna parsimonia, vel propter rari- tatem, vel quoniam sibi quisque moderaba- tur, transmarina enim diu fuêre in auctoritate, sed vbi bona sua intellexit Italia salernumque repertum, obscurata est eorum gloria. Ve- rùm & de mensis secundis & mellitis operibus aliquid degustandum: per mellita hîc intel- ligantur fercula dulciora, quæ tunc mensis se- cundis inferri solebant, vt nostra memoria Saccharati missus epularum à pistoribus dulciariis, & omnia quæ bellariorum censu continentur, & saccharei panificii operisq; structura in coenis, quæ in lanceis argeteis ad ostentationem traducuntur, magis vt delibentur, quàm vt esitentur. Nero indicebat familiaribus suis coenas, quarum vni mellita quadragenis sestertiis constiterunt: Quadragies autem sestertium, si centenis millibus aureorum nostrorum æstimentur, quanti ipsa coena æstimari poterit? hic verò diuitiarum & pecuniæ fructum non alium expectabat quàm profusionem, sordidos ac deparcos esse dicens, quibus ratio impensarum constaret, prælautos verò & magnificos, qui abuterentur ac perderent. Laudabat idem mirabaturque auunculū Caium Caligulam nullo magis nomine, quàm quòd ingenies Tiberio relictas opes breui spatio prodegisset: hic in omni vitæ parte prodigos omnes superauit, commentus nouum balnearum vsum, portentosissima quoque genera ciborum atq; coenarum, vt calidis frigidisq; vnguentis lauaretur, pretiosissimasq; margaritas aceto liquefactas sorberet, conuiuis ex auro panes, atque obsonia apponeret, aut frugi hominem esse oportere aut Cæsarem, dictitans. Is opes immensas non modo deparci, sed & sordidi Imper. Tiberii, quas annis tribus & viginti confiscauerat, non toto vertente anno absumpsit, id est, sexcenties septuagies quinquies centena millia aureorum nostrorum, æstimante Budæo.
units.tr: It is widely agreed that the conquerors of the world went mad over the distinctions between wines too. At first there was great frugality, either because of their rarity or because each man kept to moderation for himself; for foreign wines held authority for a long time, but when Italy came to know its own goods and Salernum was discovered, their glory was obscured. But we must also taste something of the second courses and honeyed dishes: by "honeyed" are meant the sweeter dishes, which were then customarily brought in with the second courses, such as, in our own memory, the sugared dishes sent from the confectioners, and everything included under the name of dessert, and the sugar-paste structures at dinners, which are carried round on silver platters for show, to be tasted rather than eaten. Nero used to announce dinners to his friends, one of which, consisting of honeyed dishes, cost four hundred thousand sesterces. Now if forty million sesterces are reckoned at a hundred thousand of our gold pieces, what price could the dinner itself be reckoned at? He, moreover, expected no other fruit of his riches and money than extravagance, saying that those who kept a record of their expenses were mean and stingy, while those who were lavish and magnificent were the ones who used up and wasted everything. The same man praised and admired his uncle Caligula for nothing more than that he squandered in a short space the vast wealth left him by Tiberius. Caligula surpassed all prodigals in every part of life: he invented a new use of baths, so that he bathed in hot and cold perfumes, and he drank down the most precious pearls dissolved in vinegar; he set before his guests bread made of gold and dishes of the same kind, saying that a man ought to be either thrifty or Caesar. He used up in less than a full year the immense wealth which Tiberius had amassed over twenty-three years and confiscated, namely, according to Budaeus, six hundred and seventy-five million of our gold pieces.

units.la: Vitellius præcipuè luxuriæ geneæq; deditus nouies millies sestertiûm paucis mensibus interuertit, teste Tacito: quadrifariam epulas dispertiebat, in ientacula, prandia, cœnas, & commessationes, quibus vt sufficeret, vomitibus assiduè vtebatur. Quod etiam factitasse Claudium Cæsarem inuenio, pinnâ in os indita, vinû enim cibosque quocunq; tempore appetebat auidissimè, conuiuia agitabat & assidua & ampla, nec triclinio vnquam abscessit, nisi distentus ac madidus, erat boletorum auidissimus: Quare per hanc occasionem venenum ei datum ab Agrippina coniuge, quo facto illa terris venenum alterum sibiq; ante omnes Neronem dedit.
units.tr: Vitellius, given above all to luxury and gluttony, squandered nine hundred million sesterces in a few months, according to Tacitus. He divided his feasts into four kinds: breakfasts, lunches, dinners and drinking-parties, and to keep up with them he constantly used vomiting. I find that Claudius Caesar did the same, putting a feather down his throat; for he craved wine and food most greedily at any hour, held frequent and lavish banquets, and never left the dining couch except stuffed and drunk. He was most greedy for mushrooms. On this occasion he was given poison by his wife Agrippina, and by that deed she gave another poison to the earth and to herself, and before all to Nero.

units.la: Verûm famosissima illa fuit supra cæteras cœna, Vitellio à fratre data, in qua duo millia electissimorum piscium & septem auium apposita traduntur: Scarorum iecinora, Phasianorum, & Pauonum cerebella, linguæ Phœnicopterum, murenarumque lactes à Carpathio vsque fretoque Hispaniæ petitæ, eam exornarunt gloriaq; palati exiterunt.
units.tr: But the most famous of all dinners was the one given by Vitellius's brother to Vitellius, at which, it is reported, two thousand of the choicest fish and seven kinds of birds were served: livers of parrotfish, brains of pheasants and peacocks, tongues of flamingos, and milt of lampreys brought from Carpathus as far as the strait of Spain; these adorned the table and were the pride of the palate.

units.la: Conuiuia M. Antonii & Cleopatræ commemorare superuacaneum est.
units.tr: It is superfluous to recall the banquets of Mark Antony and Cleopatra.

units.la: Vnum tantùm memoratu inprimis dignum adiiciam. Marcus Antonius exquisitis quotidie epulis saginabatur, & per luxum inusitatum debacchabatur: Ad eum enim Reges Orientis tis salutandi causâ confluebant, quibus impendiis exhausisse ducenta millia talentorum fertur, hoc est, centies & vicies mille aureos. Verum Cleopatra Aegypti Regina lautitiam eius omnem apparatumque fastu meretricio superbiaq; detrectabat, dictitans vna se cœna centies sestertium absumpturam. Quod equidem etsi incredibile Antonius existimaret, cupiebat tamen discere, quare condicta est cœna, in qua Regina magnificam alias epularum struem, sed quotidianam Antonio posuit: irridenti autem & computationem expostulanti illa se in ea cœna taxationem consumpturam confirmabat, quare mensam secundam inferri iubens detractum auribus vnionem aceto mersit & liquefactum absorbuit: singulare &ferè vnicum naturæ opus, vt ait Plinius, auribus gerebat Cleopatra. Quis quæso non obstupescat vno ferculo secundæ mensæ centies sestertium, id est, ducenta & quinquaginta millia aureorum absumta? tanti enim æstimatus est hic vnio Cleopatræ.
units.tr: I will add just one thing that is especially worth recording. Mark Antony was fattened daily on exquisite feasts and ran riot in unusual luxury; for kings of the East flocked to him to pay their respects, and it is said that he exhausted two hundred thousand talents on these expenses, that is, a hundred and twenty thousand gold pieces. But Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, scorned all his elegance and display with a harlot's pride and arrogance, declaring that she would spend a hundred thousand sesterces on a single dinner. Antony thought this incredible, yet he wished to learn how it could be, so a dinner was agreed upon, at which the queen served a magnificent arrangement of dishes, though one of the usual kind, to Antony. When he laughed and demanded an accounting, she insisted that she would spend the total cost on that dinner alone. Then, ordering the second course to be brought in, she took the pearl from her ear, dropped it into vinegar, and when it had dissolved, drank it down. Cleopatra wore this pearl in her ears, a unique and almost singular work of nature, as Pliny says. Who, I ask, would not be astonished that a hundred thousand sesterces, that is, two hundred and fifty thousand gold pieces, were spent on one dish of the second course? For that pearl of Cleopatra was valued at that much.

units.la: Tres historiæ prodiderunt qui experti sunt quid in gloria palati saperent margaritæ: Aesopi Tragœdi Filius primus id ausus est tentare: deinde Regina Aegypti, tertius Caius Cæsar Romanus princeps, & certum est luxum auctū, & diminutum moribus principum dominantium. tium. Lentuli quoque auguris luxus cœnarum nobilis fuisse proditur. Hic à Seneca maximum diuitiarum exemplum appellatus est, millies enim sestertium vidit, hoc est, centies centena millia aureorum: is est apud quem Cicero cœnauit, vt ipse refert in epistolis.
units.tr: Three historians have recorded those who tried what pearls taste like in the glory of the palate: first the son of Aesopus the tragic actor dared to attempt it; second, the queen of Egypt; third, Gaius Caesar, the Roman princeps. It is certain that luxury grew with these examples, and that the morals of ruling princes declined. The luxury of the augur Lentulus is also reported to have been notorious for its dinners. Seneca called him the greatest example of wealth, for he saw a thousand million sesterces, that is, a hundred million gold pieces. This is the man with whom Cicero dined, as Cicero himself reports in his letters.

units.la: Clodius, quem Milo interfecit, perdita fuit luxuria: quin & Milo ipse egregius prorsus homo, cuius æs alienum inter animi humani prodigia duxit Plinius, rerumq; memorabilium æstimator & acutus & censor grauis.
units.tr: Clodius, whom Milo killed, was a lost man through luxury; and Milo himself, an outstanding man, whose debt Pliny counted among the marvels of the human mind, was both a keen judge of memorable things and a severe censor.

units.la: Heliogabalum luxuriæ perditissimæ quoq; fuisse historiæ tradunt. Sortes is conuiuales scriptas in cochlearibus habuit tales, vt alius haberet X. Camelos, alius X. struthiones, alius X. muscas, alius decem lib. auri, alius decem lib. plumbi, alius decem ova gallinacea, alius X. vrsos, alius X. glires, alius X. lactucas, alius X. lib. bubalinæ carnis: exhibuit nauales pugnas in Euripis vino plenis. Idem nunquam minus centum sestertiis cœnauit, aliquando autem tribus millibus computatis, teste Lampridio.
units.tr: Histories also tell that Heliogabalus was the most abandoned of all in luxury. He had dinner-lots written on spoons, such that one guest would have ten camels, another ten ostriches, another ten flies, another ten pounds of gold, another ten pounds of lead, another ten hen's eggs, another ten bears, another ten dormice, another ten lettuces, another ten pounds of buffalo meat. He staged naval battles in pools filled with wine. The same man never dined for less than a hundred thousand sesterces, and sometimes his dinners were reckoned at three million, according to Lampridius.

units.la: Iulius Seuerus donauit calices singulis conuiuis per singulas potiones myrrhinos & crystallinos: dedit vasa aurea, argenteas & aureas coronas, dedit & vehicula cum mulionibus & mulabus, cum iunctuAfter iunctuaris argenteis, vt ita à conuiuio redirent: Conuiuium æstimatum ferunt sexagies sexcentum millibus sestertiorum, rum, teste Capitolino. Vnde non in cibis tantum, verum etiam in omni vitæ parte modum nullum statutum apud Romanos aliquot seculis inconfesso est. Si quis enim reputet animo ludorum cœnationumq; apparatus prodigentissimos, ædium & villarum insanas structuras, aliaq; id genus, horrescit animus, nec mirum, cùm terrarum Domini vna cum opulentia gentium victarum, mores quoque & cultus induerint, quod in Alexandro notissimum est, is enim deuicto primùm Dario luxuriosa conuiuia & epularum magnificentiam sectari cœpit, vt transiret in mores quos vicerat, immemor scilicet tantas opes his moribus amitti: & certum est paucas fuisse gentes barbaras, quæ aliquando luxuriam non sint amplexatæ, quod malum à victoriis & præda spoliisq; hostium profectum constanter asserendum.
units.tr: Julius Severus gave to each guest, at each course, cups of murrhine and crystal; he gave golden vessels, silver and gold crowns, and also carriages with muleteers and mules, with silver harness, so that they might return home from the banquet in this way. The banquet is said to have been valued at sixty-six million sesterces, according to Capitolinus. Hence for several centuries among the Romans no limit was set, not only in food but in every part of life. For if one considers in mind the most lavish preparations for games and dinners, the mad constructions of town houses and country villas, and other things of that kind, the mind shudders, and no wonder, since the lords of the lands, together with the wealth of the conquered nations, also took on their morals and customs, as is best known in the case of Alexander. For after he had first defeated Darius, he began to pursue luxurious banquets and magnificence in feasts, so that he might pass over into the morals he had conquered, forgetting, of course, that so great a wealth would be lost by these morals. And it is certain that there were few barbarian nations which did not at some time embrace luxury; this evil, it must be firmly asserted, came from victories and the plunder and spoils of enemies.

units.la: Cum itaque luxus apud Romanos ad summum fastigium culmenque ita peruenisset, nullis legibus, nullis edictis, nullaq; multa castigari coërcerive potuerunt. Verum principiis obstandum erat prisca illa seueritate & parsimonia, quæ in infantia imperii extitit. Leges equidem sumtuarias Romæ promulgatas inuenimus innumeras, sed nulla fuit, quæ capitalem luxum, at ne exilio quidem multaret, rametsi probrose obiici solitum Lucio Crasso & Lucullo. Phania lex, qua cauebatur ne quis carius obsonaret, tres tantum habuit qui parerent, Mutium scilicet Scæuolam, Cecilium Tuberonem & Rutilium Russum, qui historiā Romanam Græce scripsit, auctores Athenæus & Macrobius. Parsimonia inquit Gellius libr. noct. Attic. 2. apud veteres Romanos, & victus atque cœnarum tenuitas, non domestica solū observatione & disciplina, sed publica quoque animaduersione legumque complurium sanctionibus custodita est: Et paulo post. Senatus decretum vetus est C. Fannio & M. Valerio Messala consulibus factum, in quo iubentur principes ciuitatis, qui ludis Megalensibus antiquo ri u mutua inter se conuiuia agitarent, iurare apud consulem conceptis verbis, non amplius in singulas cœnas sumptus esse facturos, quam centenos vicenosq; æris, præter olus & far & vinum, neque vinoalienigeno, sed patrio vsuros, neq; argenti plus pondo in conuiuio quam libras 100. illaturos.
units.tr: Since luxury among the Romans had thus reached the highest summit and peak, it could not be checked or restrained by any laws, any edicts, or any fine. Yet they ought to have resisted at the beginning, with that ancient severity and frugality which existed in the infancy of the empire. We indeed find innumerable sumptuary laws promulgated at Rome, but there was none which punished capital luxury, nor even with exile, although Lucius Crassus and Lucullus were commonly and shamefully reproached with it. The Fannian law, by which it was provided that no one should buy food more expensively, had only three men to obey it: Mutius Scaevola, Caecilius Tubero and Rutilius Rufus, who wrote Roman history in Greek; the authors are Athenaeus and Macrobius. Gellius, in the second book of his Attic Nights, says: "Among the ancient Romans frugality and the simplicity of food and dinners was observed, kept not only by domestic habit and discipline but also by public censure and the sanctions of many laws." And a little later: "There is an ancient decree of the Senate, passed in the consulship of Gaius Fannius and Marcus Valerius Messala, in which the leading men of the state, who held mutual dinners among themselves during the Megalensian games, according to ancient custom, were ordered to swear before the consul in set words that they would not spend more on any single dinner than a hundred and twenty asses, apart from vegetables, spelt and wine; that they would drink native wine, not foreign; and that they would not bring more than a hundred pounds' weight of silver into the banquet."

units.la: Sed post id Senatusconsultum Lex Fannia lata est, quæ ludis Romanis, item ludis plebeis & Saturnalibus in singulos dies centenos æris insumi concessit, decemq; aliis diebus in singulis mensibus tricenos, cæteris vero omnibus diebus denos.
units.tr: But after that decree of the Senate, the Fannian Law was passed, which allowed up to one hundred asses to be spent each day at the Roman Games, the Plebeian Games, and the Saturnalia; thirty asses on ten other days in each month; and ten asses on all remaining days.

units.la: Lex deinde Licinia rogata est, quæ cum certis diebus sicut & Fannia, centenos æris consumi permi permisisset,nuptiis ducenos indulsit, caeterisque diebus tricenos, tum & carnis aridae & salsamenti certa pondera in singulos dies constituit. Has leges nonnulli obseruarunt, eas tamen postea situ obliteratas L. Sylla renouauit,quoniam videret plerosque in patrimoniis amplis helluari, & familiā pecuniamq; prandiorum gurgitibus proluere. Legem itaque tulit ad populum,qua cautum est,ut Calendis, Idibus nonisq; diebus ludorum , feriisq; quibusdam solennibus tricenos sestertios in coenā insumere ius esset atq; potestas, caeteris autem diebus omnibus non amplius ternos. Sed hæc ridicula habita est, & à nullo obseruata.
units.tr: Next the Licinian Law was proposed. Like the Fannian Law, it allowed one hundred asses to be spent on certain days, but it permitted two hundred for weddings and thirty on all other days. It also fixed set weights of dried meat and salted meat for each day. Some people kept these laws, but later, once they had fallen into disuse and been forgotten, Lucius Sulla revived them, since he saw that many were squandering their ample estates and pouring their households' money down the gullet of lavish dinners. So he proposed a law to the people providing that on the Kalends, the Ides, and the Nones, on days of games, and on certain solemn festivals, it was lawful and permitted to spend thirty sesterces on a dinner, but on all other days no more than three. Yet this was treated as ridiculous and observed by no one.

units.la: Nonnulliq; censent eum sic sanxisse , non ut modum sumptibus statueret, sed pretia minueret,ut pluribus luxuriosè viuendi facultas esset: & mirari subit,Syllam in tanta tyrannide & auorum suorum tantis funeribus &proscriptionibus,tam scrupulosè rei escariae modum voluisse statuere , & Scauri illius sui priuigni portentosissimam prodigalitate conniuentibus oculis praeteriisse.
units.tr: Some think that Sulla enacted it not to set a limit on expenses but to lower prices, so that more people would have the means to live in luxury. And one cannot help wondering that Sulla, in such a tyranny and amid the great slaughter of his ancestors' funerals and proscriptions, should have been so scrupulous about setting a limit on food, while he overlooked, with eyes closed, the monstrous extravagance of Scaurus, his stepson.

units.la: Alia autem fuit lex Æmilia, quae non sumptus coenarum,sed ciborum genus & modum praefiniebat.
units.tr: There was also another law, the Aemilian, which regulated not the amount spent on dinners but the kinds and quantities of food.

units.la: Postremo Lex Iulia ad populum peruenit, C. Augusto imperante , qua profestis quidem diebus ducēti finiuntur,Calendis,Idibus,No-nis & nis & aliis quibusdam festiuis trecenti, nuptiis & repotiis, hoc est, postridie nuptiarum sestertij mille, qui quinque & 20. aureis coronatis æstimantur: Christianorum nuptiæ nostra ætate longe luxuriosiores, & sumptuosiores, quippe vel quotidiana conuiuia longe hanc taxationē excedunt, sestertij enim ducenti in singulas cœnas quinq; æstimantur coronatis. Porro si qui essent Romani, qui simularent frugalitatē & continentiam, ij quæ lege excepta erant, id est, hortensia & quæ terræ nata vocant olera, legumina omnia, fungos & tubera ita laute condiebant, vt facile aliorum, quæ non erant excepta, sumptus superarent, eaq; non magnopere desiderarent, quo factum, vt è luxu in luxum damnosiorem lapsi sint magno sanctionum illarum contemptu ac derisu.
units.tr: Finally, the Julian Law was brought before the people in the reign of Gaius Augustus. It limited spending to two hundred sesterces on ordinary days, and to three hundred on the Kalends, the Ides, the Nones, and certain other festive days; and for weddings and wedding feasts, that is, the day after the wedding, to one thousand sesterces, which are valued at twenty-five gold crowns. In our own age the weddings of Christians are far more lavish and costly; indeed, even their daily banquets far exceed this assessment, for two hundred sesterces per dinner are valued at five crowns. Moreover, if there were any Romans who pretended to thrift and self-restraint, they dressed up those things that were exempted from the law, namely garden herbs and what they call the produce of the earth, all pulses, mushrooms, and truffles, so lavishly that they easily exceeded the expense of the items that were not exempted. Nor did they greatly miss those items. The result was that they slid from one extravagance into a more ruinous one, with great contempt and mockery of those sanctions.

units.la: Extant & aliæ censoriæ leges, teste Plinio, glandia in cœnis, gliresq; apponi vetantes. Inuenti pariter sunt principes, qui bacchanalia viuentes coercere luxum simularint.
units.tr: Other censorial laws also survive, according to Pliny, forbidding acorns and dormice to be served at dinners. Likewise there have been rulers who, while living in Bacchanalian fashion, pretended to restrain luxury.

units.la: Domitianus in summa frugum penuria & vini vbertate largissima edixit, ne quis in Italia nouellaret, vtq; in prouinciis vineæ succiderētur. Fertur etiam C. Cæsar legem sumptuariā seuere admodum obseruare iussisse, dispositis etiam circa macellum custodibus, qui ementium obsonia retinerent.
units.tr: Domitian, in a time of great scarcity of grain and an abundant glut of wine, decreed that no one in Italy should plant new vineyards, and that vines in the provinces should be cut down. It is also said that Gaius Caesar ordered a sumptuary law to be observed very strictly, even stationing guards around the market to hold back those who bought provisions.

units.la: Verum boni principes bonis suis moribus & vita proba exemplum satis præbent sobrie & modeste vivendi.
units.tr: Yet good rulers, by their good conduct and upright lives, provide sufficient example of living soberly and modestly.

units.la: Augustus in principatu suo, vitæ suæ seueri-tate atq; temperantia luxum diminuit.
units.tr: Augustus, during his principate, reduced luxury by the severity and temperance of his own life.

units.la: Hadriani modestia suis pro lege fuit.
units.tr: The moderation of Hadrian was law enough for his subjects.

units.la: Antonius Pius tali vsus est victu, vt esset opulentia sine reprehensione, parsimonia sine sordibus, & mensa eius per proprios seruos, aucupes, piscatores, ac venatores instrue-retur.
units.tr: Antoninus Pius lived on such a diet that there was abundance without reproach and thrift without squalor; his table was supplied through his own slaves, fowlers, fishermen, and hunters.

units.la: Temperantia quoque nobilitatos inuenio Phocionem, Aristidem, Phormionem, exercituum clariss.[?]duces, Epaminondam Thebanum, Agesilaum illum magnum, Cleomenem Lacedæmonium, Alexandrum Macedon. Catonem Censorium, &c.
units.tr: I find that men of distinction were also temperate: Phocion, Aristides, Phormio, most famous generals of their armies; Epaminondas of Thebes; the great Agesilaus; Cleomenes of Sparta; Alexander of Macedon; Cato the Censor, and others.

units.la: Non omiserim imperatoris cuiusdam Christiani seuerum verbum ad milites Sarracenis victos, qui cum causam in vini inopiam reiicerent, quod scilicet vinum soleat animos incendere, corporiq; vigorem agilitatemq; addere, dixit, at qui vos vicerunt aquam omnes potant, eorum enim lege Mahumetica vini potus prohibetur.
units.tr: I must not omit a stern saying of a certain Christian emperor to soldiers defeated by the Saracens. When they blamed their defeat on a shortage of wine, which of course is wont to inflame the spirits and add vigour and agility to the body, he said: "But those who defeated you all drink water; for by the Mahometan law the drinking of wine is forbidden to them."

units.la: Egregium quoq; Fabricij dictum & factum nefas duxi silentio præterire, cum nullæ sint leges, nullæq; sanctiones censoriæ, quæ magis auocare debeant à vitiis intemperantiæ, quam huiusmodi virorum vitæ exempla. Is Samnitū legatis immensum auri pondus offerentibus rogantibusque enixissime, ut id acciperet, atq; uteretur in illa sua paupertate, fertur manus planas ab auribus ad oculos, & deinceps ad nares, & ad os gulamque, atque inde ad imum ventrem deduxisse, simulque legatis ita respondisse, dum illis membris omnibus quae attigissent, obsistere atq; imperare posset; nunquam quicquam defuturum: quo verbo quid sanctius dici potuit? sed paucos habuit imitatores Romae. Certum est tunc homines bene salubriterque victutos, si ventri atque gulae vasis corporis pessimis non obtemperarint, sed eorum intemperatis cupiditatibus & importunis interpellationibus fortiter obstiterint: at eorum causa maior mehercule mortalium pars vivit, horum gratia avaritia expetitur, luxuria his conditur, his ad Indos navigatur, ad Phasin & ultra quaeruntur obsonia, horum gratia profundissima exquiruntur maria. Quin nulla sunt montium juga, nullae rupes, nulla claustra, quae non transcendantur & infringantur, ut venter saginetur.
units.tr: I think it wrong to pass over in silence the outstanding saying and deed of Fabricius, since there are no laws or censorial sanctions more capable of diverting people from the vices of intemperance than the lives and examples of such men. When envoys of the Samnites offered him an immense weight of gold and begged him most earnestly to accept it and use it in his poverty, he is said to have laid his flat hands from his ears to his eyes, then to his nostrils, then to his mouth and throat, and finally down to his lower belly; and at the same time he answered the envoys thus: "As long as I can restrain and command all these members I have touched, nothing will ever be lacking to me." What could be said more holy than that word? But he had few imitators at Rome. It is certain that men live well and healthily when they do not obey the belly and the throat, the worst vessels of the body, but resist firmly their intemperate desires and importunate demands. Yet, by Hercules, a greater part of mankind lives for their sake: for their sake avarice is pursued, luxury is prepared, ships sail to the Indies, to the Phasis and beyond, provisions are sought, and for their sake the deepest seas are searched. Indeed, there are no mountain ridges, no cliffs, no barriers that are not crossed and broken, so that the belly may be fattened.

units.la: Multi ob luxuriosam & delicatam victus rationem adepti sunt ventrem pinguissimum & distentissimum in amplitudinem.
units.tr: Many, through a luxurious and pampered way of eating, have acquired a very fat belly, swollen to an enormous size.

units.la: Ptolomaeus Euergetes 7. Aegyptiorum Rex & huius filius Alexander ob quotidianam voracitatem adeo fuere ventricosi, vt vix pedem efferre possint, raroque in conspectum populi prodirent.
units.tr: Ptolemy Euergetes, the seventh king of Egypt, and his son Alexander became so bloated from their daily gluttony that they could scarcely move a foot and rarely appeared before the public.

units.la: Dionysius Heracleorum tyrannus filius Clearchi ob intemperantissimas quoq; voluptates ad immodicam corporis molem adoleuit.
units.tr: Dionysius, tyrant of Heraclea and son of Clearchus, also grew to an immoderate bulk through his most intemperate pleasures.

units.la: Fuit item Pitho Bizantius Rhetor obesissimo aqualiculo, pariterq; eius vxor gulæ scilicet vitio & ventris intemperantia.
units.tr: Likewise there was Pitho of Byzantium, a rhetorician, with a very fat paunch, and his wife too, from the same fault of gluttony and intemperance of the belly.

units.la: Nostra memoria nobilissimarum & clarissimarum gentium viri inueniuntur, & in aulis Magnatum non infimum locum obtinentes, qui adeo ventrem tumidum & turgidum habarent, vt multis annis non licuerit pudenda contemplari: quibus tamen voracitatis quoddam vitium à natura insertum est, excusandi veniunt, neq; dubium est alios aliis fuisse & esse edaciores natura.
units.tr: In our own memory men of the noblest and most distinguished nations are found, holding no low place in the courts of the great, who had so swollen and bloated bellies that for many years it was not allowed to look upon their private parts. Yet some excuse may be offered for them, since a certain vice of voracity was implanted in them by nature; and there is no doubt that some are, and always have been, greedier than others by nature.

units.la: Exordiũ sumemus ab ipso tantopere decantato Hercule, quem neq; famem tolerare nouisse, neq; gulæ ventriq; imperare, neq; etiam modum cibis statuere prodiderunt Græci, quæ sunt ardentissimæ & intolerabilis intemperantiæ argumenta.
units.tr: We shall begin with that Hercules who is so much sung about, whom the Greeks reported to have known neither how to endure hunger, nor how to command his throat and belly, nor even how to set a limit to his food; and these are the proofs of a burning and intolerable intemperance.

units.la: Est & incredibilis Milonis Crotoniatæ edacitas, is enim vno conuictu carnis pondo 20. totidemq; panis vorasse creditur, vini vero tres-Choas exhausisse, quin & taurũ viuũ in Olym-pia hupia humeris suis circumtulisse, stadij unius curriculo praedicatur, ipsumq; postea solum die u-no vorasse. Verum in prodigioso robore prodigiosa forte minus videbitur gula.
units.tr: There is also the incredible gluttony of Milo of Croton, who is believed to have eaten at a single meal twenty pounds of meat and as much bread, and to have drunk three choes of wine. Indeed, it is reported that at Olympia he carried a live bull on his shoulders around the course of one stadium, and afterwards ate the whole of it in a single day. But in such prodigious strength a prodigious appetite will perhaps seem less remarkable.

units.la: Sed quis Valentē Iunium, vehicula cum cu-leis onusta, donec exinanirētur, sustinere soli-tū, voracē fuisse non existimauerit, quin & carpenta comprehensa una manu retinere solitū, obnixius contra nitentibus iumentis, aliaque mirabilia fecisse, traditum reperio.
units.tr: Yet who would not think Valens Junius, who used to bear carts loaded with leather bottles until they were emptied, a glutton? I find it also recorded that he was in the habit of holding back carts with one hand while the animals strained against him, and that he performed other marvels.

units.la: Athanatus aurem, quem vidisse se Plinius affirmat, thorace plumbeo indutum, cothurnisq; quingentorum pōdo calceatum, per scenam ingredi nō parci fuisse, putabitur, quemadmodum nec is, qui centenaria pondera pedibus, manibus totidem & ducenaria humeris contra scalas ferebat.
units.tr: One might suppose that Athanatus, whom Pliny says he saw, wearing a leaden breastplate and shod with buskins of five hundred pounds, did not hesitate to walk across the stage; just as he who carried weights of a hundred pounds on his feet, the same number on his hands, and two hundred on his shoulders, against a ladder.

units.la: Theagenes Thasius athleta taurum solus edebat.
units.tr: Theagenes of Thasos, the athlete, used to eat a whole bull by himself.

units.la: Astidamas athleta Milesius, qui ter in Olympia victor euasit, plerunque omnia, quae apud Aribatzanem Persarum Regem in conuiuio parata offenderet, solus absumebat: quamobrem nō inepte dixit ille, mille quidem in Graecia pestes esse, sed athletarum generis pessimam & pernitiosissimam.
units.tr: Astydamas of Miletus, an athlete who was thrice victor at Olympia, would usually eat up alone everything he found prepared at the table of Aribazanes, king of the Persians. Hence that man spoke not foolishly, saying that there are a thousand plagues in Greece, but the worst and most destructive of them is the breed of athletes.

units.la: Est in exemplis quoque Herodotus Megarensis tibicen & saltator, qui panis sex choenices & carnis lib. 20, ederet, viniq; hauriret duas Choas vno conuictu: porro & tubis duabus canere solitum Græci scripserunt.
units.tr: Among the examples there is also Herodotus of Megara, a flute-player and dancer, who at a single meal would eat six choenices of bread and twenty pounds of meat, and drink two choes of wine; and the Greeks have written that he was also accustomed to play on two flutes at once.

units.la: Celeno Phrygiæ rex voracitate & ventris ingluuie memorabili extitisse fertur. In hac quoque nomenclatura reponunt Mithridatem illum Ponti Regem maximum, aiuntque quandoq; certamen & cibarium & vinarium condixisse, constituisseque victori præmium talentum vnum argenteum, atque in eo certamine Regem ipsum declaratum victorem.
units.tr: Celeno, king of Phrygia, is said to have been remarkable for his gluttony and the excess of his belly. Some also put in this catalogue that great king of Pontus, Mithridates, and say that once he proposed a contest of eating and drinking, with a silver talent as the prize for the winner, and that in that contest the king himself was declared the victor.

units.la: Capitolinus maximum patrem narrat frequenter bibisse vno die vini amphoram Capitolinam, & edisse 40 carnis libras.
units.tr: Capitolinus relates that the elder Maximinus often drank an Capitoline amphora of wine in a single day and ate forty pounds of meat.

units.la: Gulosus ille Phago Aureliano Imperatori in delitijs fuit, quod vno in prandio ederet aprum totum, veruecem vnum, præterea porcellum & centum panes, exiccauitque ol-cam vini, quibus in ventrem exceptis percontatus est cocum, quanam hora sit redeūdum ad cœnam, teste Vopisco Digna hercule gula harpyis rapacibus.
units.tr: That gluttonous eater Phago was a favourite of the emperor Aurelian, because at one meal he ate a whole boar, a wether, besides a suckling pig and a hundred loaves, and drained a jug of wine. When he had stowed all this in his belly, he asked the cook at what hour he had to return for supper. Vopiscus is the witness. By Hercules, a gullet worthy of rapacious harpies!

units.la: Proximum nunc est, vt vinolentiæ sectatores prosequamur, bibaces & vinosos, qui circa perdenda vina occupati sunt: dederat nobis natura aquæ potum, qua cætera omnia vtuntur animantia. Verum eius benignitate non contenti multo labore magnoque impendio liquores alios quæsiuimus, qui mentem animumque obtunderent, atq; etiam adimerent, quin & corpora effœminarent & mollia reddèrent. Id vero non in vna orbis terrarum parte inuentum est, sed vbique gentium.
units.tr: Next, let us follow the devotees of drunkenness, the tipplers and winebibbers, who are busy with the destruction of wines. Nature had given us water to drink, as all the other living creatures use it. But not content with its bounty, we have, at great labour and expense, sought out other liquors that dull and even take away the mind and spirit, and that also enfeeble the body and make it soft. Yet this discovery was not made in one part of the world only, but among all nations.

units.la: Bibacitate autem nominatissimi atque celebratissimi fuerunt Græci, qui diebus festis inferias agentes pro poculis certabant, pluris facientes vinolentiam quam opes. Hinc trita vocabula sunt græcari & pergræcari. Ægyptii vino olim admodum dediti fuerunt, eo enim abundabant. Sed contrà hodiè euenit. Nam iurarunt in Mahumeris perditissimi legem, quæ vini vsum sectatoribus abdicauit: quare paucas vites illic nunc videas. Romani Tricongium Torquatum appellârunt à tribus vno imperu congiis exhaustis, & bicongium à duobus congiis Ciceronis filium. Xenarchus Rhodius Metretes dictus est à potione immodica, Maximinus, auctore Capitolino, pater, amphoram Capitolinam siccabat sæpe in die, amphora vero octo congios capit, seu duodequinquaginta sextarios.
units.tr: The Greeks were the most notorious and celebrated for drinking. On feast days, offering libations to the dead, they competed over their cups, valuing drunkenness above wealth. Hence the common words "to Grecize" and "to out-Grecize." The Egyptians once were very much given to wine, for they had plenty of it. But today the reverse has happened: the most abandoned Mahumetans have sworn to a law that forbids their followers the use of wine, so that you now see few vines there. The Romans called Torquatus "Tricongius" from the three congii he once drained at one draught, and Cicero's son "Bicongius" from two congii. Xenarchus of Rhodes was called "Metretes" from his immoderate drinking. Maximinus, the father, according to Capitolinus, often emptied the Capitoline amphora in a day; an amphora holds eight congii, or fifty-two sextarii.

units.la: Tiberius, quod ad merum pronior esset, dictus est Biberius, & pro Nerone Mero. Antiochum quoq; Magnum vinosum extitisse, historiæ testantur.
units.tr: Tiberius, because he was more inclined to unmixed wine, was called "Biberius," and Nero was given the name "Merus." Histories also testify that Antiochus the Great was fond of wine.

units.la: Alexandrum ad vina pronum fuisse, testatur Plutarchus, bibit apud Mediam vini fortis congios duos, & paulò post extinctus est; Philippus quoque pater ebrietati indulsisse multorum rum consensu dicitur: De quodam vini potatore repetitur, Syracusis tamdiu potare solitum, donec ab eo cooperta oua in terra fœtum ederent, prodente Aristotele & Plinio eius interprete.
units.tr: Plutarch testifies that Alexander was inclined to wine: at Media he drank two congii of strong wine and died shortly afterwards. It is also said, by the agreement of many, that his father Philip indulged in drunkenness. Of a certain wine-bibber it is recorded that at Syracuse he used to drink so long that eggs, covered by him in the ground, hatched chicks, as Aristotle and his interpreter Pliny report.

units.la: Cato Vticensis huic vitio affinis fuisse creditur. Bonosus Imperator, vt scribit Flauius Vopiscus, bibit quantum alius nemo: Et si quando legati barbarorum gentium vndecunq; venissent, ipsis propinauit, vt eos vino obrueret, sic enim ab ebriis consilia eliciebat. Idem Phagi cuiusdam meminit, qui vini orcam vno conuictu biberet.
units.tr: Cato of Utica is thought to have been close to this vice. The emperor Bonosus, as Flavius Vopiscus writes, drank more than anyone else. And whenever embassies of barbarian peoples came to him from wherever, he would pledge them, to overwhelm them with wine, for in that way he drew out their plans from them when they were drunk. The same author mentions a certain Phagus who drank a jar of wine at a single sitting.

units.la: Dionysius Siculus Nestor item vinolentus traditur, nam vel graui instanti pugna à potu non abstinuit.
units.tr: Dionysius of Sicily is likewise reported to have been a drunkard like Nestor, for even when a grave battle was pressing he did not abstain from drink.

units.la: Illyrii cubantes cœnant & bibunt, vt Menander scriptum reliquit, quin & suas vxores, conuictibus adhibent, quibus propinare egregium & pulcrum putant: at demum ipsæ viros e conuiuiis deturbant, aluumq; sibi falciis zonisque latis cingunt, dum potant. Primum quidem leuiter & modicè, postea vero cum liberalius bibunt, arctius validiusq;. Constat multos inuictosq; exercitus militum vinolentiâ fuisse deletos. Carthaginenses non sinebant in castra vinum deferri.
units.tr: The Illyrians dine and drink reclining, as Menander has written, and they also bring their wives to their parties, whom they consider it a fine and handsome thing to toast. At last the women themselves drive the men from the feasts, and they gird their bellies with sickles and broad belts while they drink. At first they drink lightly and moderately, but later, when they drink more freely, they tighten and strengthen their belts. It is well established that many large and invincible armies have been destroyed by wine-drinking. The Carthaginians would not allow wine to be carried into their camps.

units.la: Alcei poëtæ memorabilis fertur ebrietas: namq; semper potans inuentus est, scripsitque sua poëmata ebrius: quod & de Comico Ari-stophane proditur: quin & Epicharmum in scenam primum vinolentiam inuexisse aiunt, vt in totum dixisse liceat, poëtas vel insignes vinosos fuisse. Extant compluria nobilia exempla vinosorum, quæ audientium fastidio parcens prætereo: plura qui desiderat, legat cœnas Athenæi, in quibus magnum Asotorum catalogum reperiet,
units.tr: The drunkenness of the poet Alcaeus is recorded as remarkable: he was always found drinking, and he wrote his poems while drunk. The same is related of the comic poet Aristophanes. Indeed, they say that Epicharmus was the first to bring drunkenness onto the stage, so that, to put it all in one sentence, even distinguished poets have been drinkers. There are many famous examples of drinkers, which I pass over, sparing the disgust of my hearers. Whoever wants more should read the Banquets of Athenaeus, where he will find a great catalogue of wastrels.

units.la: Sed & fœminarum genus vini fuisse auidum poëtæ Græci scripserunt.
units.tr: But Greek poets also wrote that the female sex was greedy for wine.

units.la: Quin & annalibus Romanorum reperiuntur fœminæ vinosæ vel prisci(s illis temporibus, quibus luxus incognitus & ebrietas videbatur.
units.tr: Indeed, in the annals of the Romans, we find women who were drinkers even in those early times, when luxury was unknown and drunkenness seemed a thing of the past.

units.la: Romulo regnum obtinente Egnatius Mententinus vxorem, quod vinum è dolio bibisset interfecit, cuius cædis absolutus est à Romulo.
units.tr: While Romulus held the kingdom, Egnatius Mecennius killed his wife because she had drunk wine from the cask; he was acquitted of that killing by Romulus.

units.la: Est quoq; inter exempla, matronam quandam à suis inedia mori coactam, quod loculos in quibus erant claues vinariæ cellæ, resignauisset.
units.tr: Among the examples is also that of a matron who was forced by her family to die of starvation because she had unsealed the boxes in which were the keys to the wine cellar.

units.la: Præterea inuenimus mulierem à Cneo Domitio dote multatam quod viro inscio plus vina esset vini bibisse, quam valetudo exposceret. Polybius apud Athenæum scribit, Romanorum fœminis vinum bibere non licuisse.
units.tr: Further, we find a woman whom Gnaeus Domitius fined her dowry because, without her husband's knowledge, she had drunk more wine than her health required. Polybius, in Athenaeus, writes that Roman women were not allowed to drink wine.

units.la: Cato censuit osculum fœminis dari à propinquis,vt scirent an temetum olerent,hoc enim tunc nomen vino erat.
units.tr: Cato proposed that women should be kissed by their relatives, so that it could be known whether they smelled of wine, for at that time "temetum" was the name for wine.

units.la: Nostræ hodie cautiores sunt & callidiores, quæ à vini haustu commanducant, aut animsum saccharo intectum, fœniculum,aut coriandrū, quo diuerticulo imponunt maritis atque adulteris.
units.tr: Our women today are more cautious and more cunning: after taking wine they chew aniseed or coriander, or mint covered with sugar, and by this little trick they deceive their husbands and lovers.

units.la: Apud Massilienses lex quoque fuit, qua mulieres aquam potare iubebantur, hancque legem eandem Mileti sua ætate viguisse Theophrastus autor est. Præterea apud Romanos præter fœminas, nec seruilia vinum potabant, nec adolescentes qui annum 30. non attigis-sent.
units.tr: Among the Massilians there was also a law by which women were ordered to drink water, and Theophrastus tells us that this same law flourished at Miletus in his day. Moreover, among the Romans, besides women, neither slaves drank wine, nor young men who had not yet reached thirty.

units.la: Antiquiores quoq; Romani in conuiuiis liberaliorib. tot cyathos singulis haustibus ebibere soliti sunt, quot erant literæ in nominibus amicarum; à qua consuetudine Martialis Epigramma libr. 1. emanauit:
units.tr: The older Romans also, at more generous dinners, were accustomed to drink in each gulp as many cups as there were letters in the names of their mistresses. From this custom Martial's epigram in the first book arose:

units.la: Næniá sex cyathis, totidem Iustina bibatur,
units.tr: Let Naenia be drunk with six cups, and as many for Justina,

units.la: Quinq; Lyca, Lyde quatuor, Ida tribus,
units.tr: Lyca with five, Lyde with four, Ida with three,

units.la: Omnis ab infuso numeretur amica falerno.
units.tr: Let every mistress be counted out of the poured Falernian.

units.la: Atque inde sunt inuenta vocabula, triens, quadrans, quincunx, septunx, & reliqua quæ non magis pocula, quàm mensuras significant.
units.tr: From this custom come the words triens (a third), quadrans (a quarter), quincunx (five-twelfths), septunx (seven-twelfths), and the rest, which signify measures no less than cups.

units.la: Sed certum est Romanos potores habuisse memorabiles, quod satis indicant bicongii, tricongii atq; amphorarii: quamuis consuetudo hic plurimum valeat, nam quanto plus biberint, tanto plus sitiunt Parthi: verum sitis causas non stomachi tantum infirmitati vel firmitati, quod Budæus facit, tribuendum, cum alias unde veniant. Capacitas certè ventriculi & eius amplitudo cibi & potus maiorem copiam expetit, arguitque firmiorem constitutionem viscerisangustia verò & paruitas contra imbecillitatem, potulentorumq; ac esculentorum parsimoniam suadet.
units.tr: It is certain, however, that the Romans had remarkable drinkers, as the bicongii, tricongii and amphorarii sufficiently show, although here custom counts for a great deal: the more the Parthians drink, the thirstier they are. But the cause of thirst is not to be ascribed only to the weakness or strength of the stomach, as Budé holds, since it may come from elsewhere. The capacity and roominess of the little stomach certainly demands a greater quantity of food and drink and indicates a stronger constitution; a narrowness and smallness, on the other hand, suggests weakness and a sparing use of drink and food.

units.la: Itaq; hic tenendum, errare eos qui omnem morborum causam in intemperantiam reiiciunt, quasi hæc sola & vnica sit omnium morborum mater. Licet enim plures occumbant crapula quàm capulo, lancibus quàm lanceis, constat tamen experientiâ certisq; autoritatibus, etiam exactissimè viuentes in periculosos sæpè morbos incidisse.
units.tr: Therefore we must hold that those are wrong who attribute every cause of disease to intemperance, as if this were the sole and only mother of all diseases. For although more people perish from overindulgence than from the sword, it is nevertheless established by experience and by trustworthy authorities that even those who live most carefully often fall into dangerous diseases.

units.la: Verùm de vinolentis hactenus, nunc de priscorum quoq; poculis dicendum aliquid, quæ fuisse multiplicia & variasse etiam pro vinosorum miro ingenio & luxus inconstantia, non est obscurum iudicatu. Latini potoria & pocula appellant, græce ποτήρια.
units.tr: So much for drunkards; now something must be said about the cups of the ancients as well, which were many and varied, according to the remarkable ingenuity of the drinkers and the fickleness of luxury, as is not unknown to those who judge such things. The Latins call them potoria and pocula; in Greek they are potēria [ποτήρια].

units.la: Sed hic prius docendum, an prisci maioribus & capacioribus poculis sint vsi, quam nostra ætas. Scio enim non raro in conuiuiis liberalioribus hanc quæstionem excitari.
units.tr: But here it must first be shown whether the ancients used larger and more capacious cups than our age. For I know that this question is often raised at generous banquets.

units.la: Dicæarchus Messenius Aristotelis discipulus pulus antiquos minoribus potoriis vsos & di-lutius bibisse prodidit.
units.tr: Dicaearchus of Messene, a pupil of Aristotle, reported that the ancients used smaller drinking vessels and drank more diluted wine.

units.la: Chamæleon Heracleotes in eo libro quē de ebrietate scripsit, antiquos græcos censet haud quaquam in vsu habuisse capaciora pocula, sed idipsum esse nouitium in Græcia postea inuentum à barbararum gentium morib. translatum: quin in nulla Græciæ parte pocula ampla fuisse admissa in mensas & potus, quam à Solis magnatibus, heroibus, ab aliquo scriptum esse idem testatur.
units.tr: Chamaeleon of Heraclea, in the book he wrote on drunkenness, holds that the ancient Greeks by no means used larger cups, but that this practice was a novelty later introduced into Greece, transferred from the customs of the barbarian nations. Indeed, he testifies that in no part of Greece were large cups admitted to tables and drinking except by the great men of the Sun, the heroes; this, he says, has been written by someone else as well.

units.la: Spartanis regibus, teste Herodoto, binæ dabantur cotylæ, cæteris verò singulæ in conuiciibus, tanta erat apud eos vini parsimonia.
units.tr: According to Herodotus, the Spartan kings were each given two cotylae, while the others received only one at their feasts, so sparing was their use of wine.

units.la: Nestoris poculum apud Homerum celebratur insigni amplitudine. Vnde patere potest potorium datum cyclopi ab Vlysse paruum haudquaquam extitisse. Poculorum autem nomina recensere quædam absurdum non est, maximè quorum vsus crebrior fuerit & nobilitas præstantior.
units.tr: Nestor's cup is celebrated in Homer for its remarkable size. From this it can be seen that the cup Ulysses gave the Cyclops was by no means small. It is not absurd, however, to list some of the names of cups, especially those whose use was more frequent and whose distinction was greater.

units.la: Fuere quædam potoria gentibus peculiaria, κώθων Lacedæmoniis quod genus erit vtile & commodum in bello, vbi plerumque aquam impuram haurire necesse sit: quin & eosdem figulinis vsos in epulis nuptialibus solennibus & sacrificiis, traditur: nam in aliis conuiuiis aliis vasis potabant.
units.tr: Some cups were peculiar to certain peoples. The Lacedaemonians had the kōthōn [κώθων], a kind of vessel useful and convenient in war, where it is often necessary to draw unclean water. It is also recorded that they used earthenware vessels at solemn wedding feasts and sacrifices, for at other banquets they drank from other vessels.

units.la: Quin & Argiui in quibusdam cœnis figulina na vlurpabant. Sed inprimis Agathoclea regem ferunt potasse, fictilibus & coenasse etiam, cum tamen amicis suis & conuiuis aurea præberi curaret, ne scilicet obliuionem originis suæ ad insolentiam indueret sublatus ex humili patris figuli fortuna ad regnum.
units.tr: The Argives too, at some dinners, used earthenware. But it is said especially that King Agathocles drank and dined from earthenware, although he took care to provide gold vessels for his friends and guests. He did this, no doubt, so that his rise from humble origins, the son of a potter, to the kingship should not lead him to forget where he came from and grow arrogant.

units.la: Romæ quoque eo peruenit aliquando luxuria, vt fictilia pluris venirent quam myrrhina: vnde & collegium figulorum illic constitutum esse narrant.
units.tr: At Rome too, luxury once reached such a point that earthenware sold for more than myrrhine ware. They say that for this reason a guild of potters was established there.

units.la: Nobilitantur gentes terra sua & vasis ex ea. Vasa Arretina commendabantur.
units.tr: Peoples have been made famous by their land and by the vessels made from it. Arretine vases were highly esteemed.
