units.la: Surrentum calicum nobilitatem retinuit: Saguntum quidem in Hispania, & in Asia Pergamum, & hæc vltro citroque per maria transportabantur.
units.tr: Sorrento kept its reputation for cups; Saguntum in Spain and Pergamum in Asia likewise, and these were carried back and forth across the seas.

units.la: Sed Choæ in maxima erant gloria, Hadrianæ firmitatis nomine laudē adeptæ. Amphora vas erat condendo vino accommodatum, non mensis, quanquam Tiberium vini amphoram super coenam cuidam propinasse inuenio, quam vno impetu exhauserit. Potoria ingentia à Romanis vsurpata constat. Nam & eorum proceres sic gloriam quæsiuisse memorantur, vnde Tricongiorum & Bicongiorum præclara illa cognomina. Sed quis quæso crederet hac nostra ætate posse reperiri, qui vno impetu tres congios aut etiam amphoram exsorberet. Plinius, vbi de ebrietate vitanda locutus est, venena excogitata ad sitim quærendam pariter enarrans, cautissimos, ait, ex his balneis quoq; coqui videamus, exanimesq; efferri: iam verò alios lectum expectare non posse, imò verò nec tunicam, nudosque ibi protinus & anhelos ingentia vasa corripere velut ad ostentationem virium, ac plene infundere, vt statim euomant, rursusq; hauriant, atq; iterum, tertioq; tanquam ad perdenda vina geniti. Ex quibus verbis maximis potoriis Romanos bibisse elicitur.
units.tr: But the jugs of Choae were held in the highest glory, having won praise for their Hadrianic sturdiness. The amphora was a vessel suited to storing wine, not for the table, although I find that Tiberius once sent an amphora of wine as a toast to someone after dinner, which the man drank off in a single gulp. It is well established that the Romans used huge drinking vessels. Indeed their leading men are recorded to have sought glory in this way, whence the famous surnames Tricongius and Bicongius. But who, I ask, would believe that in our own age there could be found a man who could drain three congii, or even an amphora, in one gulp? Pliny, speaking of avoiding drunkenness, while also describing the poisons devised to quench thirst, says: "We see the most careful of these men, even from the baths, carried out half-dead. Others cannot wait for a couch, nay, not even for a tunic; naked and gasping there and then, they seize huge vessels, as if to show off their strength, and pour them in full, so that they vomit at once, drink again, and then once more, and a third time, as if born only to waste wine." From these words it is clear that the Romans drank from very large cups.

units.la: Præterea varias eorum figuras fuisse & cœlaturas non est dubium, alia enim ventrosa & patula, alia angustiora & strictiora: Inuenio crateras, pateras, calices, cyathos, Scyphos, Carchesia, in frequentiori vsu apud latinos. In Pauli Æmilii triumpho, crateres argentei, cornua, phialæ, & calices grandissimi affabreq; facti & pulcerrime ornati deferebantur.
units.tr: Moreover, there is no doubt that their shapes and engraving were varied: some were bulging and wide, others narrower and tighter. I find craters, paterae, calices, cyathi, scyphi and carchesia, which were in more frequent use among the Latins. In the triumph of Paulus Aemilius, silver mixing-bowls, horns, phialae and very large cups, skilfully made and most beautifully adorned, were carried in procession.

units.la: Crater, vt Græci putant, dicitur ἀπὸ τοῦ κεράσαι, hoc est, miscere & temperare aquam vino, vel ἀπὸ τῆς κέρατος, q. κερατὴς, quoniam in cornu olim vinum infundebatur: Mos enim fuit antiquioribus primum cornibus potare, idq; fecisse Thraces Xenophon docuit, quin & Philippū Macedonē Atheniensibus cornu propinasse ferunt. Peonios aiunt boues educare, qui cornua gestent tantæ magnitudinis, vt capere possint tres & 4. choas, quare ex iis facere pocula, quoquorum labia argento aurove circumducantur. Porro Athenienses cornibus aureis vsos in potibus quidam memoriae tradiderunt, unde Virgil. dixit:
units.tr: The crater, as the Greeks think, is so called from kerasai [κεράσαι], that is, to mix and temper water with wine, or from keras [κέρας], as if keratēs [κερατής], because wine was once poured into a horn. For the older people had the custom of drinking first from horns, as Xenophon showed was done by the Thracians; and they say that Philip of Macedon once offered a horn to the Athenians as a toast. They say the Paeonians raise oxen whose horns are so large that they can hold three or four choae, and so they make cups from them, whose rims are bound with silver or gold. Moreover, some have recorded that the Athenians used golden horns for drinking, whence Virgil said:

units.la: Crateras magnos statuunt, vinumque coronant.
units.tr: They set up great mixing-bowls and crown the wine.

units.la: Et grandem fuisse craterem oportuit, post quem Virgilius lib. 9. Aen. Rhetum sese tegentem ne ab Euryalo interficeretur, scripsit, quod etiam carmine suo indicat:
units.tr: And the crater must have been large, behind which Virgil writes that Rhetus hid himself, so that he would not be killed by Euryalus, as he also indicates in his verse:

units.la: Est magnum metuens se post cratera tegebat.
units.tr: Fearing greatly, he hid himself behind a great mixing-bowl.

units.la: Pateram quoque in auctoritate fuisse non ambigitur; nam à Virgilio saepe nominatur, praecipue vero in Didonis conuiuio: Cum primis autem principibus & proceribus peculiaris existimatur: unde Fabricius quidem ille Romanus bellicosos imperatores vetabat habere plusquam pateram & salinum ex argento. Calices, qui à Graec. κήλικες, multis modis luxuria variauit. Sed hoc quoq; non fuit satis. Gemmis potare instituerunt mores Romani, & calices Smaragdis contexere, quod Maro seuere admodum & vere reprehendit carmine suo Georgico, cum ait:
units.tr: That the patera too was held in esteem is not in doubt; for Virgil often names it, especially at Dido's banquet. It is considered especially the property of the leading men and nobles. Hence that famous Roman, Fabricius, forbade his warlike generals to have more than one patera and a salt-cellar of silver. The calices, which the Greeks call kēlikes [κήλικες], luxury has varied in many ways. But even this was not enough. The Romans began to drink from gems and to inlay cups with emeralds, which Maro, in his Georgics, rebuked most severely and truly when he said:

units.la: Hic petit excidiis vrbem miserosque penates,
units.tr: Here he seeks the destruction of the city and its wretched household gods,

units.la: Vt gemmâ bibat, & serrano dormiat ostro.
units.tr: So that he may drink from a gem and sleep on Serranian purple.

units.la: Murrhinorum vero & crystallinorum gratia in tia inuenta est ad rigidos potus, quibus pretiū fragilitas fecit: Murrhino calice 8o, sestertiis empto capaci ad sextarios sex potauit consulatis quidam ob amorem abraso eius margine, vt tamen iniuria illa pretium augeret.
units.tr: The fashion for murrhine and crystal vessels for cold drinks was also invented, for which their fragility gave them value. A certain consul, out of love, drank from a murrhine cup bought for 80,000 sesterces, large enough to hold six sextarii, after its rim had been broken off, though this injury only raised its price.

units.la: Nero amissarum rerū nuncio accepto duos calices crystallinos in suprema ira fregit illisos, vt ne quis alius biberet. Idem quoque scyphi fracti membra seruari, vt ostentarentur, curauit. Quin & capedinem quadringentis sestertiis, vt princeps Romanus pretiosissime biberet, mercatus est. Murrhina ex Oriente petebantur, illic enim plurimum nascebantur, præsertim in Parthorum ditione & Carmania.
units.tr: When Nero received news of his losses, in his fury he broke two crystal cups by dashing them together, so that no one else might drink from them. He also took care that the pieces of a broken cup should be kept and displayed. Moreover, he bought a cup for four hundred sesterces so that as Roman emperor he might drink from the most precious vessel. Murrhine ware was brought from the East, for it grew there in greatest abundance, especially in the realm of the Parthians and in Carmania.

units.la: Crystallina in summo fuerunt honore, deportanturque à Veneris ad frigidos quoq; potus quæsita crystallus, planeq; omnium consensu glacies est, nullibi enim reperitur, nisi vbi hibernæ niues maxime rigent. Nascitur sexangulis lateribus. Xenocrates testatus est vas amphorale ex ea visum.
units.tr: Crystal was held in the highest honour, and crystal sought for cold drinks is brought from the Venetian region; it is generally agreed that it is ice. It is found nowhere except where winter snows are most severe. It grows in six-sided shapes. Xenocrates testifies that a jar-shaped vessel was made from it.

units.la: Vitrea nunc sequuntur, ex quibus inprimis laudantur candida translucentia. Vsus eorum creberrimus tum Magnatibus, tū pauperibus. Sunt autem caloris impatientia vt crystallus; nisi præcedat frigidus liquor, quin & virus aut venenum non tolerare vulgo creduntur, aut acrimonia ceparum, aliorumve id genus: fiunt autem omnibus fere coloribus, nulla enim materia aut sequacior & ad picturam commodatior: raro tamen sic picti & coloribus infecti calices ad potandum vsurpantur à vitam nitidiorem viuentibus, tantum ad ostentationem habentur, nisi qui margines inauratas habere visuntur, aut raras lineas in calicis orbe rectas transfuersasque: alij ad escaria vasa, hoc est, tragematum & Saccharatorum, vitro picto vtuntur, aut rubro aut cœruleo, & hyacinthum imitante aut Sapphyrum. Inopia ligni vitreorum annonam flagellat.
units.tr: Next come vessels of glass, of which the clear, candid ones are especially praised. Their use was very common, both among the great and among the poor. They cannot bear heat any more than crystal does, unless cold liquid goes before, and they are commonly believed not to withstand poison or the sharpness of onions and things of that kind. They come in almost all colours, for no material is more pliable or better suited to painting. Yet cups painted and tinted in this way are rarely used for drinking by those who live a more refined life; they are kept merely for show, unless they are seen to have gilded rims or fine straight lines running across the circle of the cup. Others use painted glass for dishes of sweets and confections, red or blue, imitating the hyacinth or the sapphire. The lack of wood makes glass costly.

units.la: Scyphi nomen quoq; Græcum esse certum est, ἀπὸ τῆς σκαφίδος, hoc est, vasculo, quo lac aut ferum continetur, cœptiq; sunt fieri fictiles & argentei, multisq; modis ornabantur, auro, argento, gemmis & cælaturæ artificiis singularibus, ideoq; à Romanis ad potandum vsurpabatur, verum in Scyphis aurum spectasse prodigiosum habitum & luxuriosum, Plinius testis est, vbi de petoritorum & vehiculorum ornamentis & inani luxuria disserit.
units.tr: The name scyphus is also certainly Greek, from skaphidos [σκαφίδος], that is, a small vessel in which milk or whey is kept. Scyphi began to be made of earthenware and silver, and were adorned in many ways with gold, silver, gems and singular artifices of engraving. For this reason they were used for drinking by the Romans. But that it was regarded as a prodigious and luxurious display to look for gold in scyphi, Pliny bears witness, where he discusses the ornaments of litters and carriages and empty luxury.

units.la: Vasa quoq; potoria ex Onyche facta primū in Germania: quin & amphoræ ex eo lapide & vrceii: absurde labuntur hic qui Onychem vnguem interpretantur.
units.tr: Drinking vessels were also made of onyx, first in Germany; and also amphorae and small urns of that stone. Those who take onyx to mean the fingernail are clearly mistaken here.

units.la: Trulla praeterea inter vasa vinaria reponitur, quæ ex auro & ex murrhino fieri luxus excogitauit, etiam ad ventris excrementa excipienda.
units.tr: Among the wine vessels is also reckoned the trulla, which luxury devised to make from gold and murrhine ware, and also for receiving the excrement of the belly.

units.la: Fuerunt & alia pocula affabre facta & cæ-lata, vt illa duo, quæ Germanicus Cæsar dedit Cassio Syllano præceptori suo Calamidis manu cælata, quæ postea Zenodorus ita æmulatus est, vt vix vlla artis esset differentia.
units.tr: There were also other cups made skilfully and engraved, such as those two which Germanicus Caesar gave to Cassius Syllanus, his tutor, engraved by the hand of Calamis, which Zenodorus afterwards imitated so closely that there was hardly any difference in the craftsmanship.

units.la: Fiebant item potoria vasa ex Carchedonio, & hodie etiam ex argento & argento viuo, quod vitæ insidiosum arbitror, vix enim fieri potest, quin tempore atteratur & absorbeatur aurum, & reliquiæ argenti viui potibus admisceantur, quæ viscera perrumpant dira tabes: nam certum est aurificum & artificum inaurantium corpora tremore pertentari. Esse quoque Carchesium antiquissimum potorium figuræ oblongæ, testatur Virgil. Aen.
units.tr: Drinking vessels were likewise made of carchedonium, and today also of silver and quicksilver. I consider this treacherous to life, for it can hardly be avoided that gold is worn away and absorbed over time, and the remains of quicksilver get mixed into the drinks, and a dreadful wasting disease breaks through the bowels. For it is certain that goldsmiths and gilders have bodies shaken by tremors. The carchesium too was a very ancient drinking vessel of oblong shape, as Virgil testifies in the Aeneid.

units.la: Hic duo rite mero libant Carchesia Bacho Fundit humi.
units.tr: Here two men pour out Carchesia, duly filled with Bacchus's wine, onto the ground.

units.la: Nomen ei redditum putant à suprema mali in naui parte.
units.tr: They think the name was given to it from the uppermost part of a ship's mast.

units.la: Magnam denique poculorum nomenclaturam à Græcis ad Latinos transiisse extra controuersiam est, cumque nobis plus quam abunde omnis generis suppetant, facto fine riuos claudo.
units.tr: It is beyond dispute that a great stock of drinking-vessel names passed from the Greeks to the Latins. Since we have more than enough of every kind, I make an end and shut off the streams.

units.la: Audiuistis de prisci seculi inclinatis ad luxum moribus, qua gloria si nostræ ætatis mores hominesque defraudarem, magnam certe iniuriam facerem. In hac innumeri viuunt vt edant, non autem edunt vt viuant, longe à Socratis sapientissimi sententia remoti. Vina enim hac nostra ætate tam profuse prodigunturapud Christianos, vt videantur ad perdenda ea geniti: proceres, pauperes, plebs infima, infantes, pueri, viri atque fœminæ pariter vinum amplectuntur, nec sine eo vitam putant beatam, vt nulla in parte operosiorem vitam nostro seculo inueniamus quam in perdendis vinis. Apud nos enim sine lege, sine modo bibitur.
units.tr: You have heard of the manners of the earlier age, inclined to luxury. If I withheld from our own age and its people the glory of such manners, I would certainly do them a great injustice. In this age countless people live in order to eat, and do not eat in order to live, far removed from the opinion of Socrates, the wisest of men. Among Christians, wine is now squandered so lavishly that they seem born only to waste it. Nobles, the poor, the lowest commons, infants, boys, men and women alike embrace wine, and they think life is not happy without it. So in no area of life do we find a busier life in our century than in the wasting of wines. Among us, drinking has no law and no measure.

units.la: Germanorum bibacitas apud alias gentes hodie ante cuncta nobilitatur, atque inter miracula celebratur, cum singuli quaternos quartarios vno prandio hauriunt, & hodie vasa potoria cernuntur, quæ plus quam duas choas capiant, quibus hospites & externos liberalissime inuitant & proluunt: ac nullus hoc tempore est, qui luxuriosas & profusas mensas non struat, quique coquos ganeasque artifices peritissime cibos condientes & patrimonia mergentes non quærat: quam vita intemperantiam apud Christianos maxime debacchari memoria nostra videmus.
units.tr: The drinking capacity of the Germans is now, above all else, celebrated among other nations and praised as a marvel. Single men gulp down four quarts at one meal. Today there are drinking vessels that hold more than two choae, from which they lavishly invite and entertain guests and foreigners. At this time there is no one who does not set up luxurious and extravagant tables, and who does not seek out cooks and gourmet artisans, skilled at seasoning food, who sink their family fortunes. In our time we see that this intemperance of life rages most fiercely among Christians.

units.la: In conuiuiis enim nostris omnes studemus & certamus pro luxus patina & principatu.
units.tr: In our banquets, all of us strive and compete for the first place in luxury and its dishes.

units.la: Nam quo quisq; exquisitissimorum obsoniorum varia genera epularumque varios apparatus & lautos profusius dat, eo magis commendamendatur: at quanto innocentius ille victus fuit, de quo Plinius, qui tunc Asiæ præerat in Epistola quadam ad Traianum Imperatorem.
units.tr: For the more lavishly someone provides a variety of the most exquisite delicacies and sumptuous displays of feasting, the more he is praised. But how much more innocent was that fare which Pliny describes, who at that time presided over Asia, in a certain letter to the Emperor Trajan.

units.la: Coibant Christiani, ad capiendum cibum promiscuum & innoxiū. O tempora, O Christianorum mores prostratos? venimus eo, vt maxime cibis pereamus, hinc innumerosissimum illud morborum agmen ac satellitium nouum, quod indies gulæ culpa emergit: nam certum est vino potuque immodico plurimos funeris ante diem interire.
units.tr: "Christians used to gather to take food together, a common and harmless meal." O times! O the ruined morals of Christians! We have come to the point where we perish chiefly by food. From this comes that countless army of diseases and that new retinue of ailments, which daily rises from the fault of gluttony. For it is certain that very many die before their time from excessive wine and drink.

units.la: Caue vero quis putet eo hæc à me dici, vt omnem apparatum epularum abiiciam, omnéque mensarum voluptatem detester: Cum enim conuiuium, teste Nonio Matell. sit epularis amicorum accubatio, vitæq; habeat coniunctionem, & Cicero conuiuia dixit, quod tunc maxime simul viuatur, haud scio, an ad amicitiam fouendam & conseruandam quicquam [?]possit esse eximius; conuiuia enim publica à prudentibus legislatoribus in hunc finem instituta sunt: habet enim nescio quid philtri in se vinum ad benevolentiam conciliandam.
units.tr: Let no one think I say this to cast off all the furnishing of feasts, or to condemn all the pleasure of tables. For since a banquet, as Nonius Marcellus testifies, is a feast-like reclining of friends, and has a connection with life, and Cicero called them convivia because people then live together most of all, I do not know whether anything can be more excellent for fostering and preserving friendship. For public banquets were instituted by wise lawgivers for this very purpose. Wine has, I know not what, of a love-potion in it for winning goodwill.

units.la: Verum de conuiuarum numero mira est sententiarum inconstantia. Aulus Gellius à trium gratiarum numero ternarium in literas retulit, vnde forte Horatius carminibus suis ternarium numerum tantum asscripsit, cum inquit:
units.tr: Yet about the number of guests there is a remarkable inconsistency of opinions. Aulus Gellius recorded in his writings the number three from the number of the Three Graces, and perhaps for this reason Horace attributed only the number three to his guests in his poems, when he says:

units.la: Tres mihi conuiuæ prope dissentire videntur,Poscentes vario semper diuersa palato.
units.tr: Three guests at my table seem almost to disagree, always demanding different things according to their varied tastes.

units.la: Triclinij verbum à tribus lectis, qui contigui sternerentur, quibus conuiuæ ( vt nunc quoq; Turcæ & Græci) accubarent: Hinc Horatius : Sæpe tribus lectis videas cœnare quaternos.
units.tr: The word triclinium comes from three couches, which were laid side by side, on which the guests (as the Turks and Greeks still do) reclined. Hence Horace: Often you may see four men dining on three couches.

units.la: Et Iuuenalis;neglectum adhibere clientemTertia ne vacuo cessaret culcitra lecto.
units.tr: And Juvenal: to take a neglected client, lest the third mattress on an empty couch should lie idle.

units.la: Sunt apud Græcos, qui tres tantum conuiuas adhiberi censuerūt, alij quatuor, alij quinque, alij sex, vt ita posset intelligi rarius illū morem fuisse obseruatum, nisi forte apud Philosophos & literarum studiosos.
units.tr: Among the Greeks there were some who thought only three guests should be invited, others four, others five, others six. From this it can be understood that this custom was observed more rarely, except perhaps among philosophers and men devoted to learning.

units.la: Porro quæstio quoque fuit & hodie frequenter versatur, num inter epulas & conuiuandum silere oporteat omnino, an philosophandum, & de negotiis seriis loquendum. Quidam enim existimarunt serios & philosophicos sermones mensis abdicandos: atque etiam alia negocia quæ intensiorem cogitationē desiderent, nihil enim castæ philosophiæ commune esse cum turbulento Bacchho aiunt. Nā quemadmodum apud quasdam gentes non licet coniugibus viris suis conuiuia celebrare, foràsque prodire, sed concubinarum & meretricum est epulis interesse & lasciuire, producique in vulgus & pudorem exuere, ita philosophiæ arcana inter patinas & pocula minima detema detegenda sunt aut propalanda. Ifocrates orator summus, rogatus aliquando super coe-nam, ut de eloquentia sua quippiam dissereret, respondisse sic fertur, quæ præsens locus tempusque exposcit, ego non calleo, quæ ego calleo, nec loco præsenti sunt accommoda, nec tempori. Horum a. mirari subit opinionem, cum maximos & clarissimos philosophos libros peculiariter dicasse constet institutioni conviviorum. Platonem dico & Xenophontem Socratis discipulos, qui studiose & diligenter officiz cōviuialia pertractarunt. Quamob-rem de Philosophiæ fontibus in mensa aliquid propinare, non importunum videri debet, sed maxime tempestivum & utile. Mos fuit doctissimis Romanis inter cœnas aliquid legere, & etiam excerpere & adnotare, quod utrumque Plinium factitasse invenimus aliosque non paucos. Cornelius tamen Celsus a cœna intensam cogitationem non esse tutam asseruit, quin & medicorum placita decernunt, haud esse inter edendum laborandum, proinde tunc intendere lectioni animum forte non parum esse noxium quis censuerit. Id observari in ludis literarum videmus, ut cæteris prandentibus aut cœnantibus unus pulpitum conscendat, legatque aliquos Doctorum virorum commentarios, vel etiam caput ex sacro codice. Ego certe in ea sum opinione, ut morosos ac tetricos sercos sermones à mensa debere procul abesse autumem, & conuiuatorem rusticum & inurbanum, qui conuiuas suos (vt plæriq; nunc faciunt) quæstionum ambagibus & deliris propositionibus exagitat. Id vero mal. san quidam agunt, quoties hominem vel Theologiæ, vel Iurisprudentiæ, vel Medicinæ Philosophiæque peritum inuitarint ad cœnam. Accedere in primis ad cibos hilaris quisq; debet, & potibus iocos admiscere, non illos quidem histrionicos & ridiculos, sed honestos & liberales, quales vere elegantes homines solent afferre ex Musarum sacrario. Pythagoricum illud silentium, loquacitatem item & garrulitatem ante cuncta damnari videmus atque improbari. Quare modus statuendus & inter vtrumque medium. In lætitia conuiuali quis ferat medicum aliis conuiuis leges prescribentem ciborum &potuum? quis Philosophum de metaphysicis differentem? quis Iurisconsultum de nodis legum dissceptantem? quis Astronomum de Epicyclis, metopomanticum de lineis frōtis? Mathematicum de numeris terræq; mensura, &id genus alios disciplinarum professores? Qui igitur scientia aliqua clarus conuiuio adhibetur, non de ipsis, vt ait Macrobius, profunditatis suæ inter pocula secretis loquetur, nec nodosas & anxias, sed vtiles facilesque quæstiones mouebit: Scyphis enim ad lætitiam natis Nympharum rum Musarumq; societas non erit sic intempe-stiua: meminisse a. oportet conuiuia muta fere semper displicuisse: unde conuiuatori curandum, ut conuiuas adhibeat hilares, qui epulas eruditis & suauibus sermonibus condiant. Accidit tamen, ut mensarum initio fere semper conticescant conuiuae, intenti scilicet patinis, postea procedente conuiuio hilariores facti sermones & murmura exoriuntur. Cato Maior in agris coenas opiparas exhibebat, ad quas invitabat vicinos, agricolas, aequales suos & familiares: quae quidem consuetudo non solum aequalibus suis, sed & iuuentuti quoque erat gratissima, quippe propter multarum rerum experientiam, orationem memorabilem, sermonesq; prudentissimos studiosissime observabatur. Mensam autem amicitiae eximiam conciliatricem semper affirmauit: Solebat idem super mensam ciues de Republic. bene meritis laudibus exornare, contra vero malos & improbos conuitiis proscindere.
units.tr: Furthermore, there has also been, and still is frequently debated today, the question whether one should keep silent altogether during meals and while feasting, or whether one should philosophize and speak of serious matters. For some have thought that serious and philosophical discourses should be banished from the table, and also other business that requires more intense thought. They say that pure philosophy has nothing in common with the boisterous Bacchus. For just as among certain peoples it is not lawful for wives to hold banquets with their husbands or to go out in public, but it belongs to concubines and prostitutes to take part in feasts and wantonness, and to be led out before the crowd and cast off modesty, so the secrets of philosophy must not be disclosed or published among dishes and very small cups. Isocrates, the greatest orator, when once asked at a dinner to discourse on his eloquence, is said to have replied: "I am not skilled in what the present place and time demand, and what I am skilled in is suited neither to this place nor to this time." Yet it strikes me as strange that this opinion should be held, since it is established that the greatest and most famous philosophers wrote books devoted specifically to the instruction of banquets. I mean Plato and Xenophon, the disciples of Socrates, who diligently and carefully treated the duties of the table. Therefore, to offer some draught from the fountains of philosophy at table should not seem unseemly, but most timely and useful. It was the custom of the most learned Romans to read something during dinners, and also to excerpt and annotate, which we find that Pliny did, and not a few others. Yet Cornelius Celsus asserted that intense thought after dinner is not safe, and the decisions of physicians hold that one should not labour while eating. Therefore someone might judge that to direct the mind intently to reading at that time is perhaps not a little harmful. We see this observed in schools of letters, where while the others are dining or taking supper, one man mounts the pulpit and reads some commentaries of learned men, or even a chapter from the sacred book. I, for my part, am of the opinion that grave and gloomy serious discussions should be kept far away from the table, and I count a host rustic and unmannerly who harasses his guests (as most now do) with the tangled windings of questions and with absurd propositions. Indeed, some do exactly this whenever they have invited to dinner a man skilled in theology, jurisprudence, medicine or philosophy. Above all, each person ought to come to the food cheerful, and mix jests with the drinks, not those that are theatrical and ridiculous, but honourable and gentlemanly, such as truly elegant men are accustomed to bring from the sanctuary of the Muses. We see that the Pythagorean silence, and likewise chatter and garrulity, are above all condemned and rejected. Therefore a measure must be set, and a middle course between the two. In the cheerfulness of a feast, who would tolerate a physician prescribing to the other guests laws about food and drink? Who would tolerate a philosopher discoursing about metaphysics? Who a jurisconsult debating the knots of the laws? Who an astronomer about epicycles, a metoposcopist about the lines of the forehead, a mathematician about numbers and the measurement of the earth, and other professors of this sort of learning? Therefore the man who is invited to a dinner as someone famous for some science will not, as Macrobius says, speak of the secrets of his own depth among the cups, nor raise knotty and anxious questions, but useful and easy ones. For to cups born for mirth, the company of the Nymphs and Muses will not be so untimely. We should remember that silent banquets have almost always been displeasing. Hence the host must take care to invite cheerful guests, who season the feast with learned and pleasant conversation. It happens, however, that at the start of the meal the guests almost always fall silent, intent of course on their dishes, but afterwards, as the banquet proceeds, the talk and murmuring become more cheerful. Cato the Elder, on his farms, used to provide lavish dinners, to which he invited neighbours, farmers, his contemporaries and friends. This custom was most welcome not only to his contemporaries but also to the young, since, on account of his wide experience of many things, his memorable speech and most prudent conversations were observed with the greatest attentiveness. He always affirmed that the table is an excellent maker of friendships. The same man used to adorn with praises, at the table, citizens who had deserved well of the commonwealth, and on the other hand to tear apart the wicked and dishonest with reproaches.

units.la: Paulus Aemylius, qui de Perseo Rege Macedonie triumphauit, post eam victoriam instructissima conuiuia apparauit: Etenim dicebat eiusdem esse artis & disciplinae, terribilem aciem, & suaue conuiuium struere, illam vt formidolosus hostibus, hoc vt amicis gratus esset.
units.tr: Paulus Aemilius, who celebrated a triumph over Perseus, king of Macedon, prepared very lavish banquets after that victory. He used to say that it belonged to the same art and skill to draw up a dreadful battle line and to set out a pleasant feast: the one to be fearsome to enemies, the other to be welcome to friends.

units.la: Apud Homerum inuitati tum aetatibus tum studiis atq; professionibus differebant. Nestor, Aiax, Vlyffes, omnes virtute quidem præstan-tes erant, sed tamen aliter atque aliter, quippe alius oratione & eloquentia, alius corporis vi-ribus, alius vero astutia pollebat. Plato in con-uiuio suo adhibuit Eryximachum medicum. Xenophon Aristophanem poetam. Homerus voluit optimos atq; laudatos viros vocandos: Hesiodus vicinos præcipue. Solebant antiqui Spartani festa sua celebrantes Helotas, quos in seruitutem redegerant, ad vinolentiam & e-brietatem compellere: illosque temulentos, & vino madidos postea in iuuenū cōuiuiis ostendere, vt scilicet huiusmodi ebrietatis ludibrio & turpitudine iuuētus à vino deterreatur. Verum, hominum vitam, morésque & corpus deprauare, vt exemplum aliis præbeatur bene viuendi, an sit mos laudabilis, prudentioribus iudicandum relinquo.
units.tr: In Homer, the guests invited differed in age, pursuits and callings. Nestor, Ajax and Ulysses were all outstanding in virtue, yet each in his own way: one excelled in speech and eloquence, another in bodily strength, another in cunning. Plato in his Symposium admitted Eryximachus the physician; Xenophon admitted Aristophanes the poet. Homer wanted the best and most praised men to be invited; Hesiod chiefly the neighbours. The ancient Spartans, when celebrating their festivals, used to drive the Helots, whom they had reduced to slavery, into drunkenness, and afterwards showed these drunken, wine-soaked men at the banquets of the young, so that the young might be turned away from wine by the mockery and disgrace of such drunkenness. But whether it is a praiseworthy custom to corrupt men's lives, morals and bodies so as to offer others an example of living well, I leave for wiser people to judge.

units.la: Plutarchus Philosophus in primis sapiens & eruditus acerbusq; vitiorum castigator, Lacedæmoniorum illam emendationem inciuilem plane & illiberalem affirmauit. Sed ad rem. Quare detestandi sunt, inque amicorum numero non ferendi, qui nunquam, vt de Pericle tradunt historiographi, apud amicos cœnant, quamdiu in vitæ coniunctione & Republica versantur, omnemq; epularum apparatum abiiciunt, putantes, conuiuia ad deprimendam omnem animi elationem valere, nec facile in conconsuetudine expectationem grauitatis, & fe-ueritatis conseruari: Ego puto nihil magis mo-uere admirationem, quam quotidianam vitæ cum aliis consuetudinem.
units.tr: Plutarch, a philosopher above all wise and learned and a sharp critic of vices, declared that Spartan correction to be plainly uncivil and illiberal. But to the point. Those are to be detested, and not tolerated among friends, who, as the historians tell of Pericles, never dine with friends while they are engaged in the life of companionship and in public affairs, and who cast off all the preparation of feasts, thinking that banquets serve to lower all elation of spirit, and that the expectation of gravity and seriousness is not easily kept up in familiar intercourse. I think nothing wins admiration more than daily companionship with others in life.

units.la: Ipse Christus omnium exemplorum rationumq; loco nobis debet esse, quem Euangelica historia tradit, & conuiuio alios excepisse, & ad aliorum conuiuia accessisse, atq; adeo cum improbæ famæ hominibus, publicanis & meretricibus sæpenumero conuiuia inire minime dubitasse, non libidine quadam immoderataque cibi potusq; auiditate, sed, vt Hieron. cap. 9. Matth. disserit, vt occasionem haberet docendi, vtque illorum inuitationes cum spiritualibus epulis compensaret, illosque hac occasione ab improba vita ad bonam frugem perduceret. His adde Salomonis in Ecclesiaste testimonium, nihil dicentis, homini fere optabilius esse, quam lætari, conuiuari, & soluta quadam animi libertate esse: nec non Syracidis c. 31. & 32. docentis conuiuia iucunda esse, &c. Si igitur Christus cum Pharisæis, publicanis, meretricibus, & id genus aliis conuiuari solitus est, nobis quoq; an hoc liceat, quæritur? Respondetur, non simpliciter & in vniuersum omnem conuiuandi cum impiis libertatem Christianis in sacris literis interdici, quam etiam ipse Paulus reliquit liberam, 1. Cor. 10. sed nimium conuiuum prohiberi, cum videlicet quis auide magnoque studio & voluptate consuetudinem eorum sectantur cum dictis vel factis illorum superstitionibus impietatiq; praebet assensum, cum religionem veram criminandi subministrat occasionem, & Christi exemplo contrarius, in impietate & superstitionibus ipsos confirmat, cum præcipuus conuiuiorum finis sit, omnia facere ad Dei gloriam. Inordinata igitur, immoderata, luxuriosa, mostrosa, portentosa, & sumptuosa conuiuia damnantur, quæ non ex honestatis & charitatis erga Deum & proximum studio, sed ex ambitione, & inexplebili quadam voluptatum cupiditate instituuntur.
units.tr: Christ himself ought to be for us the pattern and the reason for all things, as the Gospel history tells: he both received others at table and came to the tables of others, and indeed he did not hesitate to sit at meat with men of bad repute, with tax-collectors and harlots, very often. He did this not out of some lust or immoderate eagerness for food and drink, but, as Jerome discusses on Matthew chapter 9, in order to have an occasion of teaching, to repay their invitations with spiritual feasts, and by this occasion to lead them from a wicked life to a good way of living. To this add the testimony of Solomon in Ecclesiastes, who says that for a man there is nothing almost more desirable than to rejoice, to feast and to be in a certain freedom of spirit; and likewise Sirach chapters 31 and 32, which teach that banquets are pleasant, etc. If, then, Christ was accustomed to feast with Pharisees, tax-collectors, harlots and such like, the question is put to us too: is this permitted? The answer is that Scripture does not forbid Christians simply and in general every freedom to dine with the wicked, a freedom which Paul himself left free (1 Cor. 10); but excessive feasting is forbidden, namely when someone pursues their company eagerly, with great zeal and pleasure, when he gives assent to their superstitions and impieties by words or deeds, when he gives occasion to slander the true religion, and, being contrary to Christ's example, confirms them in impiety and superstition, whereas the chief end of banquets is to do all things to the glory of God. Therefore disorderly, immoderate, luxurious, monstrous, prodigious and sumptuous banquets are condemned, which are instituted not from a zeal for honesty and charity towards God and neighbour, but from ambition and from some insatiable desire of pleasures.

units.la: Contra vero frugalia, munda, parca, moderata, iucunda, suauia (quæ honestis & liberalibus iocis sunt condita, quales vere elegantes ac eruditi homines solét afferre è Musarum sacratio) maxime probantur, sunt enim luxus exotici dolique ignara.
units.tr: On the other hand, frugal, clean, sparing, moderate, pleasant and agreeable feasts (which are seasoned with honest and liberal jests, such as truly elegant and learned men are wont to bring from the sanctuary of the Muses) are most approved, for they are free from exotic luxury and from deceit.

units.la: De his conuiuiis vere & conuenienter dicitur, quod sint mutuæ hominũ charitatis, amicitiæ, beneuolentiæque vincula & symbola. Vnde recte à conuiuendo dicuntur, vitæque coniunctione & quasi conuictu, quod tunc maxime simul viuatur, teste Cicerone lib. de senectute. Nonius Marcellus epularem amicorum accubationem vocat. Aristoteles in Ethicis conuiuationes hominum amicitiis tuendis ac stabi biliendis perquam accommodatas esse scribit, Cicero Pætum monet, vt cum viris bonis, iucundis, suiq; amantibus viuat, sermone enim familiari, qui in conuiuiis est dulcissimus, vitæ nihil aptius esse nihilque ad beate viuendum accommodatius : ac plurima alia præclara doctissimorum testimonia ad hunc conuiuiorum finem demonstrandum extant: vnum tantum producam, quod est Plutarch. lib.4.Sympos.problem. 1. vbi conuiuii finem esse dicit amicitiæ vel generationē, vel confirmationem iunctam cum voluptate, vnde conuiuium definit viuendi rationem per vini vsum in amicitiam definentem.
units.tr: Of such banquets it is truly and fittingly said that they are bonds and tokens of mutual human charity, friendship and goodwill. Hence they are rightly called convivia from living together (conviendo), and from a kind of living together with one another, because then especially men live together, as Cicero says in his book On Old Age. Nonius Marcellus calls the reclining of friends at table epularis accubatio. Aristotle in the Ethics writes that dinner-parties are very well suited to preserving and establishing friendships. Cicero advises Paetus to live with good, pleasant men who love their friends; for in familiar conversation, which is sweetest at banquets, nothing is more fitting for life, nor more suited to living happily. And many other excellent testimonies of the most learned men exist to show this end of banquets. I will produce just one, from Plutarch, Symposiacs book 4, question 1, where he says that the end of a banquet is the begetting or the strengthening of friendship joined with pleasure; whence he defines a banquet as a way of living, by the use of wine, ending in friendship.

units.la: Hinc festiue admodum Romanus ille solus aliquando cœnans eo die se nō cœnasse dixit, sed edisse tantum, innuens, cœnam semper communione & amicitia veluti condimento indigere. Neq; vero ad amicitiam tuendam stabiliendamq; tantū conuiuia valent, sed &ad simultates inimicitiasq; auferendas: graues enim diuturnasq; priuatorum hominum simultates, odiaq; conuiuiis extincta legimus, ac & iamnunc hodie sæpe homines capitalibus à se inuicem odiis dissidentes conuiuiorum occasione sibi inuicem reconciliari. Sic M. Crassus Ciceroni reconciliatus conuiuio est. Scipio & Hasdrubal conuiuio sibi inuicem reconciliati: vt vere dixisse liceat, mensa posita contentionem
units.tr: Hence that Roman, who once dined alone, very wittily said that on that day he had not dined but only eaten, implying that a meal always needs companionship and friendship as a kind of seasoning. Nor do banquets avail only to preserve and establish friendship, but also to remove enmities and feuds. For we read that grave and long-standing quarrels and hatreds between private men have been put out by banquets; and even today, men who are divided by deadly hatreds are often reconciled to one another on the occasion of a feast. So Marcus Crassus was reconciled to Cicero at a banquet; Scipio and Hasdrubal were reconciled to one another at a banquet. So one may truly say that when the table is set, strife is removed: that is, by sharing a table quarrels are often ended and goodwill restored.

units.la: nem hem tolli, hoc est mensæ communione sæpe tolli rixas, & inimicitias, gratiamq; reconciliari, cuius rei exemplum profertur de Isbosetho filio Saulis, in cuius ædib. cum exarsisset altercatio, seruus eius adornato conuiuio dicitur eam direm*isse. Habet n. nescio quid philtri in se vinum ad amorem reconciliandum. Atque hoc de conuiuiis frugalibus & moderatis, quæ si nimis sunt sordida & parca, rectè appellantur Cynica & Timonia: Cynicorum n. Philosophorum victus erat vilissimus, tenuissimus & sordidus, siliquæ videl. & legumina. Timonia à Timone, cui humanum genus exosum erat, dicta sunt, is enim vitam sequebatur feram, in cibisq; vilissimis & à reliquis hominibus propemodum damnatis acquiescebat. Huc referuntur cœnæ terrestres, quæ nil nisi terra productum continent, quas Horatius cœnas sine sanguine vocat: & passerinum conuiuium, pro exiguo bolo & minuto, quantum vel passer absumat. Sordidum denique nimisq; tenue conuiuium est absque fumo, in quo nihil cocti obsoniiq; apponitur. Quemadmodum igitur, qui nimia conuiuiorum crebritate atque frequentia, eorumq; profuso, splendido ac sumptuoso apparatu gaudent, in excessu peccant: ita contra in defectu sordide delinquunt, qui ita conuiuali consuetudine abhorrent, vt neq; alios ad se, epularumque suarum communionem nem vnquam inuitent, neq; inuitati ad aliorū conuiuia accedant, id quod fere cuiusdam immanitatis esse videtur, quippe cum ipsa natura atq; humanitas hanc vitæ coenarumq; consuetudinem postulet. II. Cum quis inuitatus liberius quidem & prompte aliorum conuiuio se sistit, at ille inuitat neminem, id quod auaritiæ ingratitudinisq; cuiusdam flagitiosissimæ vitium est, quo quis laborans ἀλλοτριοφάγος recte dicitur, cui nimirum dulce est aliena viuere quadra. Horū passim reperiūtur plurimi, quos neq; pudet, neq; piget, neq; pœnitet incōuiuetię suæ & monophagię sordidissimæ, & si quādo honestioribus liberalioribusque conuiuiis adhibentur, alienamq; quadram arrodere ac lingere illis licet, tanta ciborum ingluuie se infarciunt vno prandio coenave, quanta vix decem alii, accusari se á natura & genio existimātes, si in tanta epularum strue apparatuq; eum defraudarent. III. Cum quis ad conuiuium à se inuitatos nimis tenuiter sordideq; tractat, eosq; semifamelicos atq; sitientes dimittit, qui μικροτράπεζος potest appellari, hoc est, paruam & angustam mensam ponens: vbi tamen excipiendi, qui aduersa valetudine impediti, vel negotiorum multitudine districti, vel denique ex inopia & egestate conuiuali huiusmodi officio fungi minime possunt.
units.tr: An example of this is cited concerning Ish-bosheth, son of Saul: when a quarrel had flared up in his house, his servant, having prepared a banquet, is said to have settled it. For wine has in itself I know not what charm for reconciling love. And this is said of frugal and moderate banquets; but if they are too squalid and sparing, they are rightly called Cynic and Timonian. For the diet of the Cynic philosophers was very cheap, very meagre and squalid, namely carob-pods and pulses. Timonian banquets are named from Timon, to whom the human race was hateful: he followed a wild life and was content with the cheapest foods, which were almost rejected by other men. To this belong the "earthly" dinners, which contain nothing but what the earth produces, and which Horace calls dinners without blood; and the sparrow's banquet, a tiny morsel and a little bit, as much as a sparrow would eat. Lastly, a squalid and overly meagre banquet is one without smoke, in which nothing cooked or relish is served. Just as those who delight in too frequent and crowded banquets, and in their extravagant, splendid and sumptuous preparation, sin by excess, so, on the contrary, those sin squalidly by defect who shrink so much from social dining that they never invite others to them or to the sharing of their meals, and when invited do not go to the banquets of others. This seems almost a kind of savagery, since nature itself and humanity demand this custom of life and of dinners. II. When someone, invited, presents himself at the banquet of others more freely and readily, but he invites no one in return, this is a vice of a most shameful avarice and ingratitude, by which a man labouring under it is rightly called *allotriophagos* [ἀλλοτριοφάγος], a dweller on others' tables, for of course it is sweet to him to live on another's money. Many of these are found everywhere, who are neither ashamed, nor grieved, nor repent of their unsociability and most squalid solitary eating; and if at times they are admitted to more honourable and generous banquets, they are allowed to gnaw and lick another's dish, and they stuff themselves at a single lunch or dinner with such gluttony of food as scarcely ten others could manage, thinking themselves cheated by nature and their own genius if they were deprived of such a spread and preparation of feasts. III. When someone treats those whom he has invited to his table too meagrely and squalidly, and sends them away half-starved and thirsty, such a man may be called *mikrotrapezos* [μικροτράπεζος], that is, one who sets a small and narrow table. Yet there are those who must be received at such a table: people who are prevented by ill health, or distracted by the press of business, or who, from poverty and want, can by no means perform this office of hospitality.

units.la: Plinius Orator Plinii Auunculi nepos, non proprobabat eos, qui sordidi simul ac sumptuosi essent, qui scilicet in conuiuiis & conuictibus sibi & paucis optima quaedam caeteris vilia & minuta ponerent, vinaque lagunculis in plura describerent genera: hunc morem displicuisse Catoni Censorio, atq; etiam ipsi Plinio auunculo, maxime vero Caesari dictatori, qui pistore suum vinxit, quia alium panem subiecisset coniuiis suis, quam sibi, tradunt historiae. Hic circa cibum adeo indifferens fuit, ut quondam ab hospite conditum oleum pro viridi appositum aspernantibus caeteris, solum etiam largius dicatur appetiuisse, ne hospitem aut negligentiae aut rusticitatis videretur arguere: Eundem quoque ne inimici quidem vini parcissimum fuisse non negarunt, munditiarum tamen lautitiarumq; fuisse studiosissimum, constans opinio est.
units.tr: Pliny the Orator, nephew of the elder Pliny, did not approve of those who were at once mean and extravagant, who in their dinners and banquets set before themselves and a few friends the finest dishes, while serving the rest cheap and small fare, and who divided their wines into many kinds in little flasks. The histories relate that this custom displeased Cato the Censor, and also the elder Pliny himself, and most of all Caesar the dictator, who had his baker bound because he had served his guests a different bread from his own. In regard to food he was so indifferent that once, when the others refused a dressed oil set out in place of fresh, he alone is said to have helped himself rather freely to it, so as not to seem to reproach his host for carelessness or rudeness. Nor do even his enemies deny that he was very sparing with wine; yet it is the settled opinion that he was most attentive to neatness and refinement.

units.la: Vox mehercule praeclarissima est Plinii, non enim, inquit, quod ego, liberti mei bibunt, sed idem ego, quod liberti, gulamq; reprimendam & in ordinem redigendam censet.
units.tr: By heaven, Pliny's words are most excellent: "They drink," he says, "not what I give my freedmen, but the same as my freedmen; and he judges that gluttony must be restrained and brought back into order."

units.la: Hannibalis certe summa in victu celebratur moderatio. Is enim neq; in Italia, neque in Aphrica vsquam coenas recubuit, aut plus quam vini sextario in conuiictu indulsit. Constantinus Imperator (vt ait Marcellinus) parce sobrieq; edendo ac potando valetudinem ita retinuit tinuit firmam, vt raros contingeret morbos, sed eos non ptocul à vitæ periculo, id enim euenire corporibus à luxu intemperantiaq; remotis, diuturna experientia & probationes medendi monstrant.
units.tr: Certainly the great moderation of Hannibal in his diet is celebrated. For he never reclined at a dinner, either in Italy or in Africa, and in company he allowed himself no more than a sextarius of wine. The Emperor Constantine (as Marcellinus says) kept his health by eating and drinking so sparingly and soberly that he was rarely ill, and when he was, it was not dangerously; for long experience and trials of medicine show that this is what happens to bodies kept free of luxury and intemperance.

units.la: Seuerus nihil vnquã imperatoriæ luxuriæ, nihilq; deliciarum in exercitu ostentauit, eundem semper cibum ac potum capiens, quem cæteri milites.
units.tr: Severus never displayed any imperial luxury or delicacies in the army, always taking the same food and drink as the other soldiers.

units.la: Antonius abiectissimis cibariis militariter delectabatur.
units.tr: Antony took pleasure in the plainest rations, as a soldier would.

units.la: Pompeii modestia & facilitas insignis in victus ratione fuit, de qua re id tantum commemorasse satis erit, quod cũ morbo decũbenti & cibos fastidienti medicus ad recreandam auiditatẽ turdũ illi apponi iussisset, huncq; venalem non inuenirent famuli, quoniam id temporis nõ ferebat, à quodam indicatum est, apud Lucullum posse reperiri, qui eos toto anno in viuariis educaret: at Pompeius ad ea dixisse traditur, nos igitur sine Luculli luxu viuere non possumus? Dimisso itaq; medico alium facile parabilem cibum sumpsit.
units.tr: The modesty and easy ways of Pompey in his diet were remarkable, and it will be enough to recall one thing about him. When a physician, ordered to revive the appetite of a man lying sick who loathed his food, had prescribed thrushes for him, and his servants could not find any for sale, since it was not the season, someone informed them that they could be found at Lucullus's house, where he kept them the whole year in his fishponds. But Pompey is reported to have replied: "So then we cannot live without Lucullus's luxury?" Dismissing the physician, he took a different food that was easy to obtain.

units.la: Cato quoq; Cęsorius in ampla fortuna tenuiter vixit, ex rapis iucũdissimũ sua manu sibi parabat obsoniũ, eoq; vt salubertimo vescebatur.
units.tr: Cato the Censor, too, though his fortune was large, lived frugally; he prepared for himself with his own hand a very pleasant relish of turnips, and he ate it as most wholesome.

units.la: A puero laboribus & moderata viuendi ratione, & ex rei militaris consuetudine ad robur &bo& bonam valetudinem constantissimum na-ctus est corporis habitum in exercitu cum siti-ret, fere semper bibit aquam.
units.tr: From boyhood, through toil, a moderate way of life, and the habits of military service, he acquired strength and a most constant bodily condition of good health; in the army, when he was thirsty, he almost always drank water.

units.la: Quod si ęstu grauiori tentaretur, aceti hau-stu crebriori sitim leuabat & caloré, & si quan-do infirmior sibi videretur, vt vires pristinasinstauraret & retineret, leuiusculi vini nonnihilde gustabat, eodemq; pane, eodemq; vino, quosui, vsus est Imperator & Consul.
units.tr: If he was troubled by heavier heat, he relieved his thirst and warmth by drinking vinegar more often; and if at any time he seemed weaker, to restore and keep his former strength, he tasted a little rather light wine, and he used the same bread and the same wine as his soldiers, being both commander and consul.

units.la: Incuriam porro suorum & imprudentiamin iis, quæ ad cibos spectarent, non moleste fe-rebat, putabat enim obscœnum esse & indeco-rum, gulæ aluiq; causa graues cum seruis litessuscipere: Cōstat nihilominus ipsum eo genereduri & rigidi victus vxoré perdidisse & liberos.
units.tr: Moreover, he did not take it amiss that his people were careless and unthoughtful in matters concerning food, for he thought it shameful and unseemly to take serious trouble with slaves for the sake of gluttony and the belly. Yet it is agreed that by this kind of harsh and rigid diet he lost his wife and children.

units.la: Curius similiter Romanorum Imperator ra-pis vixisse proditur: quare cum ei Samnitū Le-gati aurum plurimū obtulissent, respōdit, illiauro nō opus esse, qui talia cœnaret, ostēdensrapam, quam foco torreret in cibos.
units.tr: Curius, likewise a Roman commander, is recorded to have lived on turnips; therefore when the envoys of the Samnites offered him a great deal of gold, he answered that he had no need of gold, since he who dined on such things, showing them a turnip which he was roasting at the hearth for his food.

units.la: Alexander ille Macedo, ventris cibiq; tem-peratissimus fuisse traditur: ad prandia enimnoctu rna itinera, ad cœnas vero prandiorumtenuitatem optima esse condimenta censebat,ideoq; coquos ab exercitu suo remouit.
units.tr: That famous Macedonian Alexander is said to have been most temperate in appetite and food; for he thought that night marches were the best seasoning for breakfasts, and that simplicity of breakfasts was the best seasoning for dinners; and therefore he removed the cooks from his army.

units.la: Is cum primum diluculasset, prandio accum-bebat, cœna vero iā appetēte nocte bibebat in-ter sacrificādum, ciborū exquisitorū adeo fuitconcontemptor, vt ad se è longinquo missa obso-niia elegantissima interamicos partiretur, nihil que ex iis sibi reliquium faceret. In rebus gerē-dis cū magnus imprimis fuit, tum vero sobrius & vigilans, non temulentus, nō imperii licen-tia bacchabundus, cuius qui minimam partem nacti sunt, temperare sibi nequiuerunt.
units.tr: When it was first light he would sit down to breakfast, but at dinner, as night was already approaching, he drank while sacrificing; he so despised exquisite foods that when dainty dishes were sent to him from afar he would share them out among his friends and keep nothing of them for himself. In managing affairs he was great above all, and moreover sober and watchful, not drunken with wine, nor wild with the licence of power; and those who obtained even the smallest share of these things could not restrain themselves.

units.la: Augustus, cibi minimi atq; vulgaris fuit, pisces enim minusculos & panem secundarium, caseum bubulum manu pressum, & ficus viri-des biferas maxime expetiisse aiunt.
units.tr: Augustus was of the least and commonest diet; they say he especially desired small fish, second-rate bread, cow's cheese pressed by hand, and green figs that bear twice a year.

units.la: Vini autem natura erat parcissimus, nec am-plius ter bibere solitus super cœnam in castris apud Mutinam. Quoties vero se largissime in-uitasset, senos sextantes non excessit: maxime delectatus est Rhetico, neque temere interdiu bibit: pro potione sumebat perfusum aqua frigida panem aut cucumeris fructum, aut la-ctucæ thyrsum, aut recens acidum me pomum vinosioris saporis.
units.tr: By nature he was very sparing with wine, and at the camp at Mutina he was accustomed to drink no more than three times over dinner. Whenever he invited guests most lavishly, he did not exceed six sextarii; he took the greatest delight in Rhaetian wine, and he did not drink by day without reason; for a drink he took bread soaked in cold water, or a cucumber, or a lettuce stalk, or a fresh sour apple of rather winy flavour.

units.la: Vescebatur ante cœnam quocunque tem-pore & loco, quod stomachus desiderasset. Prę-terea epulandi confusissimū solutissimūq; mo-dum correxit, assidue tamē conuiuabatur, verū cœnam ternis ferculis, aut, cum abundantissi-me senis præbebat.
units.tr: Before dinner he ate at whatever time and place his stomach desired. Furthermore, he corrected the most disordered and loose manner of feasting; yet he was constantly entertaining guests, but he served dinner in three courses, or, when he was most lavish, in six.

units.la: Querentem de inopia & caritate vini po-pulum Rom. seuerissima coercuit oratione, satis, prouisum à genero suo Agrippa pductis pluribus aquis, ne homines sitirent.
units.tr: The Roman people, complaining of the scarcity and dearness of wine, he restrained with a most severe speech, saying that enough provision had been made by his son-in-law Agrippa, who had brought in several aqueducts, so that men should not thirst.

units.la: De Pescenio Imperatore non absimile traditur. Nam cum in Ægypto cum exercitu esset, quererenturq; milites, quod vinum non adesset, respondit; Nilum habetis & vinum petitis? nam reuera incolæ illius amnis aquam bibunt: fuit præterea tenuis valetudinis, quam dilligentia tuebatur, vnde annum sextum & septuagesimum attigit.
units.tr: Something not unlike is recorded of the Emperor Pescennius. For when he was in Egypt with his army, and the soldiers complained that there was no wine, he replied: "You have the Nile, and do you ask for wine?" For in truth the inhabitants of that river drink water. He was moreover of a weak constitution, which he preserved by care, and so he reached the seventy-sixth year of his age.

units.la: O aurea secula; Hostantos Reges tantosq; Heroas quis crederet tam sobrie vixisse? rara namq; sobrietatis atq; fortunæ concordia est. Sit igitur & nobis modus apparatui impendioq; cœnarum. Sint simplices escæ, mensæq; simplices, nulla varietate & pernitiosa coacervatione opulentatæ. Sordidus hic mos est & detestandus. Sed his miseriis homines obnoxios reddit mala ambitio & dira habendi cupido, ostentatioq; potius prodigi luxus, quam necessitas & vtilitas. Ipse Christus Dominus noster exemplum nobis vitæ prodidit, prodiderunt Apostoli, prodiderunt tot sancti viri illius imitatores, quos si & nos imitaremur, satius esse cū Plinio concluderemus, simpliciter viuere & frugaliter, quā gulæ irritamentis delitiisq; turpiter se polluere, in amplis patrimoniis helluari, opesq; & pecuniā prandiorū gurgitib. proluere.
units.tr: O golden ages! Who would believe that such kings and such great heroes lived so soberly? For the agreement of sobriety with fortune is rare. Let there therefore be a measure also for us in the preparation and expense of dinners. Let the dishes be plain and the tables plain, not made rich with any variety or pernicious heaping up. This sordid custom is hateful and deserves to be detested. But ill ambition and the dreadful desire to possess, and the display of prodigal luxury rather than necessity and usefulness, make men liable to these miseries. Christ our Lord himself has set before us the example of life; the Apostles have set it, and so many holy men, imitators of him; if we too imitated them, we should conclude with Pliny that it is better to live simply and frugally than to pollute oneself shamefully with the incitements and delights of gluttony, to waste away in great patrimonies, and to drown wealth and money in the whirlpools of feasts.

units.la: Quod etiam Horatius vitiorum acerrimus castigator & censor carminibus suis de victu moderato verius, quâ vel vllus Philosophus, vel Medicus, vel Theologus expressit, libr.II. serm.satyr.2.
units.tr: Horace too, the sharpest chastiser and censor of vices, has expressed in his poems on moderate diet more truly than any philosopher, physician, or theologian: Book II, Satire 2.

units.la: Remitto etiam auditorem vel lectorem ad Satyram, quam scripsit Varro de cibis & lautitiis, in qua versibus comprehendit exquisitas delitias, & quae helluones terra mariq; conquirunt, pleraq; exposuit, generaque & nomina eduliorum, sicut & domicilia ciborum vt monstrosa, sic pernitiosa exprobrans recenset.
units.tr: I also refer the listener or reader to the satire which Varro wrote on foods and delicacies, in which he set down in verse the exquisite delights, and what gluttons seek by land and sea, and set forth many things, and recounts the names and kinds of dainties, as well as the dwelling-places of foods, denouncing them as monstrous and equally pernicious.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.
